title: Advertisement
questions: Do you often see advertisements when you are on your phone or computer?
What kind of advertising do you like?
Do you like advertisements?
Do you see a lot of advertising on trains or other transport?
Is there an advertisement that made an impression on you when you were a child?
Have you ever bought something because of an advertisement?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Yes, quite often, mainly in free apps and short videos. I usually skip them, but a useful demonstration can catch my attention. I try to check the product independently, since seeing an advert repeatedly does not tell me whether it is good.

I like adverts that explain one useful feature clearly, such as how a kitchen tool saves time. A short demonstration is easier to judge than a celebrity endorsement, and I can decide whether the product is relevant to me.

Only when they are brief and informative. I dislike pop-ups that cover a page or videos that interrupt something I am watching. If an advert keeps appearing, I usually remember the interruption more than the product.

Yes, especially on buses and in metro stations near campus. I notice posters while waiting, although I usually ignore them once I am on my way. The number seems to have grown as more services use screens instead of printed notices.

I remember a snack advert with a catchy tune from primary school. My classmates and I used to sing it during breaks, even though we could not recall many details about the product. It stayed in my memory because we turned it into a joke.

Yes, I once tried a snack after seeing it in an online advert. It tasted fine, but it was less exciting than the video suggested, so now I check reviews before buying. The advert introduced me to it, but it did not decide whether I would buy it again.

title: Cars
questions: Did you enjoy traveling by car when you were a kid?
What types of cars do you like?
Do you prefer to be a driver or a passenger?
What do you usually do when there is a traffic jam?
Do you think car colours are important?
Will you buy an expensive car in the future?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Yes, I enjoyed family car trips, especially because they were less common than travelling by bus. I watched the scenery for a while and usually fell asleep once the road became steady. Even a short drive felt like a small break from our normal routine.
I would choose a small electric car. It should be cheaper to run and easier to park near campus or work, which matters more to me than having a powerful engine or a flashy design.
I would rather be a passenger on a long or busy journey because I can relax and look out of the window. On a quiet short trip, though, driving would give me more control over the route.
I check the delay, put on a podcast and try not to keep watching the clock. If someone is waiting for me, I send a quick message, then accept that the traffic is outside my control.

Not particularly. I would care more about reliability and running costs than paintwork; if I had to choose, I would go for dark grey because it stays looking neat between washes. For daily use, that practical side matters more to me than making a statement.
Probably not. I would rather spend that money on travel or keep it for something more useful. An expensive car would bring higher costs, and I do not care enough about the badge to justify them.

title: Clothing
questions: What kind of clothes do you like to wear?
Do you prefer to wear comfortable and casual clothes or smart clothes?
Do you like wearing T-shirts?
Do you spend a lot of time choosing clothes?
Do you wear different styles of clothes on weekdays and weekends?
What colour clothes do you like?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: I like comfortable clothes in simple colours, especially jeans or trousers with a plain T-shirt. They are easy to match and work for most university days. I keep a smarter jacket for presentations or family occasions.

I prefer comfortable, casual clothes for most days because I walk between classes and spend a lot of time sitting in lectures. I wear something smarter for a presentation or formal event, but comfort comes first.

Yes, I wear T-shirts quite often, especially in warm weather or when I am studying at home. They are comfortable and easy to wash. I usually choose a plain one because it goes with most of my trousers.

No, not really. I usually decide in a few minutes because most of my clothes are easy to match. I might spend longer choosing something for a presentation, but I do not plan a different outfit for every day.

A little. On weekdays I usually wear comfortable clothes for lectures, while at weekends I might choose something more relaxed or meet friends in a slightly smarter outfit. I do not change my style dramatically, though.

I tend to wear navy, grey and white because those colours are easy to combine. I sometimes choose a brighter colour for a jacket or shirt, but I would not want my whole wardrobe to be difficult to match.

title: Fruit and vegetables
questions: Do people in your country like planting vegetables?
Were there any kind of fruits and vegetables you disliked as a child?
What kind of fruits and vegetables do you dislike?
Where do you usually buy fruit and vegetables?
How often do you eat fruit and vegetables?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Yes, quite a few people do, especially those with a balcony or a small garden. My grandparents grew seasonal vegetables when I was younger, and I can see why people enjoy having something fresh to pick.
I was not keen on bitter melon as a child because the taste seemed too strong. I am more open to it now, especially when it is cooked with eggs, but it still would not be my first choice.
I am not a big fan of bitter melon or fruit that is overly sour. I do eat them occasionally if they are part of a meal, but I usually choose sweeter fruit and milder vegetables.

Usually at a supermarket near home, because I can buy everything in one stop. If I have more time, I go to the local market, where I can compare the produce and choose smaller amounts of different vegetables.
I have fruit most days, usually with breakfast or as a snack between classes. Keeping apples or bananas at home makes it easy to choose something fresh, even when I have a busy study schedule.

title: Headphones
questions: Do you use headphones?
What type of headphones do you use?
When would you use headphones?
In what conditions would you not use headphones?
Is wearing headphones comfortable?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Yes, mostly when I am on a bus or listening to a lecture recording in a shared space. I take them off before crossing a road and when someone is speaking to me, because I want to stay aware of my surroundings.

I have a pair of small wireless earbuds with a charging case. They fit easily in my bag and are fine for podcasts, although I would choose over-ear headphones if I needed to block out noise for a long flight.

I use headphones on the bus or when I am listening to a lecture recording at home. I would not wear them while walking near traffic, because hearing what is around me matters more. I want to stay alert.

I take them off when I am crossing a busy road or need to listen for an announcement. I also avoid wearing them in a conversation, since it can make the other person feel that I am not paying attention.

They are comfortable for a short journey or a study session, provided the fit is right. I take them off after a while because wearing them all day can make my ears tired and stop me noticing what is happening around me.

Do you live in an apartment or a house?

What kinds of accommodation do you live in?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: I would like a bright apartment with a separate study corner and a small balcony. It would be comfortable without being difficult to maintain, and I would want public transport and shops within walking distance.

The bus stop and metro station are both within a short walk of my home, so getting to campus is fairly easy. The only drawback is that buses can be crowded at rush hour. For most daily trips, though, I do not need a car.

An apartment suits me better at the moment because it is easier to maintain and usually closer to public transport. I would still like a little outdoor space, perhaps a balcony, but I do not need a large house.
My room is fairly simple, with a bed, a desk beside the window and a bookshelf for course notes. I keep the desk clear while I am studying, because too many things around me make it harder to focus.
I like the small study corner beside the window most. It gets good daylight, and I can keep my mathematics books and laptop there. It is not a separate room, but it gives me a quiet place to work.

I have lived there for most of my life, so the neighbourhood feels very familiar. I know where to find daily essentials and which routes are quickest. I may move after graduation for work, but I would still think of it as home.
Probably for the next few years, because it is comfortable and close to the places I need to go. I may move after graduation if work takes me to another city, so I would not make a long-term promise.
My current apartment is closer to public transport and gives me a quieter place to study. The home I lived in as a child was more spacious, but it was farther from the city centre and daily services.

I live in a practical apartment with my family. It has a shared living room, a small kitchen and a quiet corner where I can study. Shops and a bus stop are nearby, so daily errands are straightforward.

We spend most of our time in the living room, especially after dinner. Someone might watch the news while the rest of us chat or use our phones. It is the easiest place for everyone to relax together.
My favourite room is the study corner in my bedroom. It is small, but the desk gets natural light and I can keep my course notes nearby. Having a familiar place to work helps me settle down quickly.

Natural light and a tidy shared space make me feel comfortable at home. I also like having a quiet corner where I can read or work through a problem without being interrupted. It does not need to look perfect.

Yes, especially because home is where people need to rest and recover. A comfortable space does not have to be expensive; enough light, a reasonable amount of quiet and furniture that works well make a noticeable difference.

I live in an apartment with my family. It suits us because it is close to public transport and shops, and we do not have to spend much time maintaining a garden. The rooms are modest, but the location is convenient.

I live with my family. We are all fairly busy during the day, but we usually see each other at dinner or in the living room afterwards. I like having company at home while still having my own study space.

I usually study at my desk, have meals with my family and relax in the living room in the evening. It is not a large apartment, so we share the space quite naturally. I like having a quiet corner where I can work.

It is a mid-sized flat in a residential building, with a shared living room and separate bedrooms. Our place is fairly practical rather than spacious, and the balcony is where we keep a few plants and dry laundry.

title: Hometown
questions: Where is your hometown?
Is that a big city or a small place?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: I grew up in a city in China, and I am now studying away from home. It is familiar to me because my family and many of my childhood memories are still there, even though I see it differently when I visit as an adult.

I would call it a medium-sized city. It has the usual shopping areas and public transport, but it is not so large that getting across town takes the whole day. That balance makes it fairly convenient to live in.

It is a medium-sized city with busy commercial streets and quieter residential areas. Public transport makes it fairly easy to get around, and there are parks where people can take a break. It feels lively without being overwhelming.

I lived there for most of my childhood, then moved away to attend university. I still go back during longer holidays, so it remains the place I associate with home, even though my daily routine is now somewhere else.

Probably for the next few years, since it is comfortable and close to the places I need to go. After graduation I may move for work, but I could imagine returning if a suitable opportunity came up. I would decide based on work and family needs.

Yes. My hometown feels familiar, and I like that local markets, relatives and familiar streets are close by. It has become busier over the years, but I still enjoy returning to places I knew as a child.

Yes, overall. Daily errands are easy because I know the area well, and I can reach shops and public transport without much planning. The main drawback is traffic at peak times, so I prefer the quieter streets near home.

I like that it feels familiar without being boring. I know where to find good food and quiet places to walk, and visiting family is easy. When I go back after a busy semester, the slower pace helps me relax.

The main drawback is traffic, particularly when people are travelling home from work. A few roads get crowded, so a short journey can take longer than expected. Apart from that, I find it a comfortable place to visit and spend time with family.

I like the familiar rhythm of my area, especially having shops and public transport within easy reach. That balance between convenience and familiarity is what makes a place feel like home to me. I appreciate having familiar places within a short trip.

We learned a little about local history at school, mainly through a few important events and well-known people. I remember the general outline, but I would like to learn more about how ordinary families lived in the past.

Yes, there are quite a lot, partly because local universities and colleges attract students from nearby areas. You see groups meeting for food or studying in cafes, although some graduates move away to find work after finishing their courses.

It is a reasonable place to start a career, especially in education, retail and local services. For more specialised jobs, graduates may have fewer choices than in a major city, so some leave for a wider job market.

Yes, I have learned more by visiting a local museum and reading short articles online. I am especially interested in how the city changed as transport and industry developed, because those changes still affect where people live today.

Mostly through family routines and school activities rather than formal lessons. We celebrated local festivals, ate familiar dishes and heard stories from older relatives. I understood more about their meaning as I grew older and started asking my family where the customs came from.

title: Jokes & Comedies
questions: Are you good at telling jokes?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Not really. I can make friends laugh when I tell a story, but I am not quick with a punchline. I usually enjoy listening to other people more than trying to perform, especially in a large group.

A few of them do, especially when we are taking a break after class. Their jokes usually come from small things that happened that day, so they feel more natural than a memorised punchline. I like the stories that make the whole group join in.

I enjoy comedies based on awkward everyday situations more than jokes that rely on insulting someone. A live comedy show sounds fun, although I would need the performer to speak clearly for the jokes to land.

Yes, I went to a small stand-up show with friends at university. The room was intimate, so the comedian could react to the audience, and even an ordinary joke felt funnier when everyone laughed together.

Yes, comedy shows are popular, particularly short online clips and stand-up performances. People share jokes that reflect everyday life, although humour can be very personal and a joke that works for one group may not work for another.

title: Mirrors

part1: Yes, but only briefly. I check whether my hair or clothes look presentable before leaving, rather than spending time studying my reflection. It is a practical habit, and I usually forget about the mirror once I am ready.
I probably look in a mirror a few times a day when I get ready or check my appearance before leaving home. I do not spend long in front of it; I just want to make sure I look presentable.
Yes, I bought a small mirror for my desk when I moved into student accommodation. It is useful when I am getting ready, but I chose a simple one because I did not want it to take up much space.
Not usually. My phone camera is enough for a quick check on an ordinary day, and I might pack a small mirror if I am going to a formal event or will be out for a long time.
I use a mirror for practical reasons, mainly to check my hair or clothes before leaving home. A full-length mirror is useful in a small room, while a smaller one is easier to carry when travelling.

title: Morning time
questions: Do you like getting up early in the morning?

Why?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: I like getting up early when I have slept enough. The morning is quiet, so I can review my plans or work through a problem before messages and classes start. I am less enthusiastic about it after a late night.
I get dressed, make tea and look over the day's tasks before leaving home. If I have an early lecture, I prepare my bag the night before so I do not have to search for notes while rushing out.

I usually ate breakfast at home and walked to primary school with a neighbour. On rainy days my father drove me, and we talked about what I had that day. I was much slower to wake up then than I am now.

We ate breakfast together because my parents wanted us to start the day calmly before school. It also gave us a few minutes to talk, although I mostly remember enjoying the routine rather than thinking about why it mattered.
When I was younger, my parents organised most of my morning routine before school. Now I check my own timetable, prepare what I need for class and decide whether to study or have breakfast first.

Not exactly. On weekdays I get ready quickly and leave for class, while at weekends I usually wake up later and have a slower breakfast. I keep the basic routine, but there is less pressure to watch the clock.

title: Music
questions: Do you prefer sad or happy music?
Does happy music make you feel more excited?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: I usually prefer mellow or happy music, depending on what I am doing. Upbeat songs lift my mood on the way to class, while softer music helps me unwind at home. I do not often choose very sad songs unless I already feel reflective.

Usually, yes. Upbeat music gives me a quick lift, especially when I am walking to class or doing a routine task. If I need to concentrate on a difficult proof, though, I prefer silence. That is my preference.

I had a few basic music lessons at school, but I never studied an instrument seriously. We learned simple rhythms and sang in a group. I enjoyed the lessons, although I prefer listening to music now rather than practising formally.

Sometimes, when I am walking or doing simple chores. I turn it off when I need to read carefully or work through a mathematics problem, because lyrics can distract me from the details. Instrumental music is easier.

part1: Occasionally, especially when I meet several people at once. I remember a name more easily if I repeat it during the conversation or connect it with something we discussed. If I forget, I would rather ask politely than pretend I remember.
When I meet someone, I try to use their name once in the conversation so I remember it. Repeating a name quietly after an introduction works better for me than trying to memorise a long list.

I try to use someone's name naturally soon after we meet, then link it to what we talked about. If I meet several people at once, I sometimes write their names down afterwards so I do not confuse them.

Not always, especially at a large event where introductions happen quickly. I usually remember a face first and need another conversation to connect it with a name. It is easier when the person has introduced themselves in a relaxed setting.

part1: From time to time, especially through university projects or people I meet in my department. I do not get a major opportunity every week, but small chances to present work or learn a new tool come up quite regularly.

Usually, yes, as long as I can manage the commitment alongside my studies. A new project can show me what I need to improve, even if it feels unfamiliar at first. I try to understand the time involved before agreeing.

Trying different things can help people discover what they enjoy, but they do not need to say yes to everything. Time and energy are limited, so I think it is better to explore a few options thoughtfully and keep the ones that feel worthwhile.

Yes. At primary school I tried a few activities, including drawing and a short sports club. I was not especially good at either, but it was fun to try them with classmates before homework and exams became a bigger part of life.

title: Outer space and stars

part1: Yes, mainly at school and through documentaries. I was especially interested in the planets because diagrams helped me picture their size and distance from the Sun. The scale is difficult to imagine, so visual explanations made the topic much easier to follow.

Yes, especially films that use space as a setting for questions about people and society. I enjoy the ideas more than complicated special effects, and a good science-fiction story can make me curious about real astronomy too.

I like science-fiction films because they use unfamiliar settings to explore questions about people and society. The ideas interest me more than complicated effects, and a good story can make me curious about real astronomy or technology afterwards.

Yes, I would. I am curious about how planets form and whether life could exist elsewhere, although I usually learn through short articles or documentaries rather than technical books. A clear explanation makes me want to learn more.

Probably not. Seeing Earth from space would be incredible, but the cost, risk and training would put me off. I would be perfectly happy visiting an observatory or seeing a clear night sky from the ground.

title: Paper

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: I carry a small notebook and pen when I expect to be out for most of the day. They are useful for jotting down an address or sketching an idea in class, and I do not have to unlock a device first.

Some people keep handwritten letters because they carry a personal message that is easy to revisit. They can be especially meaningful when they come from someone who lives far away or is no longer around. Most everyday conversations are digital now, though.

Almost never. I send messages for everyday communication, but I might write a card for a graduation or a family birthday. A handwritten note feels more deliberate, so I save it for occasions when I want the message to last.
I used to fold paper planes and make simple cards for family occasions. I liked that I could turn an ordinary sheet into something different with just a pair of scissors and a little imagination.

Yes, mostly simple things such as greeting cards and paper decorations. I made them at school and sometimes at home with my family; they were not perfect, but making something by hand was enjoyable. I kept one card on my desk.

title: Politeness
questions: What did you do to show your politeness as a child?
On what occasions should we be polite?
Do you think being polite is very important?
How did you learn to be polite as a child?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: At school I was taught to wait until a classmate had finished speaking before answering. I also held the door for people carrying books. Those habits seemed small, but teachers noticed when we treated one another patiently.

We should be polite whenever we share space or depend on other people, such as in class, at work or on public transport. Letting someone finish speaking is a small example. Courtesy makes everyday interactions smoother without requiring much effort.

Yes, because courtesy helps people disagree without making the conversation personal. In a seminar, for example, asking a question respectfully makes it easier to discuss a different idea. Good manners do not solve every problem, but they set a considerate tone.

My parents reminded me to greet relatives and wait until someone had finished speaking before I interrupted. A teacher reinforced that habit during class discussions. I did not think of it as a formal lesson, but those small reminders shaped how I speak to people now.

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Yes, I liked the playgrounds and open space. I used to run around or play simple games with other children, and we could stay there until our parents called us home. Even a short walk there clears my head after class.

Yes, although I use them differently now. I usually go for a walk or sit somewhere quiet after studying, rather than spend the whole time playing. It is an easy way to get outside without planning a trip.

Yes, especially small parks in residential areas. They would give people somewhere to walk or sit without travelling across the city. Even a few trees and benches can make a busy neighbourhood feel more pleasant.

I would like to visit a larger botanical garden outside the city. It would be interesting to see plants from different regions and spend a quiet afternoon there, perhaps taking a slow walk with a friend.

I would choose a public garden because it usually has more space and people can meet there. A private garden would be quieter, but I do not have one at home, and I like seeing families use a shared green space.

Parks today often have better paths, exercise equipment and areas for different age groups. The ones I visited as a child were simpler, with a playground and open ground. I still think children need room for unstructured play.
I usually walk slowly, find a bench and take a short break from screens. If I go with a friend, we might talk while walking rather than sit in one place. I do not need a special activity.
Yes, if there were a suitable space for it. I would be happy to play badminton or throw a frisbee with friends, as long as we were not disturbing people who came there to relax.

title: Rubbish and recycling
questions: Did you recycle when you were a kid?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

part1: Not in a very organised way. At home, my family reused bags and separated bottles when there was a collection point nearby. I understood more about recycling later at school, when teachers explained what happened to paper and plastic after collection.

It is becoming more common in cities, although the system is not equally convenient everywhere. Many apartment blocks have separate bins, but people are more likely to use them when the labels are clear and collection is regular. Awareness has improved, but habits take time to change.

I separate paper, plastic bottles and food waste when the building has clearly labelled bins. I rinse containers if needed and flatten cardboard so it takes up less space. The system is easiest to follow when the collection points are nearby and the instructions are simple.

At home I separate paper, bottles and food waste when the building provides the right containers. Small actions help most when the local system makes it easy for everyone to take part. It is much easier when the instructions are clear.

title: Science
questions: Do you like science?
When did you start to learn about science?
Which science subject is interesting to you?
What kinds of interesting things have you done with science?
Do you like watching science TV programs?
Do Chinese people often visit science museums?

part1: Yes, when it explains something I can observe in daily life. I enjoyed school experiments because they made a theory easier to remember, and I still like asking what evidence would support an explanation rather than accepting it immediately.

I first studied science seriously in primary school, but a middle-school experiment made it memorable. We changed one condition at a time and watched what happened. That was when I understood why careful observation matters as much as knowing the terms.

Physics interests me most because it uses mathematical models to describe motion and energy. I like starting with a real situation, making reasonable assumptions and seeing whether the equations predict what happens. It gives abstract calculation a clear purpose.

At school, I did a simple experiment comparing how quickly different materials warmed in sunlight. It was interesting to make a guess, collect measurements and see whether the result supported it. I enjoyed the process more than making a perfect display.

Yes, if the programme explains an idea clearly instead of relying on dramatic claims. I like visual examples about space or nature because they make abstract facts easier to picture. I usually watch short episodes when I want a break from coursework.

Many families do, especially during school holidays, when museums have activities for children. I remember trying an interactive exhibit on a school trip; it made the visit more engaging than reading display boards, although popular galleries can get crowded.

title: Secondary school
questions: Is there anything you miss about your secondary school?
What was your favourite subject at secondary school?
Were there any subjects that you found difficult at secondary school?
Do you remember your first day at secondary school?

answers.part2: The film I disliked was a supernatural mystery that a group of friends picked for a weekend movie night. Strange noises suggested that one of the guests was hiding something, but the film relied on jump scares instead of developing the characters. I guessed who was behind it well before the ending, so I started noticing how often the same trick appeared: a close-up, a pause, then a loud sound. Travelling abroad lets people experience everyday customs directly instead of relying on films or social media. Travelling abroad exposes people to different customs, food and ways of organising daily life, which can make them more open-minded. Travel is most valuable when people engage with local life instead of only visiting familiar tourist sites.

Many people in China enjoy travelling abroad because it offers a chance to experience different food, languages and ways of life. I think interest is high, but people's budgets and responsibilities shape how often they can go.

title: 保护环境的法律
prompt: Describe a law on environmental protection
cues: How you first learned about it
And explain how you feel about this law
questions: What kinds of rules do schools in China have?
Do you think school rules are important?
Are children unhappy with the school rules?
What are the rules people should obey at work?
What is the purpose of punishment?
How can parents and teachers help children understand and follow rules?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A law I have seen in practice is the requirement to separate household rubbish into recyclable, food and general waste. I first noticed it when new bins appeared near my apartment, with signs showing what belonged in each one. It benefits residents as well as the city, because less recyclable material is lost in mixed rubbish and cleaner streets make the neighbourhood more pleasant. At first, some people were unsure where to put things, so clear labels and regular collection mattered more than warnings. In my building, the food-waste bin is collected separately, and the management office posts a reminder when the schedule changes. That makes the rule visible without making residents feel they are being watched. I have also started rinsing containers before recycling them, which is a small but practical adjustment. It is easier to keep doing when the facilities are reliable. I support the rule because it turns an environmental idea into an ordinary habit. It works best when the bins are easy to reach and the collection service keeps the categories separate. Otherwise, people may feel their effort is pointless. The law has made me check packaging more carefully, and I think that small change is worthwhile.
part3: Schools usually have rules about attendance, classroom behaviour, uniforms and phone use. Some also ask students to join morning exercises or limit phone use during the school day. The purpose is to keep lessons orderly and make expectations clear. Rules are more reasonable when students understand why they exist and teachers apply them consistently. That makes the rules easier to follow.

Yes, clear school rules help protect students and give teachers a fair way to manage a shared classroom. Expectations about safety, attendance and respect make it easier for everyone to learn. Rules work better when students understand why they exist and when the same standard applies to everyone. Too many restrictions can feel controlling, so schools should focus on behaviour that affects others.

Some children dislike rules that feel strict or do not seem to have a clear reason, such as limits on phones or long homework. They are more likely to accept a rule when it protects safety or gives everyone a fair chance to learn. Schools should explain expectations and listen when a rule causes a problem. A rule can provide structure without treating students as if they have no judgement.

Employees should follow safety procedures, respect colleagues' time and protect confidential information. They also need to meet reasonable deadlines and communicate early if a problem affects their work. Exact rules vary by job, so employers should explain them clearly during training. A fair workplace applies the same standards to everyone and allows staff to raise concerns when a rule is unsafe or impractical.

Punishment is intended to discourage harmful behaviour and show that rules have consequences. It may also protect other people in the short term. However, punishment alone does not explain why an action was wrong or how to behave differently next time. For children and minor mistakes, a proportionate response with a clear explanation can teach more than a severe penalty. The goal should include prevention and learning.

They should explain the reason for a rule and apply it consistently. For example, asking children to put phones away is easier to accept when adults explain how notifications interrupt a lesson and follow the same expectation themselves. Parents and teachers can also praise a child for making the right choice, instead of relying only on punishment when something goes wrong.

title: 做困难事情并成功的人
prompt: Describe a person you know who did something difficult and was successful
cues: What difficult thing this person did
And explain how you feel about this person
questions: Is it easy to start up a company?
Does money equal success?
How can companies help protect the environment?
Is it difficult to do business in today's world?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The person I would describe is a friend from university who struggled with mathematics before entering an engineering programme. The difficult part was not one exam; he had to change how he studied after realizing that rereading notes was not enough. He began asking questions after class, keeping a list of mistakes and practising the types of problems he used to avoid. At first his marks improved only slightly, which was frustrating, but he used the feedback to adjust his weekly plan. By the end of the year, he could solve the weekly problem sheets he had once avoided, and he earned a place on the engineering programme. I admired that he did not treat an early setback as proof that he lacked ability; he looked for a better method instead. After each practice session, he rewrote one difficult question correctly without looking at his notes. His error log showed that two topics kept causing trouble, so he brought those questions to his tutor each week. On Sundays, he reviewed the log and chose what to practise next. I felt proud when he told me, because I had watched him turn a disappointing result into a routine he could keep following. His persistence has also made me more willing to examine my own mistakes.
part3: It is easier to start a small company than it used to be because people can advertise online and sell without renting a large shop. However, setting up still involves registration, costs and finding customers. A new owner also needs to understand cash flow and competition. Digital tools lower the barrier to entry, but they do not guarantee a stable business.

No, money can provide security and choices, but it is only one measure of success. Someone may earn a high salary yet have little time for family or work they find meaningful. I would also consider whether a person is healthy, has supportive relationships and feels their work contributes something useful. Financial stability matters, but it does not automatically create a satisfying life.

Companies can reduce waste in production, use energy more efficiently and design products that last longer or can be repaired. They can also be transparent about the materials and emissions in their supply chains. A business may find these changes costly at first, but saving energy and avoiding waste can reduce expenses over time. Government standards help ensure that responsible companies are not undercut by competitors doing less.

Doing business today can be difficult because customers have many choices and trends change quickly. Small firms also have to compete online with established brands while managing rent, wages and delivery costs. Technology opens new markets, but it raises expectations for fast service. Businesses that listen to customers and control spending are more likely to adapt when conditions change.

title: 包含动物的故事或书
prompt: Describe a story/book with animals in it
cues: And explain what you think of this story/book
questions: Should schools teach children about animals?
Some people think pets should not be kept in cities. What do you think?
Do many people keep pets in your country?
What are the advantages of keeping a pet?
Why do people always tell children stories with animals?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A story with animals that I remember is Charlotte's Web, which I read when I was still at school. It is about a pig called Wilbur and a spider called Charlotte, whose friendship changes how the other animals see him. I picked it up because a teacher recommended it, and the chapters were short enough to read between other assignments. What stayed with me was the contrast between the farm's ordinary routine and Charlotte's quiet effort to help her friend. I remember feeling sad near the end, but the story did not feel gloomy because it also showed loyalty and kindness. The animals make the plot appealing to children, while their choices raise questions about friendship that adults can appreciate too. I liked the barn setting and the way Wilbur's ordinary life continued while Charlotte quietly worked to help him. I especially remember Charlotte writing a message in her web to protect Wilbur. It is a simple idea, but the other characters react to it in believable ways, so the kindness has consequences rather than feeling like a lesson added at the end. The story made me sad in places, yet I finished it feeling hopeful. I would recommend it to readers who enjoy gentle stories that treat friendship and loss honestly, even if the plot moves slowly.
part3: Yes, schools can teach children how to care for animals and behave safely around unfamiliar ones. A short lesson could explain that pets need food, exercise and regular attention, not just affection. This helps children understand responsibility before they ask for a pet. Lessons should use age-appropriate examples and respect animal welfare rather than encouraging children to handle wildlife.

I would not ban pets from cities altogether. The real issue is whether an owner can provide enough space, exercise and attention, especially in a small apartment. Noise or poor hygiene can affect neighbours, so housing rules and responsible ownership matter. A city can accommodate pets if owners choose animals suited to their homes and follow basic standards of care.

Yes, cats and dogs are common pets in China, particularly in cities. People enjoy the companionship, and many treat pets as part of the family. Apartment living can make it harder to keep a large dog, so owners need to think about space, exercise and local rules. A pet is a long-term responsibility, not just something pleasant to have at home.

A pet can provide companionship and give its owner a regular routine, such as feeding it or taking it for a walk. Caring for an animal may also encourage people to spend more time outdoors and become more patient. For someone living alone, that company can be valuable. The benefit depends on having enough time and money to care for the animal properly.

Stories with animals let children explore human feelings and choices in a playful way. A fox, bear or small bird can represent curiosity, kindness or greed without making the lesson sound like a lecture. Children also enjoy imagining how an animal would speak and behave. The story can be entertaining first, while giving parents an easy way to talk about friendship or responsibility afterwards.

title: 印象深刻的聚会
prompt: Describe a party for a special event that impressed you a lot
cues: When and where it was held
What the party was held for
And explain why it impressed you a lot
questions: When do people like to hold a party?
Do you think people nowadays prefer attending big parties or small gatherings with close friends?
Why?
Are there any differences between how young people and older people celebrate events with parties?
What special events are celebrated in your country?
Do you think it’s a waste of money for governments to celebrate national events?
What festivals are the most important for people in your country?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The party I remember most was a family celebration after my cousin finished an important professional course. We held it at my aunt's home on a weekend, and about fifteen relatives came over during the afternoon. My uncle helped arrange the chairs while my cousin chose the music, so different generations had something to contribute. Nobody was expected to give a speech, and the younger children were free to move around. That informal setup suited her personality and meant the celebration felt like family time, not a formal award ceremony. We stayed for several hours, but nobody seemed in a hurry to leave. We shared a meal and looked at photographs from when she first started studying. The most memorable moment was a short slideshow her younger brother had put together; he included a few funny pictures that she had forgotten about, and everyone started telling stories from that period. It impressed me because the celebration felt personal without being expensive or carefully staged. My cousin looked relieved as well as happy, since the course had taken months of evening study. I left feeling closer to my relatives. A few days later, people were still sharing the photographs in our family chat, which showed me that the gathering had given everyone something they wanted to remember.
part3: People usually hold parties to mark a personal milestone or bring a group together, such as for a birthday, graduation, wedding or reunion. Some also organise a small gathering after finishing an important project. The event does not need to be expensive; food and time to talk are often enough. People tend to enjoy a party most when the occasion feels meaningful to them.

Many people prefer a small gathering because it is easier to talk with everyone and the atmosphere feels more personal. A large party can be exciting for a wedding or graduation, but guests may not know one another well. I would choose a smaller group for an ordinary celebration and a bigger event for a major milestone. The occasion and the guest list make the difference.

Small gatherings make it easier to have a proper conversation, especially when people have not seen one another for a while. At a large party, the energy can be exciting, but guests may only exchange a few words. The choice depends on the occasion: a graduation may suit a bigger celebration, while a quiet catch-up works better with close friends.

Younger people may prefer music, larger groups and sharing photos online, while older adults often value a meal with family and time to talk. These are only general tendencies; some older people enjoy a lively party, and some young adults prefer a quiet gathering. The occasion and the people involved shape the celebration more than age alone.

In China, people commonly celebrate birthdays, weddings and graduations, as well as traditional occasions such as the Spring Festival and Mid-Autumn Festival. Families may gather for a meal, exchange gifts or travel to see relatives. The customs differ by region, but these events give people a reason to spend time together and recognise important changes in someone's life.

Not necessarily. Public celebrations can bring people together and help younger generations understand national history, but the spending should be proportionate. A large event is difficult to justify if local services are underfunded or the cost is hidden. Governments could use public parks, schools and community groups rather than expensive displays. The value depends on whether people benefit and whether the budget is transparent.

The Spring Festival is probably the most important festival for many people in China because it is closely connected with family reunion and the start of a new year. People travel home, share a meal and give children red envelopes. The Mid-Autumn Festival is also meaningful, especially for families who cannot meet often. These traditions make time together feel distinct from an ordinary weekend.

title: 去过的无聊地方
prompt: Describe a boring place
cues: And explain why you think it is a boring place
questions: Why do most children think education is boring?
Why aren’t young people willing to listen to the experiences of older people?

Are there any solutions?

Do most people think news about celebrities is boring?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A place I found boring was a crowded service hall where I had to wait with a family member for paperwork. We went on a weekday morning, but several counters were closed and the queue moved much more slowly than expected. Most of the time we sat under bright lights, checked the number on a screen and listened for our turn. There was no window to look out of, either. The staff were polite, so my frustration came from the long wait and the lack of anything useful to do. I tried reading messages on my phone, but the signal was poor and I kept looking up in case our number appeared. Nothing memorable happened; the room felt repetitive because every few minutes brought the same announcement and another short queue. Since then I check whether an appointment can be booked online, although some services still require people to wait in person. We took turns holding our place in the queue while the other filled in the required forms, so we could not go outside for a break. An appointment system and clearer updates on delays would have made the hall easier to tolerate. I would avoid going at the busiest time again.
part3: Some children find school boring when lessons feel disconnected from their interests or they mostly copy information without taking part. The same subject can become engaging with a practical example or a chance to ask questions. Students also differ in how they learn, so one teaching style will not suit everyone. A clear purpose and appropriate challenge can make lessons feel more worthwhile.

Some young people assume older people's experience belongs to a different time and will not help with problems they face now. They may also feel that advice is being imposed rather than offered. It helps when an older person listens first and connects their experience to the young person's situation. Then the conversation feels like an exchange, not a lecture.

People can change activity, go for a short walk, call a friend or start a small task they have been putting off. The best choice depends on whether they need rest or stimulation. I sometimes leave my desk for a few minutes after studying and return with a clearer head. Boredom can also be a sign that someone needs more variety or social contact in their routine.

A class can feel boring when students spend most of the time copying notes and never see how the material connects with anything real. A long explanation with no questions also makes it hard to stay involved. In mathematics, even a short example showing where an idea is used can make a lesson more interesting. The topic matters, but the way it is taught matters just as much.

Teachers can break up long explanations with questions, short activities and examples connected to real life. Students can also say which part they find confusing instead of waiting until they lose interest. In mathematics, a small puzzle or practical application can change the pace. It will not make every subject exciting, but giving learners a role can keep more of them engaged.

Young people may feel bored if the conversation centres on topics they do not know or if they are expected only to listen. A difference in pace and communication habits can also make it harder to connect. Shared activities, such as cooking or looking through family photographs, give both generations something concrete to discuss. Boredom often reflects the way people interact, not a lack of anything to learn.

Some people find celebrity news entertaining because it offers an easy topic of conversation, while others see it as unimportant compared with local or international events. It depends on how much detail is reported and whether the story is reliable. I rarely follow it closely, but a major public figure's actions can sometimes have wider consequences.

title: 发小
prompt: Describe a friend from your childhood
cues: Where and how you met each other
And explain what made you like him/her
questions: Do you still keep in touch with your friends from childhood?
Why or why not?
How important is childhood friendship to children?

Has technology changed people's friendships?
How?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: I would talk about a friend I met in primary school, when we were put in the same group for a class activity. We lived within walking distance of each other, so after school we sometimes went home together or played badminton nearby. Afterwards, we might stop at a bakery and split a red-bean bun before walking home. Neither of us was especially good at badminton, so we kept inventing new rules whenever one of us fell behind. My friend was easy to talk to and did not make small mistakes feel embarrassing, so I felt relaxed around him. We went to different secondary schools and became less involved in each other's daily lives, but we still exchange messages now and then. When we do catch up, we usually start with an old story and then talk about study or work. I value the friendship because it began naturally, before either of us worried about making a good impression. We only meet a few times a year now, but after the first few minutes the conversation feels as easy as it did at school. We can talk honestly about what is going well and what is difficult without trying to impress each other.
part3: Yes, I still message one or two friends from childhood, although we do not meet as often as we used to. We can talk about old memories without explaining every detail, which makes the friendship feel familiar. Our studies and work have taken us in different directions, so staying close requires some effort. Even an occasional call helps us keep that connection.

We have shared memories and know a lot about each other's background, so it is easy to restart a conversation even after a long gap. We may not meet often now because study and work take us to different places, but a message on a birthday or holiday helps keep the friendship alive without forcing daily contact.

It is very important because friends give children a safe place to practise sharing, solving disagreements and being themselves. A classmate who sits with a child on the first day of school can make an unfamiliar setting feel manageable. Those early friendships may not all last, but learning how to build and repair them is useful well into adulthood.

I find social media useful for quick updates and keeping in touch with people who live far away. A group chat makes it easy to arrange a meeting or share photos. However, short messages can hide tone, and scrolling can replace a proper conversation if people are not careful. I use it as a convenient channel, but I prefer a call for anything personal or complicated.

Probably not completely. Social media is convenient for quick updates and keeping in touch across distance, but people still need face-to-face conversation to read expressions, build trust and discuss sensitive issues. The two forms can work together: a message can arrange a meeting, while an in-person conversation gives people more attention. Online contact may reduce some meetings, but I do not think it will remove them.

There is not one choice that suits everyone; the main difference is what people need from it. Regular contact lets people talk naturally, notice shared interests and build trust over time. A class project or sports club gives children something to do together before they become close friends. A friendly group can still exclude newcomers, so inclusion matters as much as the activity.

Yes, it has made it much easier to stay in touch when friends study or work in different places. At the same time, a stream of short updates can create a feeling of closeness without much real conversation. I keep up with classmates in group chats, but I would still call a close friend when something important happens. It is a useful channel, not a substitute for attention.

It has mainly changed how often and how easily people can contact one another. Friends who move to different cities can share small updates or arrange a video call, which was harder in the past. The limitation is that a stream of messages can feel shallow, so people still need focused conversations when something important happens.

title: 受欢迎的人
prompt: Describe a popular person

And explain why you think this person is popular
questions: Why do people want to be popular?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A popular person I know is a student in my department who seems to know people from several different year groups. I see him most weekdays in the department common area and at student events, where he makes an effort to include people standing on their own. He is confident but not loud, and he remembers small details from earlier conversations, which makes people feel noticed. He often turns up at department events and volunteer sign-ups, and people greet him even when they arrive with different groups. I think that kind of attention is more important than being the funniest or most fashionable person in a room. He also seems comfortable talking to people with different interests rather than staying only with his closest friends. His popularity looks less like a performance and more like the result of being approachable and dependable over time. At a recent department event, I saw him introduce a first-year student to a group discussing research projects, then make sure she had a chance to speak. Small actions like that explain why people trust him to bring different groups together. His popularity seems to come from making conversations easier for others, rather than trying to be the centre of attention.
part3: People may want to be popular because being accepted gives them a sense of belonging and makes social situations easier. Recognition can also bring opportunities, especially for performers or people building a public career. At the same time, trying to please everyone can be tiring. I think most people want to feel valued by a group, even if they do not want constant attention.

It may be easier to become widely noticed because social media lets people share their work or personality with a large audience. Staying popular is harder, though; attention can disappear quickly, and online visibility does not always mean people trust or know someone well. At school or work, reliability and kindness still matter. I think technology changes how popularity spreads more than what makes someone genuinely liked.

A good teacher explains ideas clearly, notices when students are confused and gives feedback they can act on. I remember teachers who broke a difficult problem into smaller steps instead of simply repeating the answer. Patience matters, but so does setting high expectations; students learn more when they feel supported and are still encouraged to think for themselves.

No. A good teacher can be respected without being the most popular person in class. Clear explanations, fairness and genuine attention to students matter more than trying to be liked. Some teachers set demanding work, which students may not enjoy at the time, but still value later. Popularity can make a classroom comfortable, though it is not a reliable measure of teaching quality.

It is helpful if students feel comfortable speaking to a teacher, but popularity should not be the main goal. A teacher needs to explain clearly, treat students fairly and set appropriate expectations. Some lessons are challenging, so not everyone will enjoy them. I think trust and respect are more important than being popular, because they make students more willing to ask questions and accept feedback.

Some students become popular because they are approachable, include others and take part in activities that bring classmates together. Others are admired for a skill, such as sport or music. Popularity is not always the same as having close friends, though; a student can be widely known but still feel lonely. Consistent kindness tends to create stronger relationships than attention alone.

title: 名人出演的广告
prompt: Describe an advertisement with a famous person in it
cues: And explain how you feel about the advertisement
questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of advertisements?

How useful are they?

Why?
Which is more effective, online advertising or offline advertising?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The advertisement I remember featured NBA star Stephen Curry promoting a pair of basketball shoes. I saw it in a short online video before a sports clip, so I watched the first few seconds before deciding whether to skip it. It showed him training on an outdoor court and wearing the shoes during an ordinary day, rather than only posing in a studio. The message was that the design was light and suitable for regular exercise, although the advert did not explain much about durability. The famous face made me stop scrolling, but it was the clear product demonstration that kept my attention. Although the clip looked polished, it gave me no information about how the shoes held up after months of use. A close-up showed the sole bending as the athlete ran, so the feature the advert promoted was easy to understand. The athlete wore them on an ordinary training run, and that setting felt relevant to me as a casual runner. I could not judge the comfort or durability from a short clip. I found it engaging because the demonstration was clear, but I would read independent reviews before buying. The advert left me curious, rather than persuaded by the celebrity.
part3: Advertisements help people learn that a product exists, compare features and find offers they might otherwise miss. They can also support free websites and media. The downside is that repeated or exaggerated claims may pressure people into buying things they do not need. I find adverts useful when they provide clear information, but consumers should still check reviews and prices independently.

A celebrity attracts attention, and fans may already trust or admire that person, so an endorsement can make a product memorable. It also helps a company connect the product with a particular image or lifestyle. The risk is that fame does not prove quality. I would be more persuaded if the celebrity explained a genuine reason for using it and the claims were independently supported.

Celebrity endorsements can be useful for attracting attention, especially when the person is a natural fit for the product. A well-known athlete can make running shoes memorable, for example. Still, a familiar face cannot prove that the shoes are comfortable or durable, so customers need clear product details and independent reviews. I see endorsements as a way to raise awareness, not as evidence of quality.

The most important factor is a clear and believable message. Viewers should quickly understand what the product does, who it is for and what it costs, without having to decode a slogan. Attractive images can catch attention, but they cannot make up for vague or misleading claims. If an advert gives relevant information honestly, people can decide whether the product suits them.

Some adverts are boring because they repeat the same message without showing anything useful about the product. Others interrupt a programme or use a slogan that feels unrelated to what they are selling. People see so many adverts that a generic presentation is easy to ignore. A short demonstration or a memorable real-life example is more likely to hold my attention than loud music alone.

Yes, advertising matters because it tells potential customers that a product exists and explains what makes it different. Without it, even a useful product may remain unknown. A clear advert can also help a company reach the people most likely to need what it offers. It works best when its claims are honest, since misleading promotion can damage trust and future sales.

Advertising helps a company tell potential customers what it sells and how it differs from other options. A small business may not be noticed without promotion, while a familiar brand can use adverts to introduce a new product. It only works in the long term if the claims are honest; misleading people may produce one sale but damage trust.

Online advertising is effective when a company wants to reach a specific group and measure clicks or sales. Offline advertising, such as a poster or television spot, can reach people who are not actively searching and may be harder to avoid. The better choice depends on the audience and product. A local event may benefit from posters, while an online service can be promoted more precisely on the web.

title: 和朋友度过的愉快夜晚
prompt: Describe an enjoyable evening you had with your friends

And explain why it was enjoyable
questions: Why do people need friends?
Do older people prefer spending time with family or with friends?
Do young people prefer spending time with family or with friends?
What are the differences between young people’s leisure time activities and those of old people?
What can we do to bring family members closer together?
How do people get along in a big family?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: An enjoyable evening I remember was a simple meal with a few university friends after we had submitted a group assignment. We met near campus, chose a small restaurant and took our time because none of us had an early class the next morning. At first we talked about the project, including the parts that had taken longer than expected, but the conversation soon moved on. One friend told a story about getting on the wrong bus, and everyone added a detail from a similar experience. We did not go anywhere special afterwards; we walked part of the way back and stopped for tea. I enjoyed it because the pressure of the deadline had passed, so we could talk without checking the time every few minutes. There were three of us, all classmates from the same project group, so nobody needed to explain why the deadline had been stressful. After tea, we stood outside the restaurant laughing over the bus story and chose a longer route back to campus. One friend even checked the map to show us the stop where he had boarded the wrong bus. That unplanned walk made the evening feel lighter, and I went home in a better mood.
part3: Friends give people someone to share experiences with and someone they can turn to when life becomes difficult. They can offer a different perspective from family, while still making ordinary activities more enjoyable. For example, studying with a classmate can make a stressful week feel less isolating. People do not need a large circle; a few dependable relationships can provide a strong sense of support.

It varies, but family often becomes especially important when older people need practical support or regular company. Friends matter too: people of a similar age may share long memories and interests without needing much explanation. Distance, health and personality can affect the balance. I think most older adults value both, even if they spend more time with one group.

It depends on the person and the stage of life. Young people may spend more time with friends because they share classes, hobbies and similar routines, while family offers support and a sense of belonging. During holidays, they may choose both. I do not think one relationship should replace the other; having different kinds of support is valuable.

Young people often spend leisure time with friends, online media or organised activities, while older adults may prefer walking, family visits or hobbies they have kept for years. These are broad patterns rather than rules; health, income and personality matter too. Technology has also made it easier for older people to watch programmes or contact friends online. People of every age need both social time and rest.

Families can grow closer by making time for ordinary conversation and sharing responsibilities, rather than meeting only for formal occasions. A regular meal gives relatives a chance to catch up, while helping one another with practical tasks builds trust. People will not agree on everything, so listening matters as much as being together. A warm relationship depends on respect, not simply living under one roof.

People in a big family get along better when they communicate clearly, respect personal boundaries and share responsibilities fairly. Regular meals can help relatives stay connected, but disagreements are easier to manage when people listen instead of keeping score. It also helps to avoid comparing siblings or cousins. Family members do not need identical opinions; mutual respect makes it possible to live with those differences.

title: 喜欢在家/花园种菜的人

And explain why he/she loves growing plants

Do many people grow vegetables or flowers at home in your country?
Is it easy to grow plants at home?
Why do some people like to grow plants?
Why do some people prefer to grow their own fruits and vegetables instead of buying them from the market?
Do you think students should learn to grow plant?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: My grandmother is the person I think of when I hear about growing vegetables. She keeps pots of spring onions, tomatoes, leafy greens and herbs on her sunny apartment balcony. She started with a few seedlings because she wanted fresh ingredients for everyday meals, then added more after she saw how well they grew. She mixes compost into the soil, puts the tomatoes where they get the most sun and ties the taller stems to thin sticks. Most mornings she checks the leaves and waters the pots only when the soil feels dry. When I visit, she sometimes asks me to pick ripe tomatoes and shows me how to remove a yellow leaf without damaging the stem. The balcony is small, so she moves the pots around when one plant is blocking the light from another. She enjoys the routine as much as the food; she says it is satisfying to see a plant change from week to week. I like how practical her hobby is, since she uses what she grows in her cooking and shares extra herbs with relatives. Watching her has made me consider starting with a pot of basil, though I would have to remember to care for it regularly.
part3: Growing plants at home gives people a practical hobby and a visible result to care for over time. Home-grown vegetables can feel fresh, and flowers make a balcony or garden more pleasant. Looking after them may also help people slow down after work. The disadvantages are the time and space required, and the harvest can be small, so it is not always cheaper than buying produce.

Yes, some people grow herbs, flowers or vegetables on balconies and in small community gardens, especially when they enjoy cooking or gardening. It is more difficult for people in apartments with little sunlight, so not every household can do it. Even a few pots of spring onions can be useful. People often value the routine and fresh produce as much as saving money.

It can be easy if someone starts with plants suited to the amount of light and space they have. Herbs such as mint or spring onions do not need a large garden, but they still need regular watering. Beginners may lose a plant while learning what it needs. A simple pot is a manageable start, and experience makes it easier to notice problems early.

Many people enjoy growing plants because it is calming to watch something develop through their care. Watering and pruning provide a simple routine, and even a few pots can make a room or balcony feel more lively. Some people also like learning which conditions help each plant thrive. It is a hobby with a visible reward, although it requires patience when growth is slow.

People may grow their own produce because they can choose the varieties, control how it is treated and pick it when it is ripe. Gardening also gives them a sense of independence and can be enjoyable exercise. However, a small home garden rarely supplies everything a household needs. For most people, it is a supplement to market shopping rather than a complete replacement.

Yes, growing a plant can teach students patience and basic responsibility. They need to water it regularly and notice what changes, which is a practical way to learn about living things. A school does not need a large garden; pots on a windowsill can work. It should be an enjoyable activity, though, rather than another competition with marks attached.

title: 喜欢或不喜欢的高建筑

cues: And explain why you like/dislike it
questions: Are there many tall buildings in your country?

Why are different places laid out and designed differently?

Why do some people like to remodel and decorate their homes themselves?
What kind of interior design style do most people like?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A tall building I like is a public library in the centre of a nearby city, which I visited during a weekend trip. It stood above the surrounding streets, but the ground floor was open and easy to enter rather than feeling exclusive. Inside, there were quiet reading areas, a small exhibition space and wide windows looking out over the city. I went with a friend who wanted to study for an hour, so we had time to look around between reading. What surprised me was that the building felt calm despite its size, because the rooms were clearly arranged and there was plenty of light. I liked that it served a practical purpose for local people instead of being impressive only from the outside. If I visited again, I would spend longer there and explore the upper floors, which we did not have time to see. A local photography display was on one upper floor, with old images of the same streets I had just walked through. Seeing those shopfronts beside the view from the windows made the library feel connected to its neighbourhood. My friend used the reading area while I looked at the photographs, so we both found a reason to stay. I would return to see another exhibition and explore the floors we missed.
part3: Yes, tall buildings are common in major Chinese cities, especially in residential and business districts where land is limited. They allow more people to live or work near transport and services. Smaller cities and older neighbourhoods still have lower buildings. A high-rise is practical only when lifts, fire safety and public space are planned well; otherwise density can make daily life uncomfortable.

Tall buildings in China differ in what they are used for and how they connect with the street. Some are mainly apartments, while others combine offices, shops and public facilities. Newer developments may have underground parking and shared amenities, whereas older residential towers can have smaller lifts and fewer green spaces. Their design also depends on location, land costs and local planning rules.

Places are designed around their purpose, local climate, available land and the needs of the people who use them. A market needs open, accessible space, while a hospital needs clear routes and quiet areas. Older streets may reflect transport and building methods from another period. Good design responds to those practical conditions rather than applying one layout everywhere.

Tall buildings allow many households to live near workplaces, transport and shops, which can reduce long commutes. Residents may also have shared facilities such as a gym or a reception desk. The trade-off is dependence on lifts and less private outdoor space. They work well when the surrounding area has good services and the building is maintained, rather than simply being tall.

People may decorate their home themselves to save money, express their taste or make the space fit their daily routines. Doing the work can also be satisfying, especially when they see a clear result. Some tasks require professional skills, though, and a poor repair may cost more later. Many people do small jobs themselves and hire an expert for electrical or structural work.

Many people prefer a simple, modern interior with practical storage, neutral colours and enough natural light. That style is easy to maintain and does not feel crowded in a smaller apartment. Preferences still vary: some people like traditional wooden details or brighter colours that show their personality. In the end, a comfortable layout matters more than copying a style that looks good in photographs.

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The person I would describe is a university friend who enjoys taking photographs wherever we go together. I got to know her through a class project, and I noticed her interest when she photographed our work instead of just the final presentation. She takes pictures of street scenes, food and small details in parks, usually using her phone rather than expensive equipment. Her favourite spots are the old lanes near campus and the riverside path. Before taking a picture, she waits for people to move out of the frame or asks if they mind being included. I like that she pays attention to light and background, but she does not interrupt the whole outing to get a perfect shot. Sometimes she sends me one or two photos afterwards, and they bring back details I had not noticed at the time. I enjoy going out with her because she makes an ordinary walk feel more observant without stopping every few minutes. One afternoon, she showed me two versions of a shopfront photo and asked which light looked more natural. She had taken one just before sunset, when the softer light changed the colours of the shopfront. I liked being part of that small decision; her hobby adds something to our time together instead of taking it over.
part3: Some photographers do not mind a person entering the frame because an unexpected figure can make a picture feel lively and natural. Others are trying to capture a specific scene and may wait for the space to clear. It depends on the purpose of the photo. People nearby should be considerate, especially if someone is setting up a careful portrait or landscape shot.

Photos help tourists keep a record of places and share the experience with people who were not there. A picture of a street market or mountain view can bring back small details more vividly than a written note. Social media encourages people to take even more pictures, though sometimes they focus on the camera instead of the place. A few photos are a useful memory; taking them constantly can interrupt the visit.

No, people should not take photos everywhere without considering others. It is usually fine in a public park, but museums, private homes and some workplaces may have rules to protect privacy or valuable objects. People should ask before photographing someone closely, especially a child. A quick check of signs and the people around you is a simple way to avoid making others uncomfortable.

People often take photos of family and friends, meals, pets and places they visit. These subjects are part of daily life, so the pictures become a record of relationships as well as events. Phones have also made it easy to take photos of small things people find beautiful or funny. I think the most meaningful pictures are usually the ones that remind someone of a particular moment.

Some people enjoy photography as a creative hobby: they pay attention to light, colour and the way a scene is framed. Others mainly take pictures to keep memories or share what they are doing with friends. For example, a family may take the same group photo at every holiday gathering. The reasons differ, but a photo lets people return to a moment they would otherwise remember only vaguely.

People often take photos at family gatherings, on holidays and when they see an unusual view or a moment they want to remember. Many also photograph food or everyday activities to share with friends online. The reason is not always to make an artistic image; sometimes a quick picture helps preserve a detail that might otherwise be forgotten. Phones have made taking these photos effortless.
