answers.part2: A home I like visiting belongs to my aunt, who lives in an older apartment near the city centre. It is full of books, family photographs and small objects collected over many years, so I often ask her where they came from. When relatives visit, we sit around the dining table, share tea and catch up without making a formal plan. My aunt usually puts fruit and tea on the table, then brings out old photographs when someone asks about a person in them. I like that the visit can stretch into the afternoon without anyone checking a schedule. The apartment is also close to a busy market, so there is always some street noise. From her balcony, we can see market stalls being packed away at dusk, which gives the flat a lively feel during a visit. My favourite part is hearing the stories behind familiar objects; a chipped teapot, for instance, belonged to my great-grandmother. The apartment itself is narrow, with a long hallway and a tiny kitchen. I would not choose it for daily life because the market is noisy at night, there is no separate study area and it is far from my university. I prefer to visit for an afternoon, then return to a quieter room where I can work.
part3: Many people do, particularly when they are close to the host or celebrating a family occasion. Visiting someone's home gives relatives and friends more time to talk than a quick meeting in a cafe. That said, younger people may prefer meeting outside because apartments can be small or travelling across a city takes time. The preference depends on the relationship and the reason for meeting.

When visiting friends or relatives in China, people often bring fruit, snacks or a small gift, especially for a first visit. They may share tea or a meal and spend time catching up with the host. Customs differ by family and region, so visitors usually follow the host's lead. The main purpose is to show care and strengthen the relationship, not to follow a strict ceremony.

Many people in China prefer a home that is close to work, public transport, shops and schools. In cities, apartments are common because they are more available and easier to maintain than a large house. Some families would rather have a quieter neighbourhood or more outdoor space, even if it means a longer commute. The right place depends on household size, budget and daily routines.

City homes are usually closer to jobs, public transport and services, but they tend to have less space and cost more. In the countryside, houses may have gardens or nearby farmland, although residents can have longer journeys to work, school or a hospital. These are general patterns; income and local development make a big difference. People choose based on the daily life they want.

People often bring fruit, snacks, flowers or a small item for the household when visiting someone. The choice depends on the relationship and occasion; close friends may bring something casual, while a formal visit calls for a more considered gift. In China, people sometimes take fruit or tea to a relative's home. The gesture matters more than the price, as long as it suits the host.

I see close friends most weeks, usually after class or at the weekend, while I visit relatives less often because they live farther away. We tend to meet for a meal or a family occasion. During exam periods I may be busier, so we keep in touch by message and arrange a longer visit when my schedule is calmer.

title: 喜欢的公共建筑

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A public building I enjoy visiting is the main library near the university, which I first used while looking for a quiet place to study. It has a bright reading room, long desks and smaller spaces where students can work together without disturbing everyone else. The design is simple, with clear signs and windows that bring in natural light during the day. Its pale brick exterior is less imposing than the newer teaching blocks nearby, and the entrance opens onto a small courtyard. I usually go there when I need to concentrate on a proof or prepare slides with classmates. One time, I expected to stay for an hour and ended up finishing most of a problem sheet because the atmosphere was calm. The building works well because people can use it in different ways, from quiet reading to group discussion. I appreciate that it is a shared space that does not require anyone to buy something in order to stay. During exam week, I alternate between the silent floor and group tables depending on whether I am working through proofs or discussing a step with classmates. Having both options in one building makes it useful for different kinds of study.
part3: People visit historic buildings to see how earlier generations designed and used shared spaces. The architecture can reveal what materials were available and what a community valued at the time. Some buildings also have personal or national significance, so visitors go to connect with a story they have learned about. Good interpretation helps people understand the site without damaging it through excessive tourism.

No, not as a general rule. New buildings are needed for housing and services, but traditional ones preserve local character and can show how people lived in the past. If a building is unsafe or no longer useful, adapting or replacing it may make sense. Cities should assess each site carefully and keep historic structures when they can be used safely.

It depends on someone's family size, budget and preferred lifestyle. An apartment is often easier to maintain and closer to public transport, which suits many city residents. A house offers more privacy and outdoor space, but it usually costs more and needs more upkeep. I would choose a practical apartment while studying, then reconsider if my family or work situation changed.

Yes, historic buildings are worth protecting when they help people understand a city's past or have architectural value. They can also give neighbourhoods a distinctive character. Preservation costs money, so not every old structure can be kept exactly as it is. Careful restoration and a useful new purpose can make a building part of modern life instead of leaving it empty.

They preserve evidence of how a community developed and give residents a connection with local history. Old buildings can also attract visitors and make a neighbourhood distinctive. Preservation is not always simple because repairs are expensive and modern safety standards matter, so owners may need public support or a useful new purpose for the building.

Historic buildings can be expensive to maintain because they need specialist materials and repairs, while still meeting modern safety requirements. Cities also face pressure to build housing, roads and public facilities on valuable land. If a building has no practical use, it can be hard to justify the cost. Preservation is easier when the site serves the community and people understand its historical value.

Some people prefer the countryside because it is quieter, offers more space and keeps them close to nature or family. The cost of housing may also be lower. The trade-off is fewer local jobs and services, so transport and internet access matter. A rural home suits people whose work and lifestyle fit the area; it is not automatically a better choice for everyone.

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A natural place I enjoy is a riverside path on the eastern side of my city. It has trees along the water, a paved walking route and a few benches where people stop to rest. The path is easy to reach by bus, so we can go there without setting aside a whole day. I go there about twice a month, often with a friend after dinner or on a free afternoon. The place is not completely quiet, but the sound of the water and the open view make it feel less crowded. I remember one visit after rain, when the air felt cooler and the reflections on the river were unusually clear. We walked slowly and talked about ordinary things instead of trying to cover a fixed distance. I value the path because it makes a small amount of nature part of city life, rather than something people need to travel far to find. On one autumn visit, we watched egrets standing among the reeds while cyclists passed along the path. That small detail reminded me that the river supports wildlife as well as giving residents somewhere to walk. We stayed for half an hour and sat on a shaded bench before heading home.
part3: The two goals should be planned together because economic growth depends on clean water, healthy people and reliable natural resources. A factory can create jobs, but pollution may leave nearby residents with health costs. Governments can encourage cleaner production and help workers move into new roles. Some trade-offs are unavoidable, but treating environmental protection as a later problem often makes it more expensive to solve.

Yes, being somewhere green can improve people's mood because it gives them a break from noise, screens and routine. Even a short walk through a park can help someone feel calmer after a difficult day. The effect is not identical for everyone, and access matters; a safe, well-maintained space is more inviting than a neglected one. Nature can support wellbeing, though it cannot replace treatment for serious problems.

Cities should include parks and other natural spaces because residents need places to walk, exercise and get a break from traffic and buildings. Trees can also provide shade and help manage rainwater. The spaces do not all need to be large; small gardens and riverside paths can serve nearby communities. Planning them early is easier than trying to add green space after an area is fully built.

Governments can make nature easier to reach by protecting parks, adding safe walking and cycling routes and improving public transport to green spaces. Free community activities, such as guided walks, can also encourage people who are not used to spending time outdoors. It is important to maintain the areas and keep them accessible to older people and families. People are more likely to visit when the space feels safe and welcoming.

For many people, yes, because time outdoors offers a break from screens and gives them room to walk or relax. It does not need to involve a long hike; a nearby park can be enough. However, people have different schedules and access, so it should not become another expectation. Cities can make it easier by providing safe, pleasant green spaces close to where people live.

People who want quiet or a change of pace often enjoy nature, but it appeals to more than hikers. Families may choose a park because children can move around, while photographers notice light and scenery. In my case, a riverside walk is a simple way to step away from study. What they enjoy depends on the activity and how easy the place is to reach.

answers.part2: A live event I enjoyed was a university basketball final that I watched with two classmates last spring. We went because one of my classmates followed the university team, and he explained a few rules I did not know. When the final shot went in, people around us stood up at once. That shared reaction is what I remember most clearly, more than the final score itself. I do not follow basketball closely, but being in the room made the match feel immediate in a way a video would not. Afterwards, my friends and I walked back to our dorms discussing the referee's final call. I liked the event because we shared the tension with everyone around us, not just because our preferred team won. I would go to another match if I had the chance, especially with friends who enjoy the atmosphere.
part3: People watch sports because they enjoy the competition, the skill and the feeling of supporting a team. A close match can be exciting because the result may change in the final minutes. Watching with friends adds a social element, while a major event gives supporters something to share with a large crowd. Not everyone follows sport, but it can create a strong sense of belonging.

People watch sports at home, in a pub or cafe, or at the stadium, depending on the importance of the match and their budget. Home is comfortable and gives viewers replays, while a live venue offers atmosphere and a closer sense of the action. Friends may gather together for a final or a local game. The best place depends on whether someone values convenience or the crowd.

Watching online is convenient because people can follow a match at home or on a phone, often with replays and several camera angles. It may also cost less than travelling to a stadium. The downside is that the screen cannot recreate the noise and shared excitement of a live crowd, and the stream may be delayed. Online viewing suits people who want flexibility or cannot attend in person.

Local matches with a relaxed atmosphere are usually a good choice, such as school basketball or a family-friendly football game. They are easier for children to follow than a very long event, and the venue is less overwhelming. Parents should check crowd safety and make sure the child is interested; the aim is to enjoy the game, not to force them to sit through it.

Some supporters travel abroad because a major match or tournament is a rare experience, especially if their favourite team is playing. They may also want to meet other fans and see the host city while they are there. Tickets, travel and accommodation can be expensive, so it is usually a special trip rather than a regular habit. For committed supporters, sharing the atmosphere can justify the cost.

Football and basketball attract large audiences in China, while badminton is widely played in schools and community gyms. People often follow major international tournaments on television, but local games are easier to join themselves. Facilities and media coverage influence which sports become popular. I think a sport grows when people can watch successful players and also find an affordable place to try it.

answers.part2: A noisy place I remember is a food street near the centre that I visited with friends on a weekend evening. People usually tolerate ordinary daytime sounds, such as children playing or traffic, but become less patient when noise continues late at night. Cities are generally noisier because traffic, construction, shops and large numbers of people are close together. Daily life includes natural sounds, such as wind and birds, as well as human-made noise from traffic, construction, alarms and electronic devices. The problem is mainly constant or very loud noise that disrupts rest.

No. Children need opportunities to play and express themselves, and some noise is a normal part of growing up. Adults should step in when it becomes unsafe or prevents other people from sleeping, studying or using a shared space. The rules should depend on the setting: a playground is different from a library or an apartment late at night.

Some noise is a normal part of children playing and learning, and it can show that they feel comfortable expressing themselves. The important point is where and when it happens; loud games are not suitable in a library or late at night. Adults can set limits without expecting children to be silent all the time. Outdoor spaces give them room to be active while considering other people.

title: 在团队中工作

answers.part2: Last semester I worked with three classmates on a statistics project for my mathematics degree. The project was part of a course assessment, so we had to submit both the analysis and a short explanation of our method. That stopped us from repeating work and made it easier to see where the disagreement came from. I was responsible for explaining why we kept the unusual points rather than removing them. part3: Some people prefer working alone because they can concentrate, make decisions quickly and organise the task in their own way. This can suit writing or detailed analysis, where interruptions are costly. However, working alone means they have fewer chances to check an idea with someone else. A leader should set a clear direction, listen to the team and take responsibility when something goes wrong. Yes, students should practise group work because many jobs require people to share information and divide responsibilities. A school project gives them a low-risk chance to listen, explain an idea and resolve a disagreement. Group work should not replace individual tasks, though, because each student also needs to develop their own understanding. Clear roles and fair assessment help ensure that everyone contributes.

Students often work together on presentations, science projects, class discussions and performances. A project might involve one person finding information, another checking the data and someone else presenting the result. These tasks show students how to share responsibility and combine different strengths. They work best when everyone has a clear role, so one confident student does not end up doing everything.

Teamwork gives students practice explaining their ideas, listening to different views and dividing up a task. For example, in a group presentation, one student may be good at research while another is more confident speaking to the class. They learn from each other and get a result they could not produce as easily alone. Teachers still need to make sure each student contributes.

A good leader helps a group make progress without taking every decision for themselves. They explain the goal, listen when a plan is not working and make sure quieter members can contribute. For example, during a group assignment, a strong leader checks whether everyone understands their role instead of only chasing the deadline. The result matters, but so does how the team worked together.

title: 好的购物服务

What service you received from the staff
And explain how you felt about the service
questions: Can consumption drive economic growth?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of shopping online?
What are the differences between online shopping and in-store shopping?
Why do some people not like shopping in small shops?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of shopping in small shops?
Why are shopping malls so popular in China?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: I received good service at a small electronics shop near the railway station when I needed headphones for a long train journey. I explained that I wanted something comfortable for several hours, and the assistant showed me three models within my budget. She pointed out that one pair had a shorter battery life, then let me try the fit instead of steering me towards the most expensive option. I went there in the afternoon before taking a train to visit my grandparents, so I did not have much time to compare products elsewhere. The assistant asked whether I cared more about noise cancellation or battery life and explained the difference in plain language. She also checked that the case and charging cable were included before I paid. I left quickly but did not feel that she had rushed me into a decision. I chose the pair that felt comfortable and had enough battery for the journey. Before I left, she checked the warranty and paired them with my phone, so I knew they worked. I left feeling confident rather than pressured, which is why I remember the visit as good service. Her explanation saved me time and helped me choose a model that matched my budget and actual needs.
part3: Consumer spending can support economic growth because it gives businesses income to produce goods, hire staff and invest. However, growth based only on people borrowing or buying things they do not need may not last. Investment in skills, infrastructure and useful services matters too. A healthy economy needs demand, but it also needs productive work and responsible financial decisions.

Online shopping gives people a wide choice and makes it easy to compare prices without travelling to several stores. Reviews can also help buyers learn from other people's experience. The disadvantages are that an item may look different from its picture, delivery takes time and returns can be inconvenient. I use it for familiar products, but prefer a shop when fit or quality is difficult to judge.

Online shopping is convenient and offers more choice, while a physical shop lets people examine an item and take it home immediately. Staff can answer questions in person, but prices may be harder to compare across stores. I buy books and household basics online, whereas I prefer to try on clothes. The best option depends on whether convenience or direct inspection matters more.

Some people avoid small shops because their selection is limited and prices can be higher than those of large chains. They may also have shorter opening hours or lack the convenience of buying everything in one place. For someone who is busy, those drawbacks matter. Other shoppers enjoy personal service, so the dislike is often about convenience and price rather than the shop's size itself.

Small shops can offer personal service, distinctive products and a direct connection with the local community. Customers may be able to ask the owner for advice or find something not stocked by a large chain. On the other hand, the range can be narrow and prices may be higher. I like them for a particular item, but a supermarket is more practical for a big weekly shop.

Shopping malls are popular because they combine shops, restaurants, cinemas and indoor places to spend time, which is convenient in hot, cold or rainy weather. Families can make a whole outing of it rather than shop for one item. Many malls are also close to public transport. They can be crowded and encourage extra spending, but their range of activities keeps people coming back.

title: 学习并喜欢历史的人
prompt: Describe a person who learns history and loves history
cues: And explain how you feel about him/her
questions: Besides big historical events, what else is important when learning history?
Do you think people should learn ancient history before learning modern history?
Is it important to learn how people in the past lived their lives?
How do children learn history before they attend school?
At what age do you think people should begin to learn history?
Do you think children should begin learning history from an early age?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The person I have in mind is my grandmother, who reads about local history and visits museums whenever she can. She became interested after asking her parents about the older streets where they grew up. Now she reads short histories, compares old photographs with current buildings and tells the family what has changed. When she explains a place, she focuses on how ordinary people lived rather than only naming leaders or dates. I once went with her to a small local museum and understood more from her stories than from the labels alone. Her interest has made me more curious about the background of places I used to pass without noticing. I admire the way she keeps learning at her own pace and makes the past feel connected to the present. I once walked through the old market street with her after visiting the museum. She pointed out a doorway that appeared in one of her family's photographs and explained how the shops had changed since her childhood. I liked seeing how she connected written accounts, photographs and memories instead of treating them as separate facts. Her curiosity has made local history feel personal to me, and I admire the patience she brings to learning about it.
part3: Everyday life, local customs and ordinary people's experiences are important alongside wars and political leaders. They show how society actually worked: how families earned a living, what children learned and how people travelled. Family stories and old photographs can make a period easier to picture. Studying both daily life and major events gives a fuller explanation of why societies changed.

Students do not need to study all ancient history before learning about modern events. Starting with a period that connects to their lives may help them become interested, while ancient history can explain the origins of later institutions and customs. A balanced course can move between periods and show how events relate. The order matters less than helping students understand context and compare different sources.

Yes, because knowing how people lived makes historical events less abstract. Their work, homes, food and family routines help explain what choices were available to them and why change mattered. For example, learning how people travelled can clarify why towns developed around rivers or roads. It should sit alongside political history, since ordinary experience and major events influence each other.

Before school, children can learn history informally through family stories, old photographs, festivals and visits to local places. A grandparent describing how a neighbourhood used to look gives them a simple sense of the past. They do not need dates or formal terms yet; parents can answer questions and compare old and new objects. The aim is to make them curious about how life changes.

Around six or seven is a reasonable age to begin, when children can follow a simple story and understand the idea of 'long ago'. They can start with family history or familiar local places rather than memorising dates and dynasties. More formal timelines can come later, as their reading develops. Early lessons should build curiosity and a sense of change, not test how many facts they remember.

Children can begin learning history early through family stories, local places and simple accounts of how life used to be. They do not need to memorise dates before they can understand a timeline. A visit to an old building or a conversation with a grandparent can make the past concrete. More detailed debates about evidence can come later, as their reading and reasoning develop.

title: 对结果开心的重要决定
prompt: Describe a time you made an important decision and were happy with the result
cues: How easy it was for you to make the decision
And explain why you were happy with the result
questions: Which is better, to make a decision quickly or slowly?
Do you think most people's decisions are made in their 20s?
What if people in a group have different opinions on a decision?
What little decisions do people make every day?
Do you think it is a good idea to make a small decision every day?
How can we tell the difference between an important and an easy decision?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A decision I was happy with was joining a student society during my first year at university. I was deciding whether to keep my evenings free or try an activity where I did not know anyone. I had never joined a society before, so I was unsure how much time it would take. A friend invited me to one meeting, so I went along and offered to help with a small event task. Having something practical to do made it easier to talk to people, and I gradually became part of the group. We later organised a welcome event for new students, which gave me a chance to contribute instead of just attending. The group met once a week and shared the work, so the commitment was manageable alongside coursework. I helped print a campus map and welcomed students at the door. One first-year student used it to find a group to join, then thanked us for making the society easier to approach. I was nervous about walking into the first meeting alone, but having a task made it natural to speak with people. The small jobs also made later meetings less intimidating. I am glad I joined because I found friends outside my classes and contributed to campus life.
part3: The importance and reversibility of the decision should determine the pace. For a small choice, deciding quickly saves time; for a major decision about study or work, it is sensible to compare options and ask for advice. Waiting too long can also become a problem if it means avoiding responsibility. I try to gather enough information, then set a point when I will decide.

People make important choices in their twenties, such as what to study, where to work and whether to move, but many decisions happen earlier or later as well. This decade often brings more independence, so choices can strongly affect daily life. Still, few decisions are irreversible. People can change careers or priorities, which is why I would not call one decade decisive for everyone.

They should first make sure everyone understands the goal and the reasons behind each suggestion. A short discussion can reveal that people are disagreeing about different parts of the problem. If they still differ, the group can compare evidence, agree on a trial option or ask someone responsible to decide. Recording the reasons makes it easier to review the choice later.

People make small decisions about what to eat, how to travel, what to wear and how to organise their time. Each choice seems minor, but together they shape daily routines and spending. I decide which assignment to work on first by checking its deadline and how much concentration it needs. A simple habit can save time, so not every small decision needs lengthy analysis.

Yes, small decisions give people practice taking responsibility without putting too much at risk. Choosing how to organise a study session or what to cook can help someone notice what works for them. It is still sensible to pause before decisions involving money or other people. Everyday choices build confidence, but they do not need to be treated as major life lessons.

I would look at the consequences and how difficult it would be to change the decision later. Choosing what to eat is usually easy because the cost is small and the choice is reversible. Deciding on a major or accepting a job can affect several years, so it deserves more research and advice. The amount of thought should match the possible impact.

title: 尊敬的比你年长的人
prompt: Describe someone who is older than you that you admire
cues: What kinds of things you like to do together
And explain how you feel about this person
questions: What kinds of things do the elderly remember for a long time?
What sports are popular among older people?
What do old people usually do in their daily life?
Why is there a generation gap between the young and the old?
Has old people's life quality improved when compared to the past?
What can young and old people learn from each other?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: An older person I admire is my former English teacher from secondary school. I first knew her when she taught my class, and she encouraged us to explain ideas in our own words rather than memorise model answers. Since I graduated, we have occasionally caught up at school events or over tea. We usually talk about books, changes in education and what I am studying at university; she is especially curious about how mathematics students learn to explain difficult ideas clearly. When school hosts an alumni event, we sometimes browse the library together and exchange book recommendations. I enjoy hearing her suggestions because she often chooses books I would not find by myself. She also asks thoughtful questions instead of turning every conversation into a lesson. When I was at school, she was demanding about preparation but patient when someone made a mistake, so I felt comfortable asking her for help. I still appreciate that balance. She has continued learning new digital tools for her classes, and she is open about the parts she finds difficult. That makes her example feel real rather than idealised. I admire her warmth and curiosity, and I hope I can keep learning from people younger than me as confidently as she does.
part3: Older people often remember events connected with strong emotions, such as a family milestone, a difficult period or a place where they grew up. Repeated routines and stories can also stay vivid for decades. A familiar song or smell may bring those memories back unexpectedly. I think people remember not only what happened but who was there and how that experience changed their lives.

Many older adults enjoy walking, swimming, tai chi or badminton because these activities can be adjusted to different fitness levels. Some also play table tennis or join a local exercise group for the social side. The best choice depends on health and access to facilities. Regular, moderate activity is usually easier to maintain than a demanding sport that risks injury.

Older people's routines vary, but many spend time on household tasks, walking, seeing relatives, looking after grandchildren or meeting friends. Those who have retired may have more flexibility, while others still work or provide care. I would not assume that an older person is inactive. A regular routine can give structure, but having choice and social contact is important too.

A generation gap often comes from growing up with different technology, job markets and social expectations. Older people may value a stable career because that was important in their experience, while younger adults see changing jobs as normal. Family roles and media habits can also differ. The gap becomes smaller when people ask why a view developed instead of assuming the other generation is simply wrong.

In many ways, yes: older people today often have better healthcare, safer homes and more ways to stay in touch than previous generations. However, the benefits are not shared equally, and loneliness or the cost of care can still be serious problems. Life quality depends on health, income and social support, not only on technology. Improvements matter most when older adults can remain independent and connected.

Older people can share experience about work, relationships and dealing with setbacks, while younger people may help them understand new technology or current social changes. Both sides benefit when they ask questions rather than assume the other has nothing to offer. A grandparent learning to use a video call, for example, may hear about a grandchild's life more often. The exchange should be mutual and respectful.

title: 小时候学到的新技能
prompt: Describe a new skill you learned when you were a child
cues: And explain how you felt about learning the skill
questions: Is it important for everyone to have a specialized skill?
Can a child learn skills from another child?
Do you think it is easier for children to learn new skills than for adults?
What are the differences between the way adults learn and the way children learn?
What are the differences between learning in a group and learning by yourself?
What skills should children learn before they go to school?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A skill I learned when I was around seven was riding a bicycle. My father taught me in an empty paved area near our home, away from traffic. He started by holding the back of the seat while I pushed off and kept reminding me to look ahead instead of staring at the front wheel. He also showed me how to push off with one foot and keep pedalling, since the bike was easier to balance once it was moving. I found that difficult because I was so worried about falling. At first, I wobbled after only a few metres and put my feet down too soon. My father didn't steer for me; he ran beside me and let go for a second or two without telling me, so I could concentrate on balancing rather than waiting for him to release the seat. After a few short attempts, I managed to ride from one end of the area to the other without stopping. My legs were shaky, but I was so excited that I wanted to try again straight away. I felt frustrated at first, then really proud when I turned around and realised my father wasn't holding the bike any more. I remember asking him when he had let go, and he just laughed. It was only a short ride, but at that age it felt like a big achievement.
part3: It is useful to develop a skill in depth, but not everyone needs one narrow specialisation. People also benefit from communication, problem-solving and the ability to learn something new. A specialist can contribute strong expertise to a team, while broader skills help them adapt when work changes. The right balance depends on the person's goals and the kind of work they want to do.

Yes. Children often explain things in language their classmates understand, and they may feel less nervous asking a friend than an adult. A child who has learned to use a new game or craft can show another one step at a time. Adults still need to check safety and correct misunderstandings, but peer learning can make practice more relaxed and collaborative.

Children may have more time to practise and can be less worried about making mistakes, so some skills feel easier to learn young. Adults bring experience and discipline, though, and can understand why a skill is useful. I learned mathematics at university more effectively when I could connect new ideas with earlier knowledge. Age matters less than practice, motivation and the quality of guidance.

Children often learn through play, repetition and copying people around them. Adults are more likely to connect new information with experience and a specific goal, such as learning software for work. Children may be less worried about making mistakes, while adults can be more disciplined. Neither approach is always better; the most effective method depends on the learner and what they are trying to master.

Learning alone lets people work at their own pace and focus on the parts they find difficult. A group offers immediate questions and different explanations, which can reveal a gap in someone's understanding. I often study mathematics on my own first, then discuss a proof with classmates if I am stuck. A mix is useful, because neither method suits every task.

Before school, children benefit from basic communication, listening, sharing and looking after simple needs, such as putting away their things. They do not need formal lessons in every subject. Being able to ask for help or take turns makes the first classroom experience easier. Parents can build these skills through play and daily routines rather than treating early childhood like an exam.

title: 帮助他人
prompt: Describe a time when you helped someone
cues: And explain how you felt about it
questions: Should children be taught to be kind to others?

Why?
What kind of advice should parents give to their children?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A time I helped someone was when a classmate was having trouble understanding the data section of a group assignment. We were both in the university library, and the deadline was close enough that she was starting to panic. I asked her to show me which step was unclear, then we checked the formula against a small example by hand. That made it easier to see that the issue was a wrongly labelled column, not a difficult statistical method. We corrected it together and then checked the rest of the table before sending the work to our group. I felt relieved that the problem was smaller than it first seemed, and she was able to explain the result herself afterwards. It reminded me that useful help often begins with listening carefully instead of taking over the whole task. She explained the correction to the rest of the group, then checked a second column by herself. I felt relieved that we had caught the mistake before submission and pleased that she could continue independently. I could see her confidence returning as the second check went smoothly. It reminded me that listening first helps me offer the right kind of support instead of taking over.
part3: Yes, children should learn kindness through what adults model and how they treat people around them. Simple habits, such as including a classmate or offering help when someone is upset, show that kindness is practical rather than abstract. Children also need to learn boundaries, so being kind does not mean agreeing to everything. Parents and teachers can discuss situations and let children practise responding.

People should be considerate, but helping does not mean taking over or ignoring what the other person wants. It is better to ask what support would be useful and respect their answer. For example, a classmate may need someone to explain one step rather than finish an assignment for them. Kindness works best when it protects the other person's dignity and independence.

Yes. Children can help with age-appropriate tasks such as setting the table, tidying their room or carrying light shopping. These jobs give parents practical support and teach children that a household depends on everyone's contribution. Adults should explain how to do the task and keep expectations realistic. The aim is shared responsibility, not asking a child to take on an adult's workload.

Parents should give advice when a child faces a choice or a risk they may not understand, but they should explain their reasoning and listen to the child's view. Advice is more useful when it helps a child compare options than when it simply gives an order. For everyday decisions, letting children try and learn from small mistakes can build independence and confidence.

Children are still learning to judge risk and consequences, so thoughtful advice can help them avoid mistakes they are not ready to handle alone. It is more effective when parents explain their reasons and listen to the child's view. Advice should guide a decision rather than control every detail, because children also need practice making choices.

Parents should give practical, honest advice about safety, relationships and important choices, while recognising that their children may want a different future. For example, they can help a teenager compare college options without choosing a major for them. Good advice includes reasons and leaves room for questions. It should guide a child to think, rather than make them feel that only one path is acceptable.

Parents can help by providing a quiet place, asking what the child has tried and explaining a difficult idea when needed. They should avoid completing the work for the child, because that hides what the student understands. If a problem remains unclear, it is better to contact the teacher. Support should make the child more independent over time, not create a habit of waiting for an answer.

title: 当地新闻

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A piece of local news people discussed was the opening of a new community library near a residential area. I first heard about it in a neighbourhood group, where people shared photographs of the reading rooms and children's section. The area had plenty of shops but few quiet public spaces, so families and students were pleased to have another option. I visited after it opened and found that it had study desks, a small event room and clear signs in both languages. People were interested because the building could be useful every day, not just something to look at from outside. A local teacher said she hoped to bring students there for weekend reading activities. I think the project will matter most if it stays well maintained and continues to offer events for different age groups. The teacher and residents had both raised the lack of study space at a neighbourhood meeting, so the opening felt like a result of people being heard. At the first weekend event, children joined a short reading session while older students tried the desks. I was interested because people were already using the library in different ways, rather than treating it as another new landmark. The news showed that a practical local campaign could change a shared space.
part3: Some people still read print newspapers, but many people in my area get news through apps or online editions because they are quicker to check on the way to work or class. Older readers may prefer a paper copy, while younger people often follow several sources on their phones. The format has changed, although people still want reliable local information.

It depends on what is happening and what matters to the reader. Local news affects daily life directly, such as changes to transport or schools, while international stories help people understand events with wider consequences. I usually check both: local updates are practical, and a broader view helps explain why some changes are happening. A reliable source matters more than the category.

A sense of national identity can help people feel connected to a shared history, language or set of public traditions. It may encourage civic participation and solidarity during difficult times. At the same time, it should leave room for regional and personal identities and respect people from other backgrounds. It is valuable when it creates belonging without turning into a reason to exclude others.

People can develop a sense of national identity by learning about their country's history, language and different regional traditions. Schools and museums can provide context, while festivals and community events let people take part in those traditions. It should not mean that everyone has to think or live in the same way. A stronger identity can include regional differences and respect for people with different backgrounds.

title: 很久没收到回复的信息

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: I once messaged a classmate to confirm the time of a group meeting, but she did not reply until the next morning. I sent it on a weekday afternoon because we needed to reserve a study room, and I offered two possible times. The booking page showed that spaces were filling up, so I was anxious to hear which option worked for her. I checked the chat a few times, then sent one brief follow-up before choosing a room for the later slot. That gave the group a workable plan without waiting indefinitely. I did not send any more messages that evening because I did not want to pressure her. She eventually replied the next morning and said she had been travelling home and had not seen the notification. I felt relieved that she was not ignoring me, although I was a little embarrassed by how much I had worried about it. The delay had been inconvenient, but it was not a serious problem because I had made a backup booking. Since then, when a decision depends on someone else's answer, I include a clear deadline and make a reasonable plan in the meantime. That way, I can keep the work moving without repeatedly checking my phone.
part3: People may take longer to reply when the message needs a careful answer, when they are working or travelling, or when they need to check information first. A delay is not necessarily a sign that they are ignoring someone. If the sender needs a quick decision, it helps to say so clearly; otherwise, a little patience is usually reasonable.

People may choose not to reply when a message is unwanted, rude or clearly trying to start an argument. They might also avoid answering if they do not want to share private information or feel pressured to make a decision. That is different from simply being busy. If a message matters, it is better to be clear and respectful, while accepting that the other person may not want to continue the conversation.

I would first check whether the message was delivered and whether the person needs time to respond. For a routine question, I would wait and send one brief follow-up later. If I needed an answer to make an urgent decision, I would call or contact them another way. I try not to read a delayed reply as a personal rejection without evidence.

People often text because they can send information without interrupting someone and the other person can reply when free. A message is also useful for sharing an address, link or time that needs to be checked later. A call is better for an urgent or emotional conversation, where tone matters. The choice depends on how quickly the answer is needed and how complicated the topic is.

I show respect by being clear, using a polite tone and avoiding repeated messages when someone has not replied. I also try to choose a suitable time and give enough context so the other person understands what I need. For a formal message, I check names and details before sending. Those small habits show that I value the recipient's time and do not expect an instant response.

Some people feel ignored when a message is read but not answered, especially if they expected a quick response or were asking about something important. Social media can make people assume everyone is available all the time. The sender may not know what the other person is doing, though. Clear expectations help; people should allow reasonable time unless the message is genuinely urgent.

title: 快乐人士

answers.part2: A happy person I know is a close friend from my mathematics course. I'll call him Wei.
