He also remembers to check in when someone has been quiet for a few days, which makes people feel included. I think he is happy because he invests attention in people and routines he genuinely enjoys, not because life is always easy. I admire that steady outlook. When I get stuck on coursework, his suggestion to step away briefly has helped me return with a clearer head.
part3: People often feel happiest when they have close relationships, a sense of security and some control over how they spend their time. A particular age does not guarantee that; children may have fewer responsibilities, while adults can make more independent choices. Small daily moments, such as a good conversation or finishing a task, also matter. Happiness usually comes from a combination rather than one achievement.

The arts give people a way to express feelings and share experiences that may be difficult to explain directly. A public concert or community mural can create a sense of connection among people who would not otherwise meet. Art can also help individuals process sadness or stress. It does not make every problem disappear, but it can make people feel understood and create space for a wider conversation.

A careful teacher can often notice changes, such as a child becoming unusually quiet, missing activities or struggling to focus. They may not know the reason immediately, so it helps to speak privately and avoid making assumptions. Some children hide how they feel, which is why a trusting classroom matters. Teachers can offer support and involve parents or counsellors when needed.

No, teachers cannot and should not monitor every moment. They need to supervise children for safety and notice when someone is struggling, but students also need privacy and chances to make small decisions independently. A teacher can set clear expectations and check in at suitable times. Trust and open communication are more helpful than constant observation, which could make children feel anxious.

Students are more likely to feel happy when they feel safe, have a few trusted friends and can see that they are making progress. A teacher who notices effort, not only top marks, can help a struggling student feel included. School should still be challenging, but students need time for interests and rest as well. Feeling supported makes it easier to learn.

Enjoying a job matters because people spend a large part of their lives working, and interest can help them stay motivated. But salary, security, working hours and family responsibilities matter too. Someone may accept a less enjoyable job while supporting relatives or gaining experience. I would look for a reasonable balance rather than assuming passion should outweigh every practical need.

title: 想从事医疗行业的人
prompt: Describe a person you know who would like to choose a career in the medical field (e.g. a doctor, a nurse) (e.g. a doctor, a nurse)
cues: When he/she started to think about that
What he/she would like to do
And explain why he/she would like to choose this career
questions: Do you think being a doctor is easy or difficult?
Do you think learning biology is interesting for children?
Why do some children want to become doctors?
Do you think governments should put a large amount of money into medical research?
Why is some doctors’ pay high and others’ low?
Do you think doctors should be paid more?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The person I have in mind is my cousin, who hopes to become a nurse. I have known her since we were children, but I learned more about her career plans last year when we talked after a community health event she had volunteered at. She helped older residents find the right station for basic checks and was surprised by how much reassurance a calm explanation could provide. After that, she began looking into nursing programmes and the different areas of the profession. That volunteer shift was the first time she saw the role up close. She is especially interested in patient care because she is patient, listens carefully and does not become flustered when someone asks the same question twice. She understands that nursing involves long shifts, detailed training and difficult moments, so she has been speaking with people who already work in healthcare rather than relying on television dramas. I admire that she is considering both the rewarding and demanding parts before making a commitment. After the event, she spoke with a nurse about training and shift work, which made her interest more informed. I think nursing suits her because she listens carefully and stays calm when people are worried.
part3: It is a demanding job because doctors need years of training and have to make careful decisions under pressure. They also speak with people who may be frightened or in pain, so communication matters as much as medical knowledge. Some parts are rewarding, particularly when a patient improves, but long shifts and emotional responsibility can be difficult. The experience also varies by specialty and workplace.

Yes, biology can be interesting because children can connect it with animals, plants and their own bodies. A simple activity, such as watching a seed grow, makes an idea easier to remember than a list of terms. Some topics require careful explanation, but curiosity is a good starting point. Practical examples help children see why the subject matters in everyday life.

Children may want to become doctors because they admire someone who helped their family or because the job seems respected and useful. Television and books can also make medicine look exciting. As they learn more, some discover that the work involves long training and emotional pressure. It is a good ambition to explore, but children should be able to change their minds as their interests develop.

Governments should fund medical research because its results can improve prevention and treatment for many people, including those who cannot afford private care. The work may take years, so stable public funding matters. However, projects should be reviewed openly and include common health needs, not only profitable treatments. Research spending is worthwhile when it is carefully managed and its findings are shared responsibly.

Doctors' pay varies with their speciality, experience, location and employer. A specialist who has completed many years of training may earn more than a new doctor, while public and private hospitals follow different pay systems. Demand and working hours also matter. Pay is one way to recognise expertise, but fair conditions and enough staff are important too, because long hours can affect both doctors and patients.

Doctors should receive fair pay that reflects their training, responsibility and often long hours. Whether salaries should rise across the board depends on public budgets and differences between specialties. Pay alone will not solve problems such as staff shortages or heavy workloads. Governments should also improve working conditions and make sure doctors in less popular regions have support, so patients can access care.

title: 想要颁布的环保法律
prompt: Describe an environmental law you would like your country to introduce
cues: Why people should follow the law
Whether the law will be popular
And explain how you feel about this law
questions: How does technology affect the law?
What kinds of rules do schools in China have?
Will there be a law that is universally accepted?
What environmental laws does your country already have?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: I would introduce a rule requiring large shops and takeaway businesses to offer reusable packaging or charge for disposable bags and containers. People should follow it because single-use packaging creates a lot of waste after only a few minutes of use. For example, a customer ordering takeaway could bring a cup from home or borrow a reusable container and return it at another participating shop. I would start with larger chains, which have more resources to manage the system, then give smaller businesses time to join. Return boxes near metro stations could let commuters drop containers off without going back to the original shop. I expect the law to be reasonably popular if people can see a convenient alternative, although some customers may dislike paying extra when they forget a container. Large chains could begin with a deposit-return scheme, while smaller shops receive time and guidance to adapt. Clear signs at the counter would explain how to borrow, return or bring a container, so customers would not have to guess what to do. I would support the change because it reduces waste at the point of sale, but enforcement should focus on businesses providing workable choices rather than blaming individual customers for every disposable item.
part3: Technology creates new situations that existing laws may not cover, such as how companies collect personal data or how online fraud is investigated. It can also help authorities organise evidence and make public services easier to access. Laws need to keep pace without restricting useful tools unnecessarily. The difficult part is protecting people's rights while allowing innovation, so updates should be based on real problems and explained clearly.

Many schools set expectations for punctuality, homework and how students treat one another. Some have added rules about sorting waste or keeping shared areas clean, which can help environmental habits become part of school life. The details differ from one school to another. I think rules work best when students can see the benefit, not simply the punishment for breaking them.

Probably not in every detail, because countries have different histories, values and social conditions. They may agree on broad principles such as protecting people from violence, but disagree about how those principles should be applied. International agreements can create common standards, although enforcement varies. A law is more likely to gain support when it respects local circumstances while protecting basic rights.

China has rules on air pollution, waste sorting and protecting wildlife, although enforcement can differ between places. In larger cities, residents may be asked to separate household rubbish, and factories face limits on emissions. Such rules matter most when inspections and public information are consistent. Legislation alone cannot solve environmental problems, but it gives authorities a basis to prevent damage and hold polluters responsible.

title: 想颁布的新法律
prompt: Describe a new law you would like to introduce in your country
cues: Whether this new law will be popular
How you came up with the new law
And explain how you feel about this new law
questions: What rules should students follow at school?
Do people in your country usually obey the law?
What kinds of behavior are considered as good behavior?
Do you think children can learn about the law outside of school?
What are the benefits for people to obey rules?
How can parents teach children to obey rules?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A new law I would introduce would require public buildings to provide step-free entrances and working lifts. I thought of it after seeing a wheelchair user wait at a station while staff searched for a side entrance. Under the law, new stations, libraries and public offices would have to meet accessibility standards from the start, while older buildings would receive a clear timetable for improvements. The changes would help wheelchair users, older people and parents with prams use public services more independently. I think the law would be popular with most residents because accessible entrances make buildings easier for everyone to use, although some organisations might worry about renovation costs. To address that concern, the government could offer grants and practical design advice, especially to smaller public facilities. Inspections should involve people with disabilities and check that the whole route works, from the entrance to the service desk. I would support the law because access should not depend on asking staff for a special arrangement. Seeing someone wait outside a public entrance made me uncomfortable. I would support a law that makes accessibility a routine part of construction, so public services can be used without asking staff for a special favour.
part3: Students should follow rules that protect safety and let other people learn, such as arriving on time, listening when someone else is speaking and using phones only when a lesson allows it. Rules should be clear and applied consistently. A punishment alone may stop behaviour briefly, but explaining the reason helps students make a sensible choice even when a teacher is not watching.

Most people follow ordinary laws, particularly when the rules are clear and enforcement seems fair. People are more likely to respect traffic or public safety rules when they can see how those rules protect others. Some may ignore regulations they consider unreasonable or inconsistently applied. Education and accessible ways to comply usually work better than punishment alone, although serious offences still require proper consequences.

Good behaviour usually means treating others with respect, keeping promises and considering how one's actions affect people nearby. In a shared space, that might mean waiting your turn or speaking at a reasonable volume. Expectations differ between cultures and settings, so politeness is not always expressed in the same way. The common idea is to show consideration without expecting people to behave identically.

Yes. Children see rules in everyday life, such as road signs, public transport and rules for using a sports centre. Parents can explain why a rule exists when they encounter it, while news stories can provide age-appropriate examples. School gives a structured foundation, but daily experiences help children understand how rules protect people and what can happen when they are ignored.

Following reasonable rules can protect people's safety, reduce conflict and make shared services work more fairly. Traffic rules, for example, help drivers and pedestrians predict what others will do. Rules also make expectations clearer, which is useful at school or work. They should still be reviewed when they create unnecessary barriers. People are more willing to follow rules when they understand their purpose and see them applied consistently.

Parents can explain the reason for a rule, agree on a clear consequence and follow the same standard themselves. If a child understands that a road rule protects people from injury, it feels less arbitrary than simply hearing 'because I said so'. It also helps to notice when a child makes the right choice. Consistency builds understanding better than shouting or changing expectations.

title: 拥挤地方
prompt: Describe a crowded place you went to
questions: Do you think it is a good trend to have more big cities?
Do you think there are some people who enjoy crowded places?
Why do people go to crowded places?
Will people use bikes more or less in cities in the future?
Will there be more or less green space in cities in the future?
Which cities are overcrowded in your country?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A crowded place I went to was a railway station during the Spring Festival travel period. We arrived just after lunch, when several holiday trains were due to depart. I was there with my family, and the main hall was full of people carrying bags and checking departure boards. We arrived early, but it still took time to get through the security line and find the right platform. I felt a little stressed because it was easy to lose sight of one another, so we agreed on a meeting point near the entrance. We agreed to meet beside the platform signs if anyone became separated. Before entering the platform area, my father and I carried the larger bags while my mother kept the tickets somewhere easy to reach. We checked the departure board, bought steamed buns for the ride and waited near the correct platform. Since the hall was crowded, we agreed that no one would leave for food alone. Boarding was announced later than expected, so we followed the staff's instructions and moved forward with the queue. Inside the train, we found our seats and watched travellers hurry across the hall. The station was busy but organised; following one clear plan helped us stay together and board without confusion.
part3: Larger cities can create more jobs, universities and specialist services, which attracts people looking for opportunity. But continuous growth also raises housing costs, traffic and pressure on green space. I do not think every place needs to become a megacity. A better goal is to develop several well-connected cities so people can find work and services without all moving to the same centre.

Yes. Some people enjoy the energy of a busy market, concert or shopping street, especially when they are with friends. Crowds can make an event feel lively and create a sense of shared excitement. Other people find them tiring because movement and noise are harder to manage. Whether a crowded place is enjoyable depends on the purpose, the person's temperament and whether they can leave when they want.

People go to crowded places because popular shops, transport hubs and events offer something they cannot easily find elsewhere. A concert, market or festival can feel exciting precisely because many people are sharing the same experience. At other times, people have little choice, such as commuting through a busy station. The attraction depends on the purpose; crowds are enjoyable for an event but tiring during an everyday errand.

People may use bikes more if cities provide protected lanes, secure parking and safe routes to public transport. Bikes are useful for short trips and can reduce congestion, but weather, distance and road safety affect people's choices. Electric bikes also make longer journeys easier. I expect cycling to grow in some areas, though it will work best alongside reliable buses and trains rather than replacing them.

It could go either way. Growing populations create pressure to build housing and roads, which may reduce open land, but many cities are adding pocket parks, rooftop gardens and tree-lined routes. The result depends on planning choices and whether green space is protected when new development is approved. I hope cities treat parks as essential infrastructure rather than decoration that can be removed later.

The largest cities in China, especially Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen, can feel overcrowded because they attract people for work, education and public services. The pressure is most visible in expensive housing and packed public transport during rush hour. These cities still offer valuable opportunities, so the issue is not simply population size. Better transport and more jobs in smaller cities could make growth more balanced.

title: 拥有成功商业的人
prompt: Describe a person you know who has a successful business
cues: How you got to know him/her
Why and how he/she started the business
And explain why you think the business is successful
questions: Why do some people start their own business?
Should governments provide financial support to start-ups?
Do most people prefer shopping at big stores or small stores?
What makes a business successful?
What makes a business fail?
Is it easy to set up a new business in your country?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A person I know who runs a successful business is my aunt, who owns a small cafe near a university. I have known her all my life, but I became familiar with her work when I visited the cafe during its first year. She had noticed that students nearby wanted a quiet place to study, so she started with a short menu and a few tables rather than taking on a large loan. In the beginning, she prepared drinks herself, tracked supplies and spoke directly with customers. The cafe now serves coffee, tea and simple meals, and many students return because the prices are reasonable and the atmosphere is welcoming. I think it has become successful because she understood a real local need and kept improving the service. When regular customers asked for more seating, she changed the layout; when a dish was not selling, she adjusted the menu instead of insisting on it. She also watches costs closely and treats feedback as useful information. I admire her practical approach because running a business requires more than having an appealing idea. The cafe has grown steadily without losing the friendly atmosphere that first brought people in, and that is what makes me think it is doing well.
part3: People start a business because they see a need, want more independence or hope to earn a living from an idea they care about. Someone may notice that a neighbourhood lacks a quiet cafe, for example, and decide to serve local students. The freedom is attractive, but owners also take financial risks and work long hours. A good idea needs careful planning and customers.

They can, particularly when a new business is testing useful technology, creating local jobs or addressing a social need. Support should be limited and transparent, with clear criteria and public reporting on results. Otherwise, funding may reward connections rather than a sound idea. Governments should also offer training and access to advice, since money alone cannot make an inexperienced business succeed.

Big stores are convenient because they offer a wider range and often lower prices, while small shops can provide personal service and local products. People may choose a mall for a planned shopping trip but use a neighbourhood shop for one or two items. Neither is always better. The choice depends on price, convenience and whether the shopper values a particular product or relationship with the seller.

A business succeeds when it understands what customers need and provides that service reliably at a price they can accept. Good staff and careful cost management matter just as much as an original idea. A small cafe, for instance, can build regular customers by keeping the food consistent and listening to feedback. Success usually comes from improving over time, not from one clever advertisement.

A business often fails when it cannot attract enough paying customers or spends more than it earns for too long. Owners may also ignore feedback because they are attached to the original idea. For example, a cafe can be popular at first but still struggle if rent is too high. Careful budgeting and willingness to adjust the offer can prevent some problems.

It is easier to start small than to build a stable business. Online platforms let people test a product without renting a shop, but they still need capital, registration, suppliers and customers. Competition can be intense, especially in large cities. I would say the first steps are accessible to some people, while keeping the business profitable is the harder part.

title: 推荐旅行过的地方
prompt: Describe a place you have travelled to that you would like to recommend to others others
cues: What you saw and did there
And explain why you would like to recommend it to others
questions: Where do people in your country often go for holidays?
Where do young people in your country often go for holidays?
What is the ideal length for a holiday?
How do people usually plan holidays?
Is it important to plan a holiday ahead?
Why do many countries try to attract people to visit?
How do people decide when to travel?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A place I would recommend is Hangzhou, which I visited with my family during a short holiday. We walked around West Lake, explored an older street and tried local food without planning every hour. We also bought tea near the lake and sat beside the water as families crossed the bridge. We noticed a row of old houses beside a canal, far quieter than the main shopping street. The city felt busy near the main attractions, but it was easy to find quieter paths once we moved away from the crowds. I remember the light on the lake in the early evening, when the tour groups had started to thin out. The contrast between the water, green paths and lively streets made the visit feel varied. One evening, after the tour groups had left, we followed a side lane to a small restaurant and tried a local dish we had not planned to order. The bus system made it easy to reach the lake and older streets without relying on taxis. I would recommend Hangzhou to people who enjoy walking, scenery and local food; visitors can see famous sights and still find quieter corners. I would return for a weekend so I could explore one neighbourhood slowly and leave time for another long meal.
part3: People in China often visit nearby cities, coastal destinations, mountain areas and well-known historic sites during holidays. Families may choose a place with convenient transport and activities for different ages, while some travellers prefer a quieter rural break. National holidays can make famous attractions crowded, so many people book early or travel in the off-season. Budget and the length of the break usually shape the choice.

Young people in China often choose lively cities, scenic areas or coastal destinations where they can share activities with friends. Some look for affordable food and public transport, while others travel to attend a music event or explore local culture. They may be more willing to use hostels and plan independently than families with children. Social media influences choices, but budget and available time still matter most.

There is no ideal length for everyone. A long weekend may be enough for a nearby city, while a distant destination needs more time to make the travel worthwhile. People should also consider their budget, work commitments and whether they want a relaxed visit or a full itinerary. I prefer leaving a little unplanned time, because rushing through every attraction can make a holiday feel like work.

People usually choose a destination first, then compare transport, accommodation and the time they can take off work or study. Many check reviews and weather before booking. Some prefer a detailed itinerary, while others reserve only the important parts and decide the rest after arriving. I think a plan should cover practical needs but leave room to change direction if a place is busy or the weather turns.

Some planning is useful, especially for transport, accommodation and popular attractions that may sell out. It also helps people set a budget and avoid wasting time after they arrive. I would not plan every hour, because unexpected places can be part of the fun. A few fixed arrangements with open time around them usually give a holiday both structure and flexibility.

Countries promote tourism because visitors spend money on accommodation, food, transport and local attractions, creating jobs and tax income. Tourism can also introduce a country's culture to a wider audience. The challenge is that popular sites may become crowded and local housing or services more expensive. Governments need to manage visitor numbers and direct some income back into the communities that receive tourists.

People often choose travel dates around work or school breaks, weather, cost and who is available to go with them. Families may prefer school holidays, even though flights and hotels are then more expensive. Someone with flexible work can travel in a quieter season. The best time depends on the destination; checking local weather and events can prevent an otherwise good trip from being uncomfortable.

title: 擅长做手工的人
prompt: Describe a person who is good at making things by hand
cues: What materials or technologies he/she uses
And why you think this person is good at making things by hand
questions: Does art, like music or theater, have an impact on society?
Is it good to have creative people in a team?
What impact can artistic buildings have on society?
Do children these days still like doing arts and crafts?
Why do some children enjoy making things by hand?
Do you think art classes are important for children?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: The person I have in mind is a classmate who makes small clay and paper decorations in her free time. I first noticed her work when she brought a handmade bookmark to the library, and later she showed me a few more pieces. She sketches a simple design, chooses materials she already has and changes the plan if one part does not work. The objects are not perfectly symmetrical, but that makes them feel personal rather than mass-produced. She once made a small desk organiser from leftover cardboard and painted it to match her study space. I like watching her because she is patient and does not throw something away after one mistake. Her hobby has made me appreciate the time behind handmade things, even when the finished item looks simple. For a set of clay tags she gave her family, she rolled the clay evenly, cut each shape and added initials before leaving them to dry. For her paper decorations, she uses a ruler and craft knife to cut matching pieces before folding the edges neatly. She measures carefully and adjusts when a material bends or cracks. I think she is good at making things because she plans each stage and tests whether an object is useful as well as attractive.
part3: Art can influence society by giving people a way to express experiences and discuss issues they might otherwise avoid. A play or song can make an audience see an event from another person's perspective. It does not change policy by itself, but it can shape public conversation and preserve culture. Its effect is strongest when people can access and interpret it for themselves.

Yes, particularly when a team is stuck with an approach that is not working. A creative member may suggest a different way to explain an idea or organise a task. Still, imagination needs to be balanced with practical judgement: the team should test suggestions against its goal, budget and evidence. A useful team welcomes new ideas but also decides which ones are realistic.

An artistic building can give a neighbourhood a recognisable landmark and make public spaces more enjoyable to use. Libraries, museums or concert halls can also attract visitors and support local businesses. Good design should still serve the people who use the building, not just look striking in photographs. If it is costly or difficult to access, its social value may be limited.

Yes, many children still enjoy drawing, building models or making things from paper, especially when the activity lets them choose what to create. Screens compete for their attention, but hands-on projects give an immediate result they can show someone. Schools and families can encourage it by providing simple materials and not judging every finished piece. Enjoyment matters more than producing perfect work.

Children enjoy making things by hand because they can turn an idea into something they can touch and show to others. The process also gives them room to experiment without needing a perfect result. For example, a child might change the shape of a paper model after it falls over. Simple materials keep it accessible, and praise for effort can make them more willing to try again.

Art classes are useful because they let children experiment with materials, express ideas and develop patience. They also give students who are less confident in academic subjects another way to feel capable. Not every child needs to become an artist, and classes should not focus only on producing neat work. The value is in practising observation and creativity in a supportive setting.

title: 擅长学习和说语言的人
prompt: Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages
cues: How you got to know him/her
How he/she learns a new language
And explain how you feel about him/her
questions: Are there many people who can speak foreign languages in your country?
Does speaking other languages help at work?
Do people learn any languages other than English?
Why is it easier for children to learn new things than for adults?
How do people learn new things?
What is the most important thing for learning a language well?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A friend from my department is unusually good at learning languages. I met her in an English conversation group during my second year, where she was happy to speak even when she did not know the perfect word. She speaks Mandarin at home, uses English confidently outside class and has recently begun Japanese because she enjoys its sound. She keeps a small list of useful phrases on her phone and revisits it before meeting people. Her method is simple, but she uses what she learns instead of waiting until she feels completely fluent. She practises English by listening to podcasts and talking with exchange students, but she does not worry about understanding every word. When she meets an expression she does not know, she asks for an example and tries using it later. I noticed her confidence during a group project with an international student; she kept the conversation moving and checked politely when something was unclear. She attends a beginner class once a week and uses short videos to practise between lessons. I admire her patience more than any quick progress. She is willing to make mistakes in conversation, then remember what she learned from them. Seeing that has made language practice feel less like a test and more like a skill built through regular use.
part3: Many people in China study English at school, but the number who feel comfortable speaking it in daily life is smaller. Some people also learn Japanese, Korean or other languages for work and travel. Ability varies with access to practice and education. Online media and international workplaces create more chances to use a language, but regular conversation is still the best way to build confidence.

It can help people communicate with international clients, read material that is not translated and work with colleagues in other countries. The value depends on the industry; it may be essential in tourism or trade but less important in a local role. Language ability is not enough on its own, though. People also need professional skills and the ability to explain ideas clearly.

Yes. In China, some people study Japanese, Korean, French or another language for travel, work or personal interest. English is common in education, but it is not the only useful choice. A language becomes easier to maintain when learners have a reason to use it, such as talking to friends or following media. Access to classes and regular practice also makes a difference.

Children may learn some new skills more easily because they have more time to practise and are less self-conscious about making mistakes. They also absorb sounds and routines through repeated exposure. Adults, however, can understand explanations and connect ideas to what they already know. So children may have an advantage in certain areas, but adults can learn effectively when they practise regularly and have a clear purpose.

People learn best through a mix of explanation, practice and feedback. Watching a short demonstration can introduce a new skill, but trying it themselves helps them notice what they do not yet understand. I remember mathematical ideas better when I work through a problem rather than only reread the proof. The right balance depends on the subject and learner, but active practice is hard to replace.

Regular practice is probably the most important factor because language needs to be used, not just memorised. Learners need to listen, speak, read and get feedback over time, even if each session is short. I find that noting a phrase from a podcast and trying it in conversation helps it stick. Confidence matters too; people improve faster when they are willing to make small mistakes.

title: 攒钱买特别物品
prompt: Describe a time when you saved money to buy something special
cues: Why you wanted to buy it
How you saved money for it
And explain how you felt after buying it
questions: Should people spend time on charity, or just money?
What kind of things do people usually save money for?

Should parents teach their children to spend money freely or to save money?
Should schools teach children how to manage money from a young age?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: During my second year at university, I saved for a reliable second-hand bicycle. The bus between my apartment and campus was often crowded, and walking took too long before morning classes. I set aside part of my allowance after paying for meals and transport, then stopped ordering small items online. I transferred the same amount into a separate account each week so I could see the balance grow. It took about two months to reach roughly 1,400 yuan. During that time, I compared frame sizes and asked a cycling classmate what to inspect on a used bike. We checked the brakes, gears and tyre condition before I bought one with a few scratches but no mechanical problems. The seller included a basic lock, saving me another small expense. The seller included a basic lock, which saved me another expense. I felt proud that I had waited for a safe, dependable model instead of buying the first cheap one I saw. On my first ride to an early lecture, I arrived faster than I would have by bus and did not have to wait in a crowded aisle. The purchase made my daily routine easier, and the saving plan showed me I could work towards a larger expense without putting pressure on my monthly budget.
part3: Both forms of help are valuable, and the right choice depends on someone's circumstances. Donating money lets charities pay for equipment or employ trained staff, while volunteering contributes time and personal skills. A person with little free time may be able to give a small amount instead. People should choose a reliable organisation and support it in a way they can sustain.

People often save for housing, education, travel, a car or an expensive device, depending on their age and income. Some also keep an emergency fund for medical costs or a period without work. A clear goal makes it easier to put aside a small amount regularly. Saving is useful, but people also need to decide how much they can set aside without making daily life unnecessarily restrictive.

For many people it is easier to spend because the reward is immediate, while the benefit of saving comes later. Online shopping also makes small purchases very convenient. Saving becomes easier when someone sets a clear goal and transfers a manageable amount regularly. I find it helps to wait a day before buying something non-essential, so I can decide whether I still want it.

Yes, that can be a useful age to start. Teenagers are old enough to understand a simple budget, and they can practise before they become financially independent. Parents might give them a weekly amount to manage and discuss saving, needs and online scams. Letting them make small decisions, then review the result together, is more effective than only warning them not to waste money.

Parents should teach children to save some money while also allowing them to spend a reasonable amount on things they enjoy. A child can divide pocket money into savings and spending, then decide what to buy. That gives them practice comparing choices and understanding that money is limited. The goal is not to make children afraid to spend, but to help them make thoughtful decisions.

Yes, schools can teach basic money skills such as budgeting, comparing prices and recognising online scams. These are useful whether a student later works, studies or manages a household. A classroom exercise could ask students to plan a small event within a fixed budget. Parents also influence habits, but schools can ensure every child learns the basics, even if money is rarely discussed at home.

title: 改变重要想法

answers.part2: I changed my opinion about online classes during a busy semester at university. I used to think they were less effective than in-person lessons because students could switch off their cameras and lose focus. Then I took an online statistics course with short recorded explanations, worked examples and small discussion groups. I found it useful to replay a difficult explanation at my own pace, and the discussion sessions gave me a chance to ask questions rather than study entirely alone. Before one session, I had misunderstood a step in a probability example; the lecturer drew a small diagram and let us compare answers in pairs until the reasoning became clear. She also answered questions in the chat while we worked through examples. That experience showed me that an online class could still involve active discussion. I still prefer a classroom when I need an immediate conversation with the lecturer, but I no longer assume that online learning is automatically inferior. I felt surprised that the course worked well, then slightly embarrassed that I had judged the format without trying a well-designed lesson. Now I check how a class is taught and how much students can participate before deciding whether its format suits me.
part3: Children start expressing preferences at a young age, for example about food, clothes or games. Their opinions usually become more reasoned as they gain experience and learn to explain why they feel a certain way. Adults can support this by asking questions rather than dismissing a choice immediately. Children still need guidance on safety, but making age-appropriate decisions helps them develop independent judgement.

Children begin expressing preferences quite early, but their opinions become more considered as they gain experience and learn to explain their reasons. Parents often shape early choices because they are responsible for safety, while teachers influence children through school and subject knowledge. Neither should automatically decide everything. Adults can listen, offer context and let children make age-appropriate choices so they learn to think independently.

Most children probably talk more with their parents because they share a home and everyday routines. Teachers see them regularly in a different setting and may be easier to approach about schoolwork or a subject they enjoy. The balance changes with age and family circumstances. What matters is that children have at least one trusted adult who listens without immediately judging them.

Young people often share opinions with close friends because they expect an honest response and have similar experiences. They may also talk to a parent or teacher when the issue involves a big decision and they want more perspective. Online groups make it easy to find people with the same interests, but not every reply is reliable. The best person to ask depends on the subject and the trust involved.

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A person who taught me a useful skill was Dr Hu, the teaching assistant in a Lean 4 formalization and number theory course at Peking University. The skill was formalizing number-theory proofs in Lean 4: turning informal arguments into precise definitions, lemmas, and proof steps. I used to write proofs and only notice a gap after a long argument. Dr Hu taught us to state a small lemma, check its type, and test it with a simple case before using it in a larger proof. In sessions, Dr Hu showed us how to keep each step traceable; when an error appeared, Dr Hu asked us to find the first step where the goal or assumption no longer matched. We practised on questions, and when I made a mistake, Dr Hu guided me to locate the first unresolved goal or type mismatch. At first this felt slower than rushing to the end, but I soon caught errors earlier and felt less frustrated. I still use the habit when checking formal proofs with several assumptions. I feel grateful because Dr Hu taught more than a procedure: Dr Hu showed me how to take responsibility for understanding my work. I admired Dr Hu’s patience in explaining the same idea differently without making a student feel foolish. Dr Hu is patient, rigorous, and encouraging.
part3: Self-discipline helps because progress usually comes from short, regular practice rather than one intense session. Someone learning an instrument or a language may feel awkward at first, but a routine makes it easier to continue through that stage. It also helps people notice whether a method is working. Discipline should not mean practising without rest; a realistic schedule is more sustainable.

A teacher can structure a subject, correct misunderstandings and answer questions straight away. Studying alone gives learners more control over pace and lets them revisit difficult material. I prefer to work through a mathematics problem independently first, then ask a lecturer or classmate when I cannot see where my reasoning fails. The two methods support different stages of learning.

Adults often learn a new skill by setting aside regular time and practising the part they need in daily life. Someone learning a spreadsheet for work, for instance, can follow a short lesson and then use the tool on a real task. Feedback helps them catch mistakes early. Adults may have less free time than children, so a practical goal keeps the effort manageable.

Parents and teachers can teach a skill by demonstrating it, letting the child try and giving feedback on one step at a time. For example, when teaching a child to cook, an adult can show how to measure ingredients and then supervise the child doing it. Patient repetition is more helpful than taking over whenever there is a mistake. Children learn confidence as well as the skill itself.

Children can learn skills at home, at school, through sports or arts clubs and from friends or relatives. A formal class gives them structured instruction, while everyday activities such as cooking with a parent teach practical skills. Online videos can help too, provided an adult checks that the advice is safe. Different settings suit different abilities, and regular practice matters more than the location alone.

Learning new skills helps children become more independent and discover what they enjoy. A child who learns to prepare a simple meal, for example, gains a practical ability and confidence that they can improve with practice. It is also healthy for them to try things they are not immediately good at. The aim should be exploration, not pressure to excel at everything.

title: 早起经历

cues: And how you felt about it

Why do people get up early?
What kinds of occasions need people to arrive early?

What kind of people like getting up early?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: I got up before sunrise for a family trip to a mountain trail during a school holiday. We wanted to start walking before the path became crowded and reach a viewpoint while the air was cool. I was sleepy when the alarm rang, but I packed a snack, filled a water bottle and left with my parents. We had checked the weather the night before and put our walking shoes and jackets beside the door, so we did not waste time getting ready. The drive to the trail took nearly an hour, and I dozed for part of it. Once we started walking, the cold air woke me up. My parents pointed out a few plants along the path, which gave us a reason to pause before reaching the viewpoint. As we climbed, the sky became brighter and the outline of the hills slowly appeared through the mist. I remember stopping at the top for a few quiet minutes before other visitors arrived. The early start was uncomfortable at first, and I needed a long rest later that afternoon, but I was glad we had made the effort. I would not want to wake up that early every day. For a special trip, though, seeing the landscape before it became busy made the morning feel worthwhile.
part3: One friend from my course likes getting up early because he can study in a quiet library before his lectures. He says he feels less rushed when he has reviewed his notes first. I am not always that disciplined, especially after a late night, but I can see why the routine works for him. It suits his schedule and helps him concentrate.

People get up early for different reasons, including work, school, exercise or a long commute. Some also find the morning quiet and use it for focused tasks before the day becomes busy. It is partly a matter of habit and sleep pattern, not simply discipline. Someone who works late may be more productive later in the day, so early rising does not suit everyone.

People should arrive early for occasions where missing the start would cause a problem, such as an exam, a job interview or an international flight. It gives them time to find the right place and deal with unexpected delays. For a casual meal with friends, arriving exactly on time is usually enough. How early to be depends on the consequences of being late.

Some people stay up late because work or study takes longer than expected, while others enjoy having quiet time after family responsibilities are finished. Their natural sleep patterns can also differ. Staying up late may feel relaxing, but it becomes a problem if it regularly reduces sleep and affects concentration the next day. A consistent schedule is more useful than forcing everyone to sleep at the same time.

No, not in every situation. Arriving early is sensible for an exam, interview or train because being late could cause a real problem. For a casual meeting, arriving a few minutes beforehand is enough; being extremely early may leave the other person feeling rushed. I think people should be punctual while considering the setting and whether anyone is ready to meet them.

People who start work early, have a long commute or enjoy morning exercise may prefer getting up early. Some feel more alert in the morning and like finishing important tasks before distractions begin. Others are naturally more energetic later in the day. I do not think early risers are automatically more productive; the best schedule is one that fits someone's responsibilities and lets them sleep enough.

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A person I know with healthy habits is a classmate I met in a first-year tutorial group. We became friends while working on a problem set, and I noticed that he kept a steady routine even when coursework became demanding. He walks to campus most days when the weather is reasonable, carries water and tries to stop studying at a sensible time instead of working through the night. He also plays badminton once or twice a week and usually eats a proper meal rather than relying on snacks during long study sessions. During exam periods, he still takes a short walk between tasks, which seems to help him clear his head. What I respect is that he is consistent without being strict; if he has a late night, he returns to his routine the next day instead of giving up on it. Seeing this has encouraged me to take breaks and protect my sleep, especially when I have several assignments due. I feel that his example is useful because it fits ordinary student life rather than depending on expensive equipment or a perfect schedule. His habits are not dramatic, but they are realistic enough to last through a busy semester.
part3: Yes. Local government can provide safe parks, walking routes, sports facilities and clear health information, making healthy choices easier for residents. It can also regulate food safety and support preventive care. Personal choices still matter, and policies should not shame people or dictate every habit. The most useful approach is to offer accessible options, especially in neighbourhoods with fewer services.

It can help because neighbours influence what feels normal. If there are safe paths, sports areas and shops selling fresh food, people have more chances to make healthy choices together. Social support can also encourage someone to keep a routine. Still, people need privacy and different habits, so a healthy community should offer options rather than pressure everyone to live in exactly the same way.

People can reduce everyday stress by taking a short break, exercising, talking to someone they trust or dividing a large task into smaller steps. Sleep and a predictable routine also help. I find that a brief walk clears my head when university work piles up. These habits cannot remove every cause of stress, so people may also need to change an unrealistic workload or ask for support.

Short-term stress can help someone focus before an exam or deadline, but constant stress may disrupt sleep, affect mood and make concentration harder. People may also develop headaches or neglect exercise when they are under pressure for a long time. The effect varies between individuals. Rest, social support and manageable routines can help, but persistent symptoms deserve proper medical advice rather than being ignored.

Older people may pay closer attention to health because they have more experience with illness and regular check-ups. Younger people may focus on fitness or appearance, but their habits vary widely. Work, income and access to healthcare also affect how much attention someone can give. Rather than compare generations, it is more useful to make healthy food, exercise and medical advice accessible at every age.

answers.part2: A very organised person I know is a classmate who keeps track of deadlines and small tasks without making a fuss about it. As a result, we spent less time asking what was happening and more time doing the actual work. I admire that her organisation is practical rather than perfect, and she still leaves room for unexpected changes. I have borrowed her habit of writing down the next action, because it helps me start instead of worrying about the whole task. I think being organised matters to her because she balances several demanding courses and does not want group members to be left doing last-minute work. A clear plan lets her protect time for study while still being flexible if someone needs help. I respect that she treats organisation as a way to reduce stress for everyone, not as a way to control them. Her approach makes group work feel more manageable.
part3: Yes, because managers coordinate people, deadlines and resources. If they communicate priorities clearly, staff can focus on the right work and notice risks early. A shared schedule, for example, helps a team see when one task depends on another. Managers also need flexibility, since a neat plan is not useful if they cannot adjust it when circumstances change.

Yes, but they should teach it gradually through everyday routines rather than expecting a child to manage everything perfectly. A parent might help a child pack a school bag the night before, then let them take responsibility over time. This builds independence and reduces last-minute stress. Children also need unstructured time, so being organised should support their day rather than fill every hour.

People can become more organised by writing down deadlines, breaking large tasks into steps and deciding what needs attention first. I keep a short list for coursework rather than trying to plan every hour. Reviewing it at the end of the day helps me see what is still unfinished, even during a busy week. The system works only if it stays simple enough to use.

Being organised can make success more likely because people are better able to meet deadlines, prepare steadily and notice when they need help. For example, a student who breaks revision into weekly tasks may avoid last-minute gaps. Organisation is not enough on its own, though; knowledge, opportunity and teamwork matter too. A flexible plan is more useful than a perfect-looking timetable.

It is helpful to introduce simple habits early, such as putting toys away or preparing school things the night before. These routines give children a sense of responsibility and make busy mornings calmer. Adults should keep the tasks suitable for the child's age and avoid criticising every mistake. The aim is to help them manage their own time as they grow.

Being organised saves time and reduces the chance of forgetting an important commitment. It also makes a large task feel more manageable because people can see the next step instead of worrying about everything at once. In a group project, clear roles prevent classmates from duplicating work. A routine is helpful, but it should leave room for unexpected changes.

answers.part2: An interesting video I watched recently was a short animation about the Fibonacci sequence and spiral patterns in sunflower seeds. A classmate sent it after we had discussed patterns in a mathematics tutorial, and I opened it during a break at the library cafe between lectures. I wanted to see whether the sequence had a clear example in nature, rather than only in our notes. The video began with a close-up of a sunflower, then used simple drawings to show how the numbers of seeds in neighbouring spirals can follow the sequence. I liked that the narrator treated these shapes as patterns to investigate instead of claiming that every natural object fits a perfect formula. One diagram was especially clear: it marked the spirals in opposite directions, so I could follow the count without pausing every few seconds. I later sent the link to a friend studying biology, and we talked about whether related patterns appear in leaf arrangements. The explanation made me curious rather than overwhelmed, because it connected mathematics with something I could observe outdoors. After watching it, I started noticing seed heads and pinecones on walks. It was a worthwhile study break because it left me with a question to think about, not just another clip to scroll past.
part3: In China, many people watch short comedy clips, food and travel videos, livestreams and practical tutorials. Short videos fit into a commute or study break, while longer programmes are popular when viewers want a detailed story. The choice varies by age and interest. I often watch a tutorial when I need to learn a specific tool, because it lets me see the steps rather than just read about them.

Videos are helpful when someone needs to see a process, such as how to use equipment or carry out an experiment. Books are usually better for detailed explanations because readers can pause, review a section and follow a longer argument. I use videos to get an overview, then read when I need accuracy or depth. The more helpful format depends on the subject and the learner's purpose.

Videos are useful for skills that can be shown step by step, such as basic cooking, drawing techniques or using a computer program. A learner can pause, replay a difficult part and compare it with their own attempt. They are less effective when someone needs personal feedback or safety supervision, so a video is often a helpful starting point rather than a complete substitute for practice.

There can be differences in format and subject. Younger viewers often watch short clips about games, music or current trends, while older people may choose longer programmes, news or cooking videos. But personal interests matter more than age: I know older relatives who watch travel clips and young people who enjoy documentaries. Recommendation systems also shape what each group sees.

There may be differences in what some young men and women choose, but I would not treat them as fixed rules. Friends, personal interests and online recommendations often shape viewing habits more than gender. One group might share sports clips while another shares fashion videos, but plenty of people enjoy both. It is better to ask about someone's interests than assume from their gender.

A video can spread quickly when its idea is easy to understand and prompts a strong reaction, such as laughter, surprise or sympathy. A useful tip may also be shared because viewers want to help someone else. Timing and platform recommendations matter, but they cannot make every clip popular. People are more likely to pass it on when it feels original, short enough to watch and relevant to their friends.

answers.part2: One activity I do regularly but often regret is scrolling through short videos when I am tired. Because the next video starts immediately, I can lose half an hour without remembering much of what I saw. It happens more often when I have been studying for several hours and want an easy way to switch off. I have started putting my phone across the room and setting a short timer when I need a break. That does not stop me every time, but it makes me notice the choice instead of scrolling automatically. I would rather use the time for a walk or a proper rest, which leaves me feeling more refreshed. The timer does not make me productive every minute, but it helps me choose when to stop instead of losing track of time. I still watch clips for fun; I just try to do it deliberately. The difference is whether I feel rested afterwards or annoyed that I have put off something important. A short break is still useful, but I feel better when I decide its length before opening the app.
part3: People may ignore rules when they see them as unfair, confusing or impossible to follow. Others take risks because they assume the rule will not be enforced or because convenience matters more in the moment. Clear explanations and practical ways to comply can improve cooperation. Enforcement may be necessary, but it works best alongside trust; a rule that treats people inconsistently is likely to lose respect.

People often feel pressured by deadlines, financial responsibilities, family expectations and the sense that they must keep up with others. Students may face several assignments at once, while parents balance work and care. Pressure is not always harmful; a clear short-term goal can motivate someone. It becomes a problem when demands continue without enough control, rest or support.

It depends on what I mean by a waste of time. I may keep watching a short comedy clip because a brief break helps me relax, even though it is not productive. If I notice that I have been scrolling for half an hour and feel no better, I try to stop and move on. Enjoyment is worthwhile, but I need to notice when a habit stops being enjoyable.

I try to protect time for sleep, exercise and people close to me instead of filling every free hour with work. During a busy week, I set a clear stopping time and choose the most important tasks first. That is not always possible near a deadline, but I can recover afterwards. A realistic routine is more sustainable than expecting perfect balance every day.

A routine is useful because it reduces the number of small decisions people need to make and helps them protect time for sleep, study or exercise. My weekdays are easier when I know when I will work on coursework. A routine can become restrictive if every hour is fixed, though. It should provide structure while leaving room for rest and unexpected plans.

A manageable amount of pressure can help people prepare for an exam or meet a deadline, so it can give a task a sense of urgency. Too much stress for too long affects sleep, health and concentration. I would say pressure is useful only when people also have enough support and recovery time. Short breaks can help restore a sense of control.

answers.part2: A food my family often eats on a special occasion is dumplings during the Spring Festival. We usually make them together at home on New Year's Eve. Someone chops cabbage and mixes it with minced pork, spring onions and seasoning, while the rest of us spoon the filling onto round wrappers and fold the edges closed. We buy the wrappers from a local market, but prepare the filling ourselves. My grandmother checks that the dumplings are sealed before we put them into boiling water. When they rise to the surface, we take them out and serve them with vinegar. Everyone has a slightly different folding style, so the preparation is lively rather than exact. One year my uncle hid a coin in a dumpling, and the person who found it became the subject of jokes for the rest of dinner. The dish is special because several generations take part, from preparing the filling to setting the table. Dumplings are available at other times of year, but making them together has become part of how our family welcomes the new year. I enjoy the unhurried work and conversation as much as eating them. The familiar taste also reminds me of relatives who taught me how to fold them when I was younger.
part3: Special foods help mark an occasion and bring people together around a shared custom. In China, families often eat dumplings during Lunar New Year because preparing and sharing them is part of the celebration. Some foods also carry symbolic meanings, such as wishing someone good luck. The recipe may change over time, but eating it together helps people feel connected to family and tradition.

Everyday food is usually chosen for convenience, cost and nutrition, so it tends to be familiar and quick to prepare. Festival food may take longer to make and is often shared with relatives as part of a tradition. In China, dumplings are associated with the Spring Festival, while mooncakes are linked to the Mid-Autumn Festival. The special dish helps people recognise the occasion and feel connected to family.

Yes. People today have wider access to food from different countries and can order meals quickly, while previous generations relied more on seasonal ingredients and home cooking. Work patterns have also changed how often families eat together. Traditional dishes have not disappeared, but convenience foods are more common. The difference is partly about choice and partly about how much time people have.

It depends on the occasion and a person's schedule. Eating at home is usually cheaper and gives people more control over ingredients, while restaurants offer convenience and a chance to socialise. Many families do both: they cook on ordinary weekdays and eat out when they celebrate or want a break from preparing food. Budget and working hours often decide what is practical.

answers.part2: I watched an interview with Chinese novelist Yu Hua, whose novel To Live I had read in translation. The interviewer asked how the writer turns ordinary memories into fictional characters. He explained that he keeps notes about conversations and places, then combines details instead of copying one real person directly. I was interested because I had always imagined writers began with a complete plot, whereas he described collecting small observations first. I liked hearing about the decisions behind the books, not just seeing the writer promote a new release. Afterwards, I looked up one of his earlier essays and noticed how carefully he described ordinary settings. part3: People should dress neatly and choose clothes that suit the workplace, rather than assuming every interview requires a formal suit. The main aim is to look respectful and professional without letting the outfit distract from the conversation.

Interviews allow employers to hear how a candidate explains their experience and responds to questions, which is difficult to judge from a CV alone. Both sides can decide whether the work and working style are a suitable match.

People should read about the organisation, understand the main duties and prepare a few examples that show how they have handled relevant tasks. It is also useful to practise concise answers and plan the journey so they arrive on time. They should prepare questions about the role rather than memorise a script. That preparation makes it easier to speak naturally and judge whether the job is right for them.

Some people see interviews as a waste of time when questions are repetitive or the employer has already made a decision. Applicants may spend hours travelling or preparing and then receive no feedback. A well-run interview is still useful because both sides can discuss expectations and working style. Clear questions and a prompt response make the process feel respectful and worth the effort.

Some people dislike interviews because they feel nervous when they are being judged or find it uncomfortable to talk about their achievements. Others have had an unfair experience where questions seemed unrelated to the job. A structured interview with clear expectations can reduce some of that pressure. Candidates should have a chance to give examples and ask questions, rather than being expected to perform perfectly under stress.

People are interviewed when someone needs to understand their experience, views or suitability for a particular role. Job applicants are the most familiar example, but journalists also interview experts, witnesses and public figures. Researchers may speak to participants to learn about their experiences. The questions should fit the purpose and treat the person fairly. An interview is useful because it lets people explain details in their own words.
