The chapters were short, so I could read a little before bed without losing track of the story. Reading a few pages each night made it easy to keep the story with me between study sessions. I finished it over about two weeks. The characters made mistakes and changed their minds, which felt more believable than a perfect friendship. One scene made me laugh: the main character prepared a serious apology, but her neighbour's dog ran off with the note before she could deliver it. I enjoyed the book because its humour softened a difficult situation without pretending that an apology fixes everything immediately. By the end, the two friends had started speaking honestly again, and I felt cheerful and relaxed rather than weighed down by the week's work. The story also reminded me of a time I had misunderstood a friend and cleared it up by talking. I recommended the novel to a classmate who wanted something warm to read over the break. It was not a major literary discovery, but finishing it left me in a noticeably better mood.
part3: Readers in China enjoy a broad range, including novels, practical nonfiction, history and online fiction. The popular choice depends on age and free time; some people read short stories on their phones during a commute, while others prefer a printed book at home. Online platforms make new writers easier to discover. A book becomes widely read when its subject connects with people's interests or daily concerns.

No, people do not need to read the book first. A film can stand on its own, and watching it may encourage someone to read the original afterwards. Reading first gives more detail and lets people imagine the characters before seeing an actor's interpretation. I prefer whichever format suits my time and interest; comparing the two can be enjoyable, but it should not feel like homework.

Success books can be useful when they offer practical ideas or examples that readers can adapt to their own lives. They are not a formula, because people's goals, resources and responsibilities differ. Some books also make success sound easier than it is. I would take one useful suggestion and test whether it works for me, rather than assume that following every step guarantees the same result.

People may read fewer printed books, but they still read messages, articles and other material on screens every day. The bigger difference may be that attention is divided between short posts and longer writing. Some people read less for pleasure because work and entertainment compete for time. Libraries and digital books make reading accessible, so habits vary more than a simple decline suggests.

Reading on a phone is often broken into short periods by alerts and other tasks, so people may find it harder to concentrate on a long book. Printed reading may have declined for some, but people still read messages, articles and work documents. The main change may be attention and format rather than reading disappearing altogether.

Movies are easier for some people because images, music and acting tell the story without requiring long periods of reading. They can also be watched together, which makes them a social activity. Books give readers more detail and room to imagine characters for themselves, though they take more time. I do not think one is better; people choose the format that fits their mood and attention.

Parents can make books easy to reach, read aloud together and let children choose subjects they are genuinely curious about. A regular bedtime story can make reading feel like time together instead of homework. It is also useful for children to see adults reading for enjoyment. If every book is followed by a test, children may focus on getting the answer right rather than enjoying the story.

title: 近期改变
prompt: Describe a change that you made recently
cues: What you did for the change
And explain how you feel about the change
questions: Do you think it is good to change one’s daily routine?
Do you think it is good to change jobs?
Is it good for people to get a job promotion?
Do people often make plans around their regular routines?
Who tend to change their daily routine more, young people or old people?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: Recently I moved my most demanding study sessions from late at night to the morning. I made the change during a busy semester when I was finishing coursework and preparing for exams. After midnight, I was rereading the same page and making careless mistakes, so I tried doing one difficult task before my first class instead. The night before, I now choose a specific exercise, put the relevant notes on my desk and set a realistic start time. For example, I might work through a proof before breakfast and leave routine review for the afternoon. I do not schedule an early session after a late night, because that would make the routine hard to maintain. During the first week, I sometimes wanted to turn off the alarm, but finishing one problem before class helped me see a concrete benefit. I now concentrate better in the morning and have more relaxed evenings, although the routine does not work on days when I have an early lecture. I feel less rushed because I no longer depend on a long late-night session to make progress. It is a modest change, but it has made my study time more dependable, so I plan to keep it next semester.
part3: A routine is worth changing when it no longer supports someone's needs. For example, studying earlier in the day may help a student who is too tired to focus late at night. Changes do not need to be dramatic; trying one adjustment for a week gives useful evidence. If a routine already works well, there is no reason to replace it just for novelty.

Changing jobs can be a good decision if someone has stopped learning, is underpaid or needs a healthier working environment. It can also bring uncertainty, so people should consider savings, responsibilities and the quality of the new offer first. I would not change just for novelty, but staying in a poor fit indefinitely is not ideal either.

A promotion can be positive if it brings recognition, better pay or a chance to develop new skills. It may also involve longer hours, more pressure or less time with colleagues doing work someone enjoys. The title alone does not guarantee greater satisfaction. People should consider the responsibilities and support attached to the role before deciding whether it suits them.

Yes. People often schedule plans around work, classes, meals and family responsibilities because those routines take up much of the day. A student might arrange exercise after lectures or meet friends on a free evening. Weekends allow more flexibility, but regular commitments still shape them. Planning around a routine makes activities easier to keep up over time.

Young people often change routines more because they move between education, new jobs and different social groups. Older adults may have a more settled schedule, although retirement or health changes can alter it significantly. These are general patterns, not rules. A person's responsibilities and circumstances matter more than age alone. Some routine is helpful, but everyone needs room to adapt when life changes.

title: 近期改变的计划
prompt: Describe a plan that you had to change recently
cues: What made you change the plan
And how you felt about the change
questions: Do people often change their plans?
Would you tell others if you change your plan?
Why do you think parents still make plans for their children nowadays?
How does technology help people make plans?
What kind of plans do people often make?
Do you think people like the process of making plans more, or the moment of carrying them out?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: Recently, my group had to change the plan for a presentation in one of my final-year mathematics courses. We intended to meet in person the day before presenting, but one teammate became ill and could not travel to campus. We moved the discussion online and reassigned the sections so the essential analysis would be finished first. Our teammate sent us the notes he had prepared before becoming ill, which helped us understand what he had already completed. We used a shared document to mark which slides needed revision and agreed not to add new material unless it was essential. I checked in with him later so he could review the section with his name on it without having to attend the meeting. That kept the work fair while allowing him to rest. I took responsibility for explaining our data because I already knew how we had cleaned it. We also agreed on a time to stop editing, which kept us from making last-minute changes all night. The new version had fewer slides than we had planned, but each person still contributed and the main result was clear. I felt stressed when the original plan fell through, then relieved once we divided the work. It taught me to leave room for changes and to tell the group early when something is not going to work.
part3: Yes, plans often change when the weather, work or other people's schedules shift. Students may move a group meeting because someone has a deadline, for instance. A plan is helpful, but it should not become so rigid that a small change causes stress. I try to keep the main goal clear and adjust the timing when new information makes the original arrangement impractical.

Yes, especially if the change affects their time or preparation. I would explain as soon as I knew, rather than wait until the last minute, and suggest another option if possible. For a casual personal plan, a short message is enough. In group work, I would also clarify which tasks need to be reassigned so everyone knows what to do next.

Parents make plans because they want to give their children security and access to opportunities, especially around education and health. They may arrange lessons or save for university because those decisions involve time and money. The risk is planning every hour and leaving no room for the child's own interests. Support is helpful, but children also need a say in choices that shape their lives.

Calendar apps and shared documents help people keep deadlines, appointments and group tasks in one place. A reminder is useful when several classmates need to meet around different schedules. Technology also makes it easy to change a plan and tell everyone quickly. It cannot decide what matters most, though, so people still need to review priorities rather than follow every notification automatically.

People commonly plan study or work tasks, trips, family events and how to manage their money. Some plans cover only the next day, while others involve a career or a move to another city. Planning helps people see what needs to happen first, but it should leave room for changes. I find a weekly study plan useful as long as I can adjust it when new work appears.

Some people enjoy planning because it lets them imagine possibilities and feel prepared; others prefer acting, since progress becomes visible only once they begin. I like making a basic plan for study, but I get more satisfaction from finishing the work. Planning can become an end in itself if someone keeps adjusting details. A useful plan should make action easier, not delay it.

title: 遇到的科技问题
prompt: Describe a challenging technological problem you faced
cues: When and where you faced it
And explain how you solved it
questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of AI?
Do you think people today should learn about AI technology?
Should children learn to use AI?
How can AI help in our lives?
Do you think students are overly reliant on AI?
What can teachers do to stop students relying too much on AI?
What can teachers do to stop students from relying too much on AI?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A technology problem I remember happened just before a group presentation in a university classroom. My laptop would not connect to the projector, although the slides looked normal on my screen. The projector showed a "no signal" message, and the rest of the group was waiting while our classmates began to arrive. I checked the cable and display settings, then restarted the laptop, but neither step worked. We did not have time to search for another cable, so a classmate checked the classroom computer and found a saved PDF copy of our slides. We opened it, tested the first few pages and began the presentation only a few minutes late. I checked the title and first graph against our notes to make sure we had opened the correct file. I was tense because I was responsible for explaining our results, but I felt relieved once the backup worked. After class, I connected my laptop to another screen and discovered that a recent update had changed its display setting. That explained why it had worked in the previous lesson. The problem was challenging because I had to keep the group moving while troubleshooting, not because the solution was complicated. Since then, I test the projector before an audience arrives and keep important files in both editable and PDF formats.
part3: AI can process information quickly, automate routine tasks and help people generate ideas. However, it may produce inaccurate answers, reflect bias in its training data or make people less willing to check sources. It can also affect jobs that involve repetitive work. I see it as a useful tool when a person understands its limits and remains responsible for decisions, especially where accuracy or fairness matters.

Yes, people should understand the basics of AI so they can use it carefully and recognise its limits. Students and workers may encounter AI tools in ordinary tasks, from translation to data analysis. They do not all need to become programmers, but they should know that outputs can be inaccurate or biased. Basic digital judgement is now part of being an informed user.

Children should learn what AI can and cannot do before relying on it for schoolwork. They need to check facts, protect personal information and understand that a confident answer may still be wrong. A teacher can demonstrate how to compare an AI response with a reliable source. The aim is informed use, not teaching every child to build AI systems or encouraging them to avoid the technology entirely.

AI can help people with routine tasks such as organising a schedule, translating a basic message or summarising a long document. In education, it can offer another explanation when a student is stuck. It is most useful when it saves time without replacing judgement. I would still check important information against reliable sources, because a fluent answer can sound convincing even when some details are wrong.

Some students rely on AI too much when they submit answers without checking them or use it to avoid practising difficult skills. Used carefully, it can explain a concept in another way or help organise revision. The key is whether the student can still solve a similar problem independently and explain the reasoning in their own words.

Teachers can design tasks that require students to explain their reasoning, discuss sources and show how they reached an answer. In a mathematics assignment, for example, students could compare an AI-generated solution with their own working and identify an error. Clear rules about when tools are allowed also help. Simply banning AI may be hard to enforce and misses a chance to teach responsible use.

Teachers can set tasks that require students to explain their reasoning, check sources and connect ideas to class discussions, rather than submit an AI answer unchanged. They can teach students to compare the tool's claims with reliable material and discuss where it may be wrong. A blanket ban is hard to enforce. Clear rules and assessment of the student's process encourage responsible use.

title: 重要决定
prompt: Describe an important decision that you made
cues: What the results of the decision were
And explain why it was important

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: One important decision I made was to focus on statistics and data analysis alongside my mathematics degree. In my second year, I enjoyed theoretical courses but wanted to understand how mathematical ideas could answer practical questions. I chose the optional statistics course and began learning basic programming so I could work with real data. It took extra effort because I had to explain results in plain language as well as calculate them correctly. I compared the course outlines and asked a lecturer what each option involved before enrolling. A later group project gave me practical experience: I cleaned a public data set, checked unusual values and presented our conclusion to the class. During the presentation, classmates asked about one chart, so I revised its labels and explained the result more clearly the next time. After the course, I could use a short Python script to check the data rather than calculate each entry by hand. I did not give up pure mathematics; I added another direction to explore before graduation. The decision mattered because it turned a general interest in applications into skills I could build on. I felt reassured that I had tested the subject before making a larger commitment, and I am more confident about the careers I might pursue.
part3: Yes, children sometimes need to make decisions about friends, activities or how to respond when something feels unfair. Adults should guide them and explain likely consequences, but making every choice for them prevents them from learning. The level of responsibility should match their age; a child can choose an after-school club, while a serious health or safety decision needs adult involvement. Practice builds confidence gradually.

After graduation, teenagers may choose a university, vocational training, a first job or a gap period. The decision matters, but it does not determine their entire life because people can change direction later. They should compare the cost, their interests and the opportunities available, then talk to someone with relevant experience. Parents can advise them, but the young person should have a real voice in the choice.

Children can ask parents or teachers because those adults know them and can explain possible consequences. For a school subject or activity, a teacher may understand the options better; for a family matter, a parent may have more context. A trusted older sibling can also be approachable. Adults should help children think through a choice rather than immediately make it for them.

Yes, adverts can make a product familiar and draw attention to features or discounts. A clear demonstration may help someone discover an item they genuinely need. However, repeated claims or celebrity endorsements can also encourage impulse purchases. I try to compare the price, quality and independent reviews before buying, especially when the product is expensive. Advertising informs me, but it should not make the decision for me.

Advertising can be useful when it gives people clear information about a product, its price or a new service. It also helps businesses reach customers. The downside is that repeated or misleading adverts can encourage people to buy things they do not need. I think its influence is positive when claims are honest and easy to verify, and harmful when emotion is used to hide important facts.

People usually gather information, compare likely outcomes and think about what matters most to them. For a university choice, someone might compare the course, cost and distance from home, then ask current students about their experience. There is rarely a perfect option, so setting a deadline can prevent endless delay. Advice helps, but the person who will live with the result should make the final decision.

title: 钦佩的运动员

cues: What he/she is like in real life
questions: Why are there so few top athletes?
What is the most popular sport in your country?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: A successful sportsperson I admire is the Chinese badminton player Chen Yufei. I first followed her during the Tokyo Olympic Games in 2021, when she won the women's singles gold medal. What I remember from that final is how composed she looked in the longer rallies, even when the score was close. I have never met her, of course, but interviews give me the impression that she is thoughtful and grounded rather than interested in showing off. She has spoken about the hard training behind her results, and I respect that she keeps working through pressure instead of expecting talent to do everything. Winning Olympic gold is a remarkable achievement, but I also admire the discipline needed to reach that level over many years. As someone who plays badminton casually, I notice how quickly a player has to decide where to move and how much energy to save. Watching her made me more interested in the strategy of the sport, not just the final score. I would not assume I know her personality from television, but the way she discusses training and competition seems sincere. Her success motivates me to practise patiently, even when progress in my own studies or sport feels slow.
part3: Very few people reach the top because it takes a combination of talent, years of structured training, good coaching and strong physical and mental health. Access to facilities and financial support also affects who can continue. Many talented athletes face injuries or other responsibilities before reaching elite level. Success is not only individual ability; it also depends on the system that supports people along the way.

Football is probably the most widely followed sport in China, especially during major international competitions. Basketball also has a large following, and badminton is common as a recreational activity. Football's popularity comes partly from its global profile and the excitement of supporting a team. However, what people play most often may differ from what they watch, depending on local facilities and friends.

Some talents are visible early, such as a strong interest in music or sport, but it can take time to recognise others. A quiet child may be good at careful observation or helping classmates, which is less obvious in a competition. Adults should offer children different activities and notice what they enjoy and practise. Early labels can be limiting, so opportunities matter more than deciding a talent too quickly.

Talent can give an athlete an early advantage, but practice, coaching and discipline are essential for long-term performance. Someone may have natural speed yet struggle if they do not train consistently or work well with a team. Access to good facilities also matters. I think talent helps people start, while effort and support often determine how far they progress.

An athlete needs discipline, resilience and the ability to learn from a coach, as well as physical ability in their sport. They have to practise consistently and recover properly after setbacks or injuries. In team sports, communication and cooperation matter too. Natural talent can help someone begin, but long-term progress depends on good habits and staying focused when results are disappointing.

Yes. Physical education gives students regular movement, teaches basic skills and can help them manage stress after lessons. It also lets children try sports they may not have access to outside school. Not every student is competitive, so classes should include different activities and focus on participation as well as performance. Schools need safe facilities and enough choice for students with different abilities.

Why are some young people keen on being fans of superstars?

Do you think it is necessary to be ambitious when working in a team in a company?
Should parents support their children in pursuing their ambitions?

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: One long-term goal I have is to become a data analyst who can explain evidence clearly enough to support practical decisions. I have been thinking seriously about this for about two years, since a statistics assignment showed me that the same data can lead to different conclusions if it is interpreted carelessly. I do not expect to reach the goal immediately after graduation. I would first like to learn how teams collect and validate information, then gradually take on projects where I have to present findings to non-specialists. That progression gives me clear skills to work on now. During that assignment, I checked the data for missing entries and wrote a note explaining one limitation. Seeing how those small checks affected the conclusion made the work feel useful beyond the calculation itself. I am finishing my mathematics degree now and building my programming and communication skills. After graduation, I hope to begin in an entry-level role, learn from experienced colleagues and take responsibility for larger projects over time. I know the exact industry may change as I gain experience, so I am focusing on skills that transfer across fields. I chose this goal because I enjoy both careful calculation and asking what a result means outside a textbook. Reaching it would not just mean getting a job title; I would want to produce analysis that other people can understand and use responsibly.
part3: A society should aim to give people access to education, healthcare, safety and fair opportunities, while protecting the environment for future generations. These goals are connected: it is difficult to study or work well when someone lacks stable housing or basic medical care. Economic growth matters, but it should improve people's lives broadly rather than benefit only a small group. Progress should include quality of life, not just income.

Goals can give people direction and help them decide how to use their time. A student might set a goal to finish a degree or improve a skill, then break it into manageable steps. Goals should be flexible, though; circumstances and interests can change. I think they are useful when they guide choices without making people feel that one missed target means they have failed.

Many people in their early twenties want to finish their education, find work that suits them and become more financially independent. Some also hope to travel or build a stable relationship, although priorities vary. For me, completing my mathematics degree and gaining practical experience are important next steps. People often revise their goals as they learn more about themselves, so a useful plan should leave room to change direction.

Yes, children need guidance because they are still learning to judge risks and think through consequences. Advice is most useful when adults explain the reason and listen to the child's response, rather than simply giving orders. For a small choice, like joining a club, parents can help compare options and let the child decide. That builds judgement instead of dependence.

Young people often aim to finish their education, find work they can develop in and become more independent. Some also want to travel, support their family or build a creative project. Goals vary with money, health and opportunity, so it is unfair to assume everyone wants the same career. A useful goal gives direction but can change as someone learns more about what suits them.

People can make a goal manageable by turning it into smaller steps, setting a realistic schedule and checking progress regularly. If someone wants to work in data analysis, they might first improve spreadsheet skills and complete a small project. Feedback helps them adjust their plan. Persistence matters, but so does changing methods when they do not work. A goal should guide effort rather than become a source of constant pressure.

Ambitions can help children imagine possibilities and stay interested in learning, even if their plans change later. A child who wants to be an engineer might become curious about building and mathematics. Adults should encourage that curiosity without expecting the child to make a final career decision too early. Ambition is useful when it gives direction and hope, not when it becomes pressure to achieve a particular status.

Seeking a senior position can be positive if someone wants greater responsibility and is prepared to develop the skills it requires. The role may also bring higher pay and a chance to influence decisions. However, status alone is a weak reason to pursue it, because management can involve stress and difficult conversations. People should consider whether the work itself suits them, not only the title.

Young people may admire a superstar's talent, style or success and feel part of a community of fans. Following someone can also provide entertainment and a shared topic with friends. Social media makes it easy to see updates and join discussions. It becomes less healthy if a fan spends beyond their means or treats the celebrity's public image as a complete picture of their private life.

Ambition can motivate someone to learn, take responsibility and keep going after a setback. It becomes unhealthy when success matters more than relationships, health or fair treatment of others. A person can aim high while staying open to a different route. I admire ambition most when it is connected to genuine interest and steady effort, rather than only a desire for status.

Ambition can help an employee take responsibility and look for ways to improve, but it should not come at the team's expense. In a project, people need to share credit and help colleagues meet the common goal. Someone can be motivated without competing for every promotion. A healthy workplace recognises individual progress while making sure people cooperate and communicate openly.

Yes, parents should encourage their children's interests and help them explore realistic ways to pursue them. That might mean finding a class, discussing costs or connecting them with someone in the field. Support does not mean guaranteeing success or choosing the path for them. Children need room to change their minds as they learn what the work actually involves.

I keep a few old things if they have a clear memory attached, such as photographs or a small gift from a friend. I do not want to store everything, so I usually keep items that still feel meaningful.

Only if an item has a clear memory attached, such as a photograph or a gift from a friend. I do not like keeping everything because it makes a room cluttered. The memory matters more to me than the object itself.

I have kept a few old photographs and a small notebook from secondary school. They are not valuable objects, but they remind me of classmates and routines I might otherwise forget. I do not keep everything; I choose items with a clear memory attached.

part1: Yes, I use a computer almost every day for coursework. A laptop is much more comfortable than a phone for writing proofs, checking data and joining online meetings. I would also use a tablet for reading, but it would not replace my laptop.

I use a laptop when I need to write an assignment, analyse data or follow a lecture online. For checking a message or reading a short article, my phone is enough. The task and how long I need to focus determine the device.

I first used a family computer in primary school, mainly to play simple games and type short homework assignments. I remember needing both hands to find the right keys. Later, school projects taught me how useful it could be for research.

Without computers, my coursework would take longer because lecture notes, research papers and data tools are mostly online. I could still read books and write by hand, but collaborating with classmates would be less convenient. I would manage, though.

It would be difficult if the battery were dead and I had no charger, or if the internet failed during an online task. On the move, a phone is easier to carry. For detailed work, though, I need a proper keyboard.

part1: Yes, for a meal or a study session. My apartment is not very large, so I would invite a few close friends rather than organise a big gathering. We could order food, talk comfortably and avoid the noise of a crowded cafe.

Yes, I have a friend from secondary school whom I have known for several years. We do not meet every week now, but we can pick up a conversation easily when we do. Keeping in touch feels natural because we have shared so many ordinary experiences.

I usually meet one or two close friends after class for a meal or a walk. We talk about coursework, family and what we might do after graduation. It is a simple way to keep in touch during a busy semester.

answers.part2: A person I met only once recently was a volunteer at a community event near my university. I was helping direct visitors last month when a family with a young child looked unsure about where to go. part3: It is usually better to avoid intrusive questions about income, health, relationships or politics until you know the person and understand what they are comfortable discussing. Being on time, listening carefully and showing genuine interest usually makes a better impression than trying to sound impressive. A true friend is dependable, listens without immediately judging and can be honest when something needs to be said. Trust grows through small actions repeated over time, not grand promises.

Shared interests make it easier to start a conversation and spend time together, but they are not essential for a lasting friendship. What matters more is whether both people listen and make an effort to stay connected.

People often make friends when they meet regularly around a shared activity, such as starting school, joining a club or working on a project. A new class or workplace creates an easy reason to speak, while celebrations and trips can bring people together more casually. The occasion may start the connection, but friendship usually grows through repeated contact and trust. Not everyone becomes close immediately, and that is normal.

In China, people often make friends through school, university, work, shared hobbies or introductions from relatives and classmates. Students may become closer by eating together after class or cooperating on group assignments. Online groups can help people find others with the same interest, but meeting regularly usually builds stronger trust. The way people connect is changing, although spending time together remains important.

sources.file: 2026年9-12月最新雅思口语题库终版-0920(3)(4).pdf

answers.part2: I once lost my student card in the main library while moving between a printer and the study area. I only noticed when I reached the entrance gate and could not tap in. I retraced the route from the printer to the entrance, checking the floor and the places where I had put my papers. I asked the students sitting near the printer if they had seen it and gave the receptionist my name and course in case it had been turned in. The library staff checked their lost-property box and asked me to describe the card before returning it, which made me realise they handled these situations regularly. I also froze the card's payment function in the campus app while I searched. That precaution made me calmer because losing it would not affect my account. A receptionist had found it beside the queue and kept it behind the counter, so I got it back within about ten minutes. I felt anxious while I was searching because the card also lets me borrow books and enter some campus buildings. After I found it, I put it in a zipped pocket instead of carrying it loose with receipts. The experience was not serious in the end, but I was surprised by how quickly a small mistake disrupted my routine. Now I check for my card before leaving a library or classroom.
part3: People often feel frustrated or worried after losing something, especially if it contains money or personal information. They may replay their recent movements and blame themselves, which does not always help. It is better to check likely places calmly and contact the venue. If a bank card or phone is missing, protecting the account should come before finding the object itself.

A simple routine helps: keep keys and cards in the same place, check a seat before leaving and avoid carrying more than necessary. Labels or a tracking function can help with valuable items, although privacy settings matter. I try to put my student card in one pocket every time. Small habits are more reliable than assuming we will remember everything when we are rushed.

Anyone can lose things, but it is more likely when someone is tired, rushing or trying to manage several tasks at once. People may also misplace belongings in crowded places where they keep moving between queues or seats. I would not describe them as careless by nature; a busy day can distract almost anyone. Slowing down briefly before leaving often makes a difference.

On balance, yes, but the details matter. People are less likely to lose something when they have a consistent place for it and check before leaving. A labelled lost-property desk at a station gives the owner a clear place to ask and the finder a safe way to return it. Rewards can help, but clear reporting and protecting personal information matter just as much.

Most people retrace their steps and check the places they visited most recently. If they lost something in a shop or station, they can ask staff or contact lost property. For a phone or bank card, they should lock it or cancel access quickly. Posting online may help, but they should avoid sharing personal details that could let someone misuse the item.

People commonly lose small everyday items such as keys, travel cards, earphones and umbrellas because they take them in and out of bags. Phones and wallets are less easily replaced, so losing them causes more concern. Items are often left on public transport or in cafes when someone is distracted. Keeping essentials in one consistent pocket or compartment makes them easier to check.

answers.part2: Linear algebra was one of the most impressive courses in my mathematics degree. I took it in my second year, and most classes combined a short lecture with examples we worked through at the board. For one assignment, we had to show how a matrix transformation affected a set of points and then explain the result in words. I enjoyed comparing my diagram with the formal proof because each showed a different side of the same idea. The course was challenging, but the structure helped me see what each definition was for. We studied matrices and vector spaces, but the lecturer also used diagrams to show how a transformation could stretch or rotate a shape. At first I found the proofs difficult, so I worked through examples with classmates and asked about steps I could not justify. Later, I recognised the same ideas in computer graphics and data analysis, which made the subject feel connected to other fields. The course impressed me because it rewarded understanding rather than memorising a sequence of calculations. One assignment required us to explain a method in writing, and I realised that a correct result is not enough if nobody can follow the reasoning. I still use that lesson when I present mathematical work: I try to make the assumptions and each step clear.
part3: History helps us understand how present-day institutions, borders and social attitudes developed. It can also show how decisions made under pressure created consequences that lasted for generations. Learning about a local event, for example, can explain why a neighbourhood has a particular character. History does not give a perfect guide to the future, but it helps people question simple explanations and recognise patterns.

People need to remember appointments, deadlines, household tasks and small details such as keys or travel cards. A calendar or a consistent place for important items can reduce the effort of keeping everything in mind. I use reminders for university deadlines but avoid recording every minor task. The aim is to support memory, not fill the day with alerts that become easy to ignore.

Yes, reminders, calendars and searchable notes can help people manage appointments and retrieve information. For learning, spaced quizzes and digital flashcards can encourage regular review. But storing an answer is not the same as understanding it, so people still need to practise recalling ideas without looking. Technology works best as support for active learning. It can also reduce anxiety about forgetting routine tasks.

Digital calendars and reminder apps can store dates and tasks, so people do not have to keep every detail in mind. Searchable notes are also useful for finding information later. However, relying on reminders without understanding the material is different from learning it. I think technology supports memory best when people use it to review and practise.

They help in different ways. Photos bring back the appearance and feeling of a moment quickly, while words can record names, reasons or details that are not visible in a picture. For a trip, I might take a photo and write one sentence about why the place mattered. Combining the two gives me a fuller memory than relying on either one alone.

Many people value objects that remind them of a person or an important time, such as a photograph, a ticket or a handwritten note. The object may have little resale value, but its story makes it meaningful. People differ in how much they keep; some prefer a few important things, while others save many mementos. The personal connection matters more than the object itself.

Memory differs because of attention, sleep, practice and the way people connect new information with what they already know. A student who reviews a formula by using it in several problems may remember it better than someone who reads it once. There are natural differences too, but habits matter. Good memory is not only a fixed talent; people can improve how they learn and recall.

answers.part2: A city I would like to visit again is Hangzhou, where I spent three days with my family last summer. The lake was especially peaceful in the early evening, when the light changed and local people came out for a walk. I would return for a few more days and spend a morning at a local museum before taking the metro to a residential district for dinner. On the first trip, we stayed near the lake and only saw a small part of the city. part3: Governments can improve safety by maintaining roads and public spaces, enforcing fair laws and making emergency services easy to reach. Safety measures need regular review so they do not restrict people's rights unnecessarily. Good design and prevention can often solve a problem before punishment is needed.

Cities change as populations grow and people's needs shift. New housing, shops and transport links can make daily life more convenient, while older areas may be renovated or replaced. In my city, new buildings have appeared around busy roads, but green space has not always kept up. Change is useful when it improves residents' lives and preserves the places that give a neighbourhood its identity.

I would not say one group is naturally friendlier. In a small community, people may recognise their neighbours more often, while city residents have more interactions with strangers and may keep to themselves. That can create different habits rather than different personalities. Whether people are welcoming depends on the situation and the individuals, so I would avoid judging friendliness by where someone lives.

No, it is very unlikely that everyone will move to cities. Some people prefer rural life, and farming, energy and environmental work require people outside urban areas. Cities also have limits in housing, transport and water supply. More people may move to urban areas for jobs and education, but balanced regional development can reduce pressure on a few large centres.

Large cities can suit older people when they have good hospitals, accessible transport and nearby shops, but crowds and high living costs may be difficult. Smaller towns can feel calmer and make it easier to know neighbours, though specialist services may be farther away. There is no single best place. Safety, family support and the older person's own preferences should guide the choice.

Cities usually offer more jobs, universities, hospitals and public transport, but they can be crowded and expensive. The countryside often has more open space and a closer connection to nature, while services may be farther away. These are broad differences rather than rules; smaller towns can combine some advantages of both. The contrast also depends on the size of the town.

answers.part2: A change that saves me time is preparing the main materials for a study session before I sit down to work. Technology saves time when it automates repetitive tasks or makes information easier to find. Online banking and digital calendars are good examples. Technology saves time by automating repetitive steps and making information easy to retrieve. A calendar can organise deadlines, while a spreadsheet can calculate figures that would take longer by hand. Parents can help children learn to use time sensibly by showing them how to prepare for school, break a task into steps and leave time for rest. The goal should be independence, not filling every minute with planned activity. A child can practise packing a bag the night before, for example. Parents should guide them while allowing room for play and their own choices.

Good time management makes it easier to meet commitments and protect time for important work, so it can support success. It is not enough on its own: people also need skills, opportunities and sometimes support from others. A student who plans revision can use study time more effectively, but an unrealistic schedule will not help. The useful habit is setting priorities and adjusting when circumstances change.

Yes, simple time-management habits can help children balance homework, rest and activities without feeling rushed. They might use a short checklist or decide which assignment to start first. Adults should teach them to estimate time and leave breaks, rather than schedule every minute. The skill is useful because it helps children become more independent as schoolwork grows.

Schools can teach students to break a large assignment into stages, estimate how long each will take and set an earlier personal deadline. Teachers can show how to use a weekly planner and review it after a project. Students need practice, not just advice to 'be organised'. Schools should also coordinate major deadlines where possible, because time management cannot solve an unreasonable workload on its own.

answers.part2: An app I use regularly is a calendar and task manager on my phone. I discovered it after a classmate showed me how she tracked deadlines when several of our assignments overlapped. I downloaded it during my first year at university and now check it each evening and before the start of a new week. I have kept using it throughout my degree. I add exam dates, group meetings and short reminders about what to bring. For a large assignment, I break the work into a few smaller tasks so I can see what needs attention first. The weekly view is useful because I do not have to keep every date in my head, but I avoid adding every small activity or the screen becomes another source of noise. I still use paper for longer study plans because a phone can tempt me to open unrelated messages. The app has helped me miss fewer deadlines, although it cannot decide which task matters most. I like it because it supports a routine without turning planning into a complicated project. I found it through a classmate, but I have adjusted the reminders to suit my own habits. It is practical precisely because I can keep it simple.
part3: Younger people often try new apps quickly and use several for messaging, entertainment and payments. Older adults may prefer familiar apps, especially if menus change frequently or instructions are difficult to read. These are broad tendencies, not rules; confidence and experience matter as much as age. App designers should make basic tasks clear and provide support, so people do not need to be technically confident to use essential services.

Some people dislike apps because they worry about privacy, find the menus confusing or receive too many notifications. Others prefer speaking to a person when a service is important, such as banking or healthcare. Apps can save time, but poor design may make simple tasks frustrating. Companies should explain how data is used and offer another way to get help, rather than assuming everyone wants to do everything on a phone.

Messaging and short-video apps are widely used in China, along with shopping, payment and map services. People rely on them for everyday tasks because several useful functions can sit in one place. Their popularity also reflects habit: friends and businesses are already using the same platforms. Convenience is a major reason, although people still need to manage screen time and protect personal information.

People keep these apps because they save time on routine tasks and connect them with services their friends already use. A payment app, for example, can settle a bill in seconds, while a map helps someone compare routes. Convenience is the main reason, although people still need to protect personal information and control screen time.

Parents should set reasonable limits, especially for younger children, but the rules should depend on what the child is doing. A time limit can protect sleep and homework, while educational software may be useful for longer. It helps to agree on the rules together and keep devices out of the bedroom at night. A complete ban is difficult to maintain and does not teach children how to manage screen time themselves.

Some limits are sensible because long sessions can displace sleep, exercise and homework. Parents can set a clear daily window, agree on a stopping time and keep devices away during meals or bedtime. The rule works better when children understand the reason and have other activities available, rather than feeling that games have been banned without discussion.

Yes, many young people rely on apps for maps, schedules, study materials and keeping in touch. They are convenient, but dependence becomes a problem if someone cannot make a simple plan without notifications or loses access when a device runs out of battery. Schools can teach practical digital habits, such as checking information and keeping an offline copy of important work, rather than telling students to avoid apps altogether.

A complete ban may protect younger children from harmful content and pressure to compare themselves with others, but it is difficult to enforce and may stop them learning how to use social media safely. I would prefer age-appropriate limits, parental guidance and stronger privacy settings. Schools can teach digital judgement as well. Children need protection, but they also need to build responsible habits gradually.

answers.part2: I once attended my cousin's birthday dinner with my parents and younger brother, but I did not enjoy the music at the venue. part3: People enjoy a range of music events today, from large pop concerts and festivals to small live-house performances and classical concerts. Yes, basic music education helps children listen carefully, notice rhythm and experience making something together. It does not need to lead to professional training; singing or trying a simple instrument can be enough. Some students may discover a lasting interest, while others gain confidence and enjoy the activity. Schools should make lessons welcoming rather than judge every child by performance.

Young people may follow current pop, hip-hop or electronic music through short videos, while older listeners often return to songs they heard when they were younger. That is a general pattern, not a rule; taste depends on personality and social circles. Music can also bring generations together when a family shares a song. New styles appear, but people of every age enjoy both familiar and unfamiliar sounds.

In China, people can attend pop concerts, music festivals, classical performances, folk music shows and smaller local gigs. Large concerts are common in major cities, while universities often hold inexpensive performances by student groups. Traditional instruments are also featured at cultural events. The range depends on where someone lives, but online platforms make it easier to discover local performances and buy tickets.

Music can make exercise feel less repetitive and help people keep a steady pace, especially during a run or workout. Some choose energetic songs to improve their mood, while others listen to something calm when stretching. It is not suitable for every activity, because people need to hear instructions or traffic in some settings. The choice depends on safety and the kind of exercise.

At home, people can choose the volume, pause the music and listen whenever it suits them. A concert offers stronger sound and the energy of a crowd, so even familiar songs can feel new. It also costs more and requires travel, whereas home listening is convenient. I would listen at home most days, but go to a concert for an artist I particularly like.

title: 为家人骄傲

answers.part2: A time I felt proud of a family member was when my younger cousin completed a difficult professional qualification. She had been studying after work for months and often used weekends to review material she found challenging. Before the final assessment, she was nervous but had made a realistic plan and practised with sample questions. When she passed, our family had dinner together and she explained which parts had been hardest. I was proud not only of the result but of how steadily she worked without letting one poor practice test discourage her. Her success made the qualification feel like the end of a long effort rather than a lucky moment. It reminded me that supporting someone through the process can be as meaningful as celebrating the final result. At dinner, she described how she had rearranged her shifts to attend evening classes, and our aunt brought the notes she had used to quiz her. The table was noisy, but she could finally laugh about the practice tests that had worried her. I felt proud to have seen the months of preparation turn into a qualification she could use at work, and glad our family had time to celebrate together.
part3: Parents may feel proud when children make a sustained effort, treat others well or handle a setback with more independence. Good grades can be one reason, but they are not the only measure of progress. A child who admits a mistake and tries to fix it may show maturity that a test score cannot capture. Pride is strongest when it recognises the person, not just the result.

Parents can reward children when the reward recognises effort or a meaningful improvement, rather than every routine action. A small treat after a child has practised something consistently can encourage them, but praise and time together also matter. Parents should explain what they are recognising, so children understand the behaviour. Rewards work best as one form of encouragement, not the main reason to act well.

Rewards can recognise effort, but parents should avoid making every routine task depend on a prize. They could praise persistence or agree on a modest reward for a longer goal, while also helping the child notice their own progress. That way, encouragement supports responsibility instead of teaching children to expect payment for every small action.

Rewards can encourage a child when they recognise real effort, but giving one for every small action may make the child expect a prize before helping. Praise and a chance to feel capable are also powerful. I think rewards work best when they are occasional and proportionate, with the reason explained. Children should learn that responsibility and kindness matter even when no reward is offered.

Frequent rewards can make a child focus on the prize rather than the effort or responsibility involved. They may also expect something in return for every ordinary task. A reward can be useful for recognising a genuine improvement, but praise, encouragement and a chance to try independently are important too. The response should fit the child's age and effort.

Adults may feel proud after completing a difficult project, learning a new skill or supporting someone through a hard period. The achievement does not have to be public; keeping a promise to yourself can matter just as much. For example, finishing a degree while balancing other responsibilities can represent years of steady effort. Pride is most meaningful when it reflects something the person values.

Rewards may encourage a child to practise, especially when a new task feels difficult, but they do not automatically build lasting motivation. A child who reads only to earn a prize may stop when the reward disappears. Specific praise and helping the child notice their progress can work alongside occasional rewards. The goal is for them to value the skill itself, not just what they receive.

Working hard can help children learn, but doing it only for grades may make them anxious and less curious. A student might memorise a method for an exam without understanding when it is useful. Teachers and parents should recognise improvement and clear thinking as well as marks. Grades matter for some opportunities, but they should be feedback rather than a child's only reason to study.

part3: Children can help with age-appropriate chores, such as tidying their room, setting the table or looking after a pet with an adult's guidance. Yes, children can do age-appropriate chores such as putting away toys, setting the table or sorting laundry. People looking for a job often need practical feedback on their CV, interview practice and information about what the role is really like. It depends on the problem. Colleagues are often the right people for a work task because they understand the system and can offer practical advice. Yes, simple chores can teach children to take responsibility for a shared home and look after themselves. Tasks such as clearing a table or putting away laundry are appropriate when matched to the child's age. Asking for help should be seen as responsible when someone has already tried to solve the problem.

title: 别人帮助解决问题

part3: Schools can help children develop their abilities by offering challenging work, useful feedback and different ways to explore a subject. part3: Big cities usually have extensive public transport, large hospitals, universities, shopping centres and a wide range of cultural venues. Modern cities often suit young people because universities, jobs and public transport are concentrated there. A famous city can bring high housing costs, crowded public spaces and a large number of tourists, which may make ordinary errands less convenient for residents. Tourism is easier to live with when visitor numbers are managed and neighbourhood needs are considered.

I would choose a city with a long history if I had time to explore, because older streets and buildings show how people's lives changed. A well-developed city may be more convenient for transport and services, so it can suit a shorter work trip. The two qualities can exist together. My choice depends on whether I want to learn about a place or simply move around efficiently.

It is usually a mixture. Some people choose a city because it offers work, education, cultural events and services they enjoy. Others move because their field has few jobs elsewhere or their family needs access to a hospital or university. People may want the opportunities but not the expense or pace. Their reasons can change as work and family circumstances change.

A city is more liveable when planners protect ordinary neighbourhoods and keep housing, schools and healthcare accessible, rather than focusing only on attractions.

It depends on what travellers want from the visit. A modern city may appeal to people interested in shopping, new architecture and convenient transport, while a historical city offers older streets, museums and local stories. Some cities combine both. I would choose a historical destination when I have time to explore, but a modern one can be easier for a short business trip.

title: 发挥想象力
prompt: Describe a time you needed to use your imagination
cues: Why you needed to use imagination
How difficult or easy it was
And explain how you felt about it
questions: Do you think adults can have lots of imagination?
Do you think imagination is essential for scientists?
What kinds of jobs need imagination?
What subjects are helpful for children's imagination?
What games help develop children's imagination?
How important is imagination to children?

answers.part2: Last September, during orientation week, I used my imagination to help plan a welcome activity for new students in my department. We wanted people to talk to classmates they did not know, but a standard round of introductions felt awkward. I suggested a campus puzzle in which small groups followed clues to familiar places and worked out the route together. One clue described the building with the large clock, while another pointed to the courtyard where students often eat lunch. The challenge was making the clues interesting without assuming that newcomers already knew the campus. I asked two students outside our organising group to test them, and they misunderstood one reference, so I rewrote it in clearer language. On the day, groups found the locations in different orders and compared their guesses at the end. Some teams took a longer route, but everyone finished without feeling lost. One group used a different landmark and still reached the same place, which made the puzzle feel more like play than a test. I felt pleased when I saw students chatting while they worked, because the activity gave them a reason to cooperate without putting anyone on the spot. It was more difficult than I expected to imagine how a first-year student would interpret each clue, but solving that problem made the event more welcoming.
part3: Yes, imagination is not limited to children. Adults use it to design products, solve work problems and picture different ways a project might develop. They may have less unstructured time, and experience can make them cautious, but those limits do not remove creativity. A scientist, for instance, needs to imagine an explanation before testing it against evidence. Practice can keep that ability active.

It is important because scientists need to propose explanations that are not obvious from the first set of results. They then test those ideas through observation or experiments, so imagination alone is not enough. For example, a researcher may consider several reasons for an unexpected result before designing a way to compare them. Creativity helps generate questions; evidence determines which answers hold up.

Imagination is useful in design, advertising, research and teaching, but it can help in almost any job. A scientist may picture a different explanation for a result, while a designer imagines how people will use a product. Creativity still needs practical limits and evidence. It is not only about producing art; it also helps people find a new approach when a familiar method is not working.

Art and music give children space to experiment, while science and language lessons can also encourage them to ask questions and invent explanations. The teaching method matters more than the subject title: an open-ended task invites more ideas than copying a single answer. Children benefit from having time to try something, make mistakes and revise it. A mix of subjects helps them see problems from different angles.

Building blocks, role-play and drawing games can all encourage imagination because children make choices and invent their own rules. A simple set of blocks might become a bridge, a shop or a space station. Some video games also allow players to design worlds, although too much screen time is not ideal. The important part is leaving room for a child to create rather than only follow instructions.

Imagination helps children explore possibilities, practise empathy and solve problems in a playful way. When they invent a story, they have to think about what different characters might do. It can also make learning more engaging. Children still need facts and routines, but creative play gives them a safe space to test ideas. Adults can encourage it by asking questions instead of correcting every unusual answer.

title: 喜欢画画的孩子
prompt: Describe a child who loves drawing/painting
cues: Who he/she is How/when you knew him/her
And explain why you think he/she loves drawing/painting
questions: What is the right age for a child to learn drawing?
Why do most children draw more often than adults do?
Why do some people visit galleries or museums instead of viewing artworks online?
Do you think galleries and museums should be free of charge?
How do artworks inspire people?
What are the differences between reading a book and visiting a museum?

answers.part2: I have known my younger cousin since she was born, and I began noticing her love of drawing when she was about six. Now she draws three or four times a week, usually at the dining table with coloured pencils and a small notebook after finishing her homework. Rather than copying a picture exactly, she changes the colours or adds a background she has invented herself. One afternoon she drew our family dog as a detective, complete with a tiny hat and a magnifying glass. She spent a long time adding details but did not get upset when one line went wrong. Her parents put a few drawings on the wall, which seems to encourage her without turning it into a competition. I enjoy watching her work because drawing gives her a quiet way to express ideas and notice small things. She showed me the finished detective dog and explained why she had drawn each detail. I liked that she was making choices for herself rather than trying to copy a perfect picture. Drawing gives her a quiet activity she can return to, and the stories she adds make each page feel personal to her. She sometimes gives a drawing to a relative, then remembers exactly which part that person liked best.
part3: There is no single right age. A child can start drawing as soon as they enjoy holding a crayon and making marks, and the activity should remain playful at first. Adults can offer safe materials and encouragement without correcting every picture. As children grow, they may learn techniques if they are interested. The main goal is to let them explore ideas, not to produce technically perfect art.

Children often draw more because they have more unstructured time and are less worried that the result must look realistic. Drawing lets them invent characters or describe an experience before they have the words for it. Adults may stop because work takes up time or they judge their ability too harshly. If adults treat it as a relaxing activity rather than a test, they can enjoy drawing too.

Seeing art in person lets people notice its real size, texture and detail, which a screen may flatten. A gallery also gives visitors a quiet place to concentrate and compare works in the same setting. Online images are more convenient and let people explore collections from home, but they cannot fully recreate the experience. Many people use both: online to discover art and galleries to see it closely.

Public museums should ideally offer free entry to their main collections, so cost does not prevent families or students from learning. Special exhibitions may charge a modest fee because they can be expensive to organise. Museums still need funding for staff and conservation, so governments or sponsors can help cover the cost. Free access is valuable when it is paired with stable support for the institution.

Art can inspire people by showing a familiar subject from an unexpected point of view or expressing an emotion they recognise. A painting may make someone notice the colour and light in an ordinary street, while a sculpture can prompt questions about shape and space. People respond differently, so inspiration is personal. It can encourage someone to create something themselves or simply look at daily life more carefully.

A book lets someone explore a subject at their own pace and return to details later. A museum offers objects, images and displays that make history or science feel more tangible. For example, reading about an old tool is different from seeing its size and wear in person. Books are easier to access, while museums can make a strong impression. The two forms often complement each other.

title: 坏掉的电子设备
prompt: Describe a time when you had a problem with using an electronic device
cues: And explain how you solved the problem at last
questions: Why are people keen on buying new electronic devices?
What impact do electronic devices have on people?

answers.part2: I had a problem with my wireless earbuds on a train journey last winter. They had worked the day before, but when I tried to use them, only one side connected and the other kept flashing. I first checked the battery and switched off Bluetooth on my laptop in case the earbuds were reconnecting to it. Then I removed them from the laptop's saved devices and tried pairing them with my phone, but the same side kept flashing. The train was leaving in about twenty minutes, so I looked up the reset instructions in the manual I had saved. I held the button on the case for a few seconds, waited for both lights to flash and paired them again. This time both earbuds connected. I played part of the lecture to check that the sound was clear in both earbuds before putting them away, then packed them before the train reached my stop. I was relieved because I had downloaded a lecture in advance and could listen without using mobile data. Later, I cleaned the charging contacts and tested them at home to make sure the fix had worked. The issue has not returned. I learned to check a device's basic settings before assuming it is completely broken.
part3: People may want a faster device, a better camera or features that make work and entertainment easier. Advertising and frequent product launches also create pressure to upgrade, even when an older model still works. I would replace a device when it no longer meets a real need, rather than simply because a newer version is available.

Devices make communication, study and many daily tasks quicker, and they give people access to information wherever they are. At the same time, constant notifications can interrupt concentration and long screen use can affect sleep. The effect depends on habits: setting boundaries and choosing when to check a phone can preserve the benefits. Different users may experience both sides in one day.

title: 完美工作
prompt: Describe a perfect job you would like to have in the future
cues: What you need to learn to get this job
And explain why you think it is a perfect job for you
questions: What kind of job can be called a ‘dream job’?
What jobs do children want to do when they grow up?
Do people’s ideal jobs change as they grow up?
What should people consider when choosing jobs?
Is salary the main reason why people choose a certain job?
What kind of jobs are the most popular in your country?

answers.part2: My ideal job would be as a data analyst working on practical questions in education, health or public services. I first learned about this role at a careers talk at my university, where an alumnus explained how analysts turn records into evidence for decisions. I would spend part of the week checking data and asking whether a pattern is meaningful, then explain the result to colleagues who are not specialists. A typical day might include a short meeting to understand the question, time to clean and analyse the data, and a discussion about what the results can and cannot show. I would not want to sit alone with a spreadsheet all day; speaking with the people who use the findings would help me understand the context. To get this job, I need to build stronger programming and data-visualisation skills, and practise explaining uncertainty in plain language. I would value a manager who gives clear feedback and trusts staff to organise their work. It would suit me because I like moving between careful calculations and conversations about what a result means. I would find the work worthwhile if my analysis helped a school or clinic decide where to direct limited resources, even when the answer was less simple than expected.
part3: A dream job is different for each person, but it usually combines work they find meaningful with conditions they can sustain. Some value a creative role, others want stability or time for family. For me, a job using data to solve practical problems sounds appealing because it connects with my mathematics degree. Salary matters, but a job should also suit someone's strengths and priorities.

Children often mention visible jobs such as doctor, teacher, police officer or athlete because they have seen those roles in daily life or on television. Their answers can change as they meet new people and learn what a job involves. I think adults should take the interest seriously without asking a child to decide too early. Curiosity is more useful than a fixed career plan at that age.

Yes, people's idea of an ideal job often changes with age and experience. A teenager may focus on interest or status, while someone supporting a family might place more weight on stable hours and income. Work experience can reveal what kind of environment suits them. That does not mean people give up their ambitions; they may redefine success to fit their responsibilities and values.

People should consider what tasks they enjoy, what skills they have and whether the working conditions fit their lives. Salary and job security matter, but so do commute time, opportunities to learn and workplace culture. Someone choosing between two roles could speak to people already doing that work. A good decision balances practical needs with the kind of life the person wants outside work.

Salary is important because people need to cover housing, food and family expenses, but it is rarely the only factor. Some also consider job security, location, working hours, colleagues and whether the work feels meaningful. A high salary may not compensate for constant stress. People usually weigh these factors differently according to their stage of life and financial responsibilities.

In China, many young people aim for jobs in technology, healthcare, education, finance or government because these fields can offer stable prospects and room to develop. Popular choices change with the economy, and people do not all value the same things. Some prefer a secure salary, while others look for flexibility or meaningful work. A job's reputation is only one part of whether it suits someone.

title: 对家庭重要的东西
prompt: Describe something important that has been kept in your family for a long time
cues: And explain why it is important to your family
questions: What things do families keep for a long time?
What’s the difference between things valued by people in the past and today?
What kinds of things are kept in museums?
What’s the influence of technology on museums?
What are the benefits of technology for learning history?
Why do people visit museums?

answers.part2: My family has kept an old recipe notebook for about thirty years. My grandmother started writing in it when she set up her first home, and she gave it to my mother when my grandparents moved to a smaller flat. My mother has kept it in our kitchen ever since, and both of them still add corrections or notes. My grandmother still corrects a measurement when she remembers a better way to make a dish. Knowing that different people have added to it over the years is part of why we want to preserve it. She wrote down dishes she made for relatives, sometimes adding a note about who liked a particular version. Some pages are stained, and the measurements are not always exact, so my mother asks her to explain the steps when she cooks from it. The notebook has no financial value, but it carries handwriting and small corrections that no printed recipe would have. When we prepare one of the dishes, relatives often remember learning it in the same kitchen years ago. I think it matters because it connects a practical family habit with people and occasions we might otherwise forget. I would like us to keep using it rather than storing it away. Each time someone adds a clearer measurement or a new note, the book becomes a record of the family changing together.
part3: Families often keep photographs, jewellery, letters, recipe books or furniture that belonged to an older relative. These things may not be expensive, but they carry memories of people and occasions. My family has kept a handwritten recipe notebook because it reminds us of meals prepared together. Objects stay meaningful when someone explains their story and passes that story on to younger family members.

People in the past often valued objects that were difficult to replace, such as handmade furniture, tools or family photographs. Today, digital devices and online files are part of daily life, and people may replace them more often as technology changes. The difference is partly practical: production and storage have changed. Emotional value still matters, though, which is why people keep both old objects and digital memories.

Museums keep objects that help explain a subject or a period, such as tools, clothing, artworks, documents and archaeological finds. Some also collect recordings and photographs, which show how people lived rather than only what leaders did. Curators have to protect fragile items and provide context so visitors understand why they matter. A small ordinary object can be as revealing as a famous artefact.

Technology helps museums explain objects through audio guides, digital maps, short films and interactive displays. Visitors can zoom in on details or explore a collection online before travelling. These tools are useful for people who need different ways to access information. However, screens should support the exhibits rather than distract from them. A well-designed display answers a question and helps visitors notice the real object more carefully.

Technology can make history easier to picture by showing old maps, timelines, recordings and digital reconstructions of places. Students can compare sources online and access material that is not available in their local library. This makes learning more interactive, but the information still needs to be checked for accuracy and context. Used well, technology helps learners investigate evidence instead of simply memorising dates.

People visit museums to learn about history, art or science in a way that feels more direct than reading a short summary. Seeing an object in person can make its size, material and age easier to understand. Museums also offer activities for families and school groups. A good exhibition tells a clear story and gives visitors enough context without overwhelming them with dates and labels.

title: 微笑的场合
prompt: Describe an occasion when many people were smiling
cues: And explain why most people were smiling
