questions: Do you think people who like to smile are more friendly?
Why do most people smile in photographs?
Do women smile more than men?
Why?
Do people smile more when they are younger or older?
Is smiling important in your culture?
Are there any occasions when people need to pretend to smile?

answers.part2: Last winter, many people were smiling at a family dinner after my cousin completed a demanding qualification. Relatives came to a small restaurant, and she arrived carrying the certificate she had been waiting for. People congratulated her, but the happiest moment came when an uncle told a funny story about her studying at the kitchen table as a child. She laughed because the story was exaggerated, then corrected two details while everyone else added their own memories. The atmosphere was warm rather than formal, and even relatives who had not spoken much began joining the conversation. I felt pleased because the celebration recognised the work behind her result, not only the certificate itself. People were smiling for different reasons: my cousin was relieved, the older relatives were proud and the children were amused by the story. One of them asked to hold the certificate while we took a family photo, and my cousin laughed when he nearly covered her name with his thumb. My aunt recorded the moment and sent the photograph to our family chat that evening. My aunt captured that moment on her phone. I liked that nobody had to follow a formal schedule; everyone felt comfortable joining the conversation. The smiles came from celebrating her effort together, not from posing for a camera.
part3: A smile can make someone seem approachable, but it does not prove they are friendly. Some people smile because they feel nervous or want to be polite, while others are warm but have a more serious expression. I would pay more attention to how someone listens and treats people over time. First impressions matter, but they are only a small part of judging character.

People often smile in photographs because they want to look friendly and show that they are enjoying the moment. In a group picture, one person's smile can encourage everyone else to join in. Some people smile automatically because they know a camera is pointed at them, even if they feel tired. The expression can be genuine or simply a social habit, depending on the occasion.

They may appear to in some settings, but I would be careful about making a general claim. Social expectations can encourage women to smile to seem friendly, while men may be discouraged from showing certain emotions. The difference also depends on the situation and personality. In a relaxed conversation, people of any gender smile when they feel comfortable or amused.

It is difficult to say that one gender smiles more by nature. Social expectations can encourage women to appear warm and approachable, while men may be expected to look more serious in some settings. Personal temperament and the situation matter a lot. I would avoid interpreting someone's expression without considering the context and their usual manner.

It is hard to say that one age group smiles more in every situation. Children may show excitement more openly, while adults sometimes control their expressions because of work or social expectations. Personality and the setting matter as much as age. A quiet older person can be very happy, so I would not use smiling alone to judge someone's mood.

A smile is a common way to show warmth or politeness, especially when greeting someone or thanking them. Still, people do not smile in every situation, and a serious expression is not necessarily unfriendly. The meaning depends on context and personality. I think being respectful matters more than displaying a particular expression, although a genuine smile can make a first meeting feel easier.

Yes, people sometimes smile politely in a formal photograph, at work or when greeting someone even if they are tired. It can make an interaction smoother, but constantly hiding genuine feelings can be exhausting. I think a brief polite smile is normal; people should not be expected to look cheerful in every situation. The setting affects how sincere an expression feels.

title: 想从事的短期海外工作
prompt: Describe a short-term job you want to have in a foreign country
cues: And explain why you want to do it
questions: What short-term jobs do young people do in other countries?
What challenges do young people face when working abroad?
What are the benefits of working for an international company?
What personal skills are required to work in an international company?
What kind of work can young people do in foreign countries?
Why are some people unwilling to work in other countries?

answers.part2: A short-term job I would like to try abroad is a summer research assistant position in Singapore. I found the position on my university's careers website, which lists summer placements with partner universities. The role would involve helping a team organise data or check calculations, so it connects closely with my mathematics degree. Working in another country would also give me a chance to use English in everyday conversations, not only in class. I expect the first few weeks would be challenging, especially learning a new team's routines and getting used to the city. Still, a short placement would feel manageable because I could focus on one project and return to my studies afterwards. I would want a supervisor who explains expectations clearly and gives interns a chance to ask questions. Even if the work were mostly basic, seeing how an international research group shares ideas would be valuable experience for me. A month in Singapore would let me contribute to one defined research task and learn how people from different academic backgrounds discuss evidence. I would also have to manage everyday tasks, such as asking for clarification and finding my way around, in English. I would like to try that kind of independence before considering a longer move abroad.
part3: Young people abroad may take seasonal work in tourism, hospitality, agriculture or language support, depending on their visa and skills. Some also join internships or short research placements related to their studies. These jobs can provide income and experience, but applicants should check the contract, accommodation and legal requirements. A short placement is most useful when the work offers learning as well as a chance to see another country.

Young people working abroad may face a language barrier, unfamiliar workplace expectations and the stress of arranging housing or transport. Being far from family can also feel difficult when something goes wrong. A clear contract, a supportive supervisor and basic knowledge of local rules help. The first weeks may be demanding, but the experience can build confidence if the worker has a realistic plan and someone to contact for advice.

Working for an international company can expose employees to different markets, colleagues and ways of solving problems. They may use another language, learn how decisions affect customers in several countries and build a wider professional network. That experience can be useful for future roles. It can also involve time-zone meetings and rapid changes, so the benefits depend on whether someone enjoys adapting to different working styles.

Clear communication and adaptability are essential because colleagues may have different first languages and expectations. Employees also need to listen carefully, explain their reasoning and check that everyone understands a decision. Reliability matters when teams work across time zones and cannot always meet in person. Technical knowledge is important too, but people who respect cultural differences are more likely to collaborate effectively.

Young people can look for internships, language-assistant roles or temporary work in cafes and hotels, depending on their qualifications and visa conditions. An internship may connect directly with a degree, while seasonal service work can build communication skills and help cover travel costs. Before accepting anything, they should check the contract, pay and accommodation carefully. Legal status and personal safety come first.

Some people do not want to work abroad because they would be far from family, have to adapt to another language or risk losing a stable job at home. Others may not see a clear career benefit for the disruption. Those concerns are reasonable, especially for people with care responsibilities. Working abroad suits some people, but it should be a genuine choice rather than something everyone is expected to do.

title: 想拥有的科技产品
prompt: Describe a piece of technology (not a phone) that you would like to own
cues: And explain why you would like to own it
questions: What are the differences between the technology of the past and that of today?
What technology do young people like to use?
What are the differences between online and face-to-face communication?
Do you think technology has changed the way people communicate?
What negative effects does technology have on people’s relationships?
What are the differences between making friends in real life and online?

answers.part2: I would like to own a lightweight e-ink tablet with a stylus. As a mathematics student, I read lecture PDFs and often need to mark a proof or write a question beside a formula. At the moment I switch between a laptop and paper notes, which is awkward when I am travelling between campus and home. An e-ink screen would be easier on my eyes for long reading sessions, and I could keep course materials in one place. I would want a reliable battery and simple file transfer rather than a lot of entertainment features. I first heard about this kind of tablet from a classmate who uses one to annotate lecture notes. The models I have compared cost roughly two to three thousand yuan, depending on screen size and storage, so I would need to save before buying one. I would test the writing feel in a shop if possible, because a stylus that lags would make it frustrating for equations. That price seems reasonable only if it works well for several years. It is not essential, so I would wait until I could afford a model with good handwriting recognition. The main reason I want it is that it could make my study materials easier to search and carry, not because it is a new gadget.
part3: Technology today is generally smaller, faster and connected to the internet, so one phone can perform tasks that once required several devices. Older equipment was often less connected but could be easier to repair and had fewer distractions. The change has made information and communication more convenient, while raising concerns about privacy and constant notifications. Each period's technology reflects what people needed and could afford at the time.

Young people commonly use smartphones, laptops and wireless headphones for studying, communicating and entertainment. Many rely on messaging apps and video platforms because their friends use them too. Students may also use tablets or software for note-taking and coursework. Preferences depend on budget and interests, but convenience is a major factor. I think young people choose devices that combine several uses rather than buying separate tools for each task.

Online communication is convenient and gives people time to think before replying, but it can be harder to understand tone or notice when someone feels uncomfortable. Face-to-face conversation provides expressions, pauses and immediate feedback, so it is often better for sensitive discussions. I use messages for practical arrangements and talk in person when trust or a detailed explanation matters.

Yes, people can now send a message or share a photo instantly, even across countries. That makes it easier to maintain friendships, but short messages can miss tone and encourage people to reply without giving full attention. I use group chats for practical updates and call a close friend for a serious conversation. The technology has changed the speed and format more than the need to communicate.

Technology can interrupt face-to-face conversations when people keep checking their phones, and short messages can be misunderstood without tone or expression. Social media may also make someone compare their private life with carefully selected posts. Still, it helps distant friends stay connected. The effect depends on how it is used: setting a phone aside during important conversations can protect attention without giving up the benefits.

Online friendships often begin through a shared interest, and people can connect even when they live in different countries. In person, friends share more everyday experiences and can read each other's reactions more easily. Both can become meaningful, but trust online may take longer because people cannot always verify what they are told. I think regular honest conversation matters in either setting.

title: 想见的名人
prompt: Describe a famous person you would like to meet
cues: How you knew him/her How/where you would like to meet him/her
And explain why you would like to meet him/her
questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of being a famous child?
What can today’s children do to become famous?
What can children do with their fame?
Do people become famous because of their talent?
Is it easy to become famous in your country?
Do you want to be a famous person?

answers.part2: A famous person I would like to meet is the writer Yu Hua, whose books I have read in translation. I would like to meet him at a public book event, where I could ask how he decides which ordinary memories belong in a story. I am curious whether he plans a character's development in advance or discovers it while drafting. I might feel nervous at first, so I would prepare one or two questions and then listen rather than trying to impress him. I admire the way his novels describe difficult experiences in clear language without making the people in them seem simple. I first became interested in his work after a friend recommended one of his novels, and I later read another during a university break. A book festival would suit me because the discussion would give the audience some context before questions. I would keep the conversation focused on one question about how a character changes while he is writing. Meeting him would make the books more vivid for me by connecting the finished stories with the decisions behind them. Even a brief conversation would be memorable, and I would not expect special treatment. I would be satisfied with a thoughtful answer rather than a photograph or a long private conversation.
part3: A famous child may gain opportunities, income and access to experiences that other children do not have. However, public attention can affect privacy, friendships and education before the child is mature enough to manage it. Adults may also make decisions for financial reasons. The child's safety and consent should come first, and they should be able to step away from public life without being treated as ungrateful.

Children can become known by developing a skill, taking part in sport or performance, or sharing creative work online with adult guidance. However, fame should not be the main goal of childhood. Public attention can affect privacy and education, and children may not understand the long-term consequences of posting content. Adults should protect them and make sure participation is voluntary.

Children who become famous can use their influence to support a cause, share a talent or encourage others who have a similar interest. They might also save some of their income for education or future plans. But adults should help them manage public attention and protect their privacy. Fame can disappear, so it is important that a child keeps a normal routine and does not feel responsible for entertaining an audience all the time.

Talent can help someone stand out in music, sport or another field, but it is rarely the only reason they become famous. Training, opportunity, timing and media coverage all matter. Some talented people remain unknown because they lack access to an audience, while others become popular through a memorable personality or a widely shared event.

Social media can make it possible for someone to reach a large audience quickly, especially through music, sport or entertaining videos. However, becoming widely known is not the same as building a stable career, and attention can disappear just as quickly. Most people who remain successful need a skill, consistent work and some luck. A large audience is difficult to maintain over time.

Not particularly. Being recognised might create opportunities, but it would also reduce privacy and make ordinary activities more complicated. I would rather be respected for doing useful work within my field than have strangers know my name. A small audience that values what I contribute would be enough for me. I would still welcome recognition from people in my profession.

title: 擅长做计划的人
prompt: Describe a person who makes plans a lot and is good at planning
cues: And explain how you feel about this person
questions: Do you think it’s important to plan ahead?
What activities do we need to plan ahead?
Do you think children should plan their future careers?
Should children ask their teachers or parents for advice when making plans?
Is making study plans popular among young people?
Do you think choosing a college major is closely related to a person’s future career?

answers.part2: A classmate I know is very good at planning group work. I got to know her through a second-year group presentation, when several deadlines were close together. She made a simple timeline, but she also asked everyone how much time their section would realistically take. When one person fell behind, she moved the review meeting instead of blaming them. Her plans make it easier for me to start because I can see the next step, and I have adopted that method for my own assignments. For a presentation, she divides the work into research, drafting and checking, then agrees on an internal deadline before the official one. When we had to revise a set of charts, she moved the checking task earlier so we still had time to review the slides. She checked in briefly rather than messaging constantly, so we could focus on our tasks and still raise problems early. She also left a buffer before the final deadline, which gave us time to correct mistakes without rushing. I felt I could rely on her because she stayed calm under pressure. I like working with her because she makes responsibilities clear without controlling how everyone completes them. Her planning reduces last-minute stress, and I have borrowed her habit of writing down one immediate next step.
part3: Planning ahead is useful for commitments that involve time, money or other people. It helps someone see what needs to happen first and avoid leaving important tasks until the last minute. A group assignment needs early agreement on roles so one person is not left doing everything. Small everyday choices do not need detailed plans, though; flexibility is valuable when circumstances change.

People benefit from planning ahead for activities that involve other people, travel, deadlines or significant costs. A group trip needs transport and accommodation arranged early, while a university project needs time reserved for research and revision. Small daily tasks may not need a detailed plan. Planning is most helpful when a late decision would create stress or limit people's options.

Children can think about what interests them, but they should not be expected to choose a fixed career too early. Trying different subjects and activities helps them discover strengths they may not know about yet. Parents and teachers can explain possible paths without deciding for them. A flexible idea of the future gives children direction while leaving room to change.

Yes, especially for decisions that affect school, safety or family schedules. Parents understand the child's needs, while teachers may know more about academic choices. Children should be able to hear both views and explain what they want. Adults can point out consequences without making every decision for them, so the child gradually learns how to plan independently.

Many students make study plans, particularly before exams or when several assignments are due together. A timetable can help them divide a large task into smaller pieces and avoid leaving everything until the last day. Others prefer a looser approach or use reminders on their phones. The method matters less than having a realistic way to keep track of priorities.

It can be related, especially in fields that require specific training such as medicine or engineering. In other areas, a degree develops transferable skills that can lead to several kinds of work. A mathematics graduate, for example, might work in education, finance or data analysis. Students should consider career options, but their major does not determine every job they can do.

title: 最近看过的电视/网络节目
prompt: Describe a TV show/online program you have watched recently
cues: And explain how you feel about it
questions: What are the differences between the TV programs young people like to watch and those old people like to watch?
What makes a popular TV or online program?
What kinds of TV or online programs are popular in your country?

answers.part2: Last week I watched a short online documentary about how green spaces support wildlife in cities. I found it on a nature channel and watched it at home after finishing my evening study. I usually watch a short programme like this about once a week, often when I want a quiet break. The episode followed birds nesting near roads and insects living in small patches of plants between buildings. I had assumed wildlife needed a large park, but the programme showed how smaller planted areas can connect habitats across a city. One sequence followed a bird moving between a roadside tree and a community garden, which made the idea easy to picture. I sent the episode to a friend who enjoys nature, and we compared it with the green strips near our own neighbourhood. I liked the calm filming, but the best part was that it changed what I notice on my usual walk. Now I look for planted spaces that link larger parks instead of seeing each one as an isolated patch. It was relaxing to watch and gave me a practical way to think about city design. I would watch another episode when I have a proper break rather than letting videos run in the background.
part3: Young people often watch short online videos, reality shows and series they can follow on demand, while older viewers may prefer news, traditional dramas or programmes they watch at a fixed time. There is considerable overlap, especially when families watch together. The difference is partly about platform and habit, not only age. People choose content that matches their interests and how much time they have.

A popular programme usually has a clear idea, engaging presenters and episodes that give viewers a reason to return. It might be funny, useful or connected to a topic people are already discussing. Good pacing matters, especially online, where viewers can leave quickly. Popularity also grows when people recommend a programme to friends, but a large audience does not necessarily mean it has lasting quality.

In China, short videos, reality shows, dramas, comedy programmes and practical tutorials all attract large audiences. People choose different formats depending on how much time they have; a short clip fits a commute, while a drama is something to watch in the evening. Online services make it easy to follow a niche interest as well as mainstream entertainment. Trends change quickly as new platforms appear.

title: 有趣/著名的城市
prompt: Describe a city that you think is very interesting/famous
cues: And explain why you think it is very interesting/famous
questions: What advantages can tourism bring to a city?
Why do some young people like to live in cities?
Do most elderly people live in the city or in the countryside?
Do you think well-developed tourism will have negative effects on local people?
What are the benefits of urbanization?
Do you think the big cities in China today will become even larger in the future?

answers.part2: A city I find interesting is Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province, which I visited with friends for a long weekend. I first heard more about it from a travel programme on Sichuan food, then became curious about the city itself. Chengdu is especially famous for Sichuan cuisine and its giant panda research base. We tried local food, visited a museum and spent an afternoon in a park where people were playing mahjong and dancing. The city felt lively but not constantly rushed, and getting around by public transport was straightforward. I noticed how newer shopping areas sit beside older streets and teahouses, so the city did not feel as if it had one single character. We left time between activities and found a small restaurant that was not in our original plan. That unscheduled stop became one of my favourite parts of the trip because it felt more local and relaxed. A teahouse beside a modern shopping centre showed how different routines fit into the same neighbourhood. What I found most striking was how the city shifted from quiet parks to busy markets within a short walk. The visit broadened my impression beyond the spicy food I had first seen on television. I would like to explore a residential district next time and see how the atmosphere differs from the parks and central streets we visited.
part3: Tourism brings customers to hotels, restaurants, shops and cultural sites, which can support local jobs and encourage investment in transport or public spaces. Visitors may also help preserve interest in historic buildings and local traditions. The benefits are less convincing if most income goes to outside companies or residents face rising rents. A city should manage tourism so local people share the gains and everyday services remain usable.

Young people often choose cities because they offer universities, varied jobs, public transport and places to meet friends. Living nearby can make it easier to try different careers and activities. The disadvantages are high rent, crowds and a faster pace. Some people later move to a smaller place when their priorities change. City life is attractive when its opportunities justify the cost and pressure.

Many older people in China live in cities because their children, hospitals and public services are nearby, although some remain in rural areas where they grew up. The pattern varies by region and family circumstances. Older residents may move to a city for care, while others prefer the familiar community and slower pace of their hometown.

It can bring jobs and income, but heavy tourism may raise rents, crowd public transport and make everyday shops cater mainly to visitors. Noise and waste can also affect residents. The impact depends on planning: local people should have a say, and some tourism income needs to support housing, transport and public spaces they use.

Urbanization can bring people closer to jobs, universities, hospitals and public transport. When services are concentrated, governments may provide them more efficiently, and businesses can find workers and customers in one area. Cities also create opportunities for cultural exchange. The benefits depend on planning; if housing and transport do not keep up, congestion and inequality can worsen. Growth works best when people can afford to live near the opportunities it creates.

Some large Chinese cities may keep growing because they offer jobs, universities and transport links that smaller places cannot match. However, high housing costs and congestion could encourage people and companies to move to surrounding cities. Growth may happen across a region rather than only inside one centre. Planning transport and public services early will determine whether that expansion improves people's lives.

title: 有趣的建筑
prompt: Describe an interesting building
cues: And explain why you think it is interesting
questions: What types of buildings are popular in your country?
Is it worth spending a lot of money on the exterior appearance of a building?
Is it more important for a building to look good on the outside or on the inside?
Why do people like to visit historical sites?
Do you think it’s reasonable to charge an entry fee for visiting interesting buildings?
Is it better to live in a new building or an old one?

answers.part2: An interesting building I remember is an old railway station in the historic centre of my hometown, which now serves as a public arts centre. I visited it with a classmate after our exams because we wanted to see a local photography exhibition. From outside, its long brick walls and iron roof looked very different from the glass shops nearby. A narrow ticket window still remained beside the entrance. The roof's ironwork was visible from the central hall. Inside, the original platform beams were still visible, and the old waiting rooms had become small galleries and a cafe. A guide explained that trains once connected the town with nearby villages before faster transport became common. I liked standing in the central hall because its scale still suggested people arriving and leaving, even though visitors now came to see paintings or meet friends. The exhibition showed old photographs of the same streets outside, so we could compare how the area had changed. I also noticed that local families used the cafe, while students sat at tables to work. The building was not preserved as an empty monument; it had a practical role in the community. That combination of history and everyday use made it interesting to me, and I would return for another exhibition.
part3: Apartment blocks are common in Chinese cities because they make efficient use of limited urban land. People also value shopping centres, public libraries and transport hubs that combine several services in one place. In smaller towns, low-rise housing is more common. What becomes popular depends on the cost of land and how people travel; a useful building needs to fit its neighbourhood, not just look impressive.

A building's exterior matters because it affects the street and can make a public space more welcoming, but spending a very large amount only for decoration is hard to justify. Safety, accessibility and long-term maintenance should come first. A thoughtful design can be attractive without using expensive materials. The budget should reflect how the building will be used and how many people benefit from it.

The inside is more important because people need rooms that are comfortable, safe and practical every day. The outside still matters when a building shapes a public street or represents a cultural place. Ideally, the design works well in both ways, but appearance should not come at the expense of ventilation, accessibility or useful space. A building is successful when people enjoy using it, not only photographing it.

Historical sites let people see details that are difficult to picture from a textbook, such as the scale of a building or how a street was laid out. Visitors may also feel connected to local stories and earlier generations. A guide or museum display can make the visit more meaningful. Some people go for architecture or photographs, but the strongest impression often comes from understanding how the place was used.

An entry fee can be reasonable when it pays for maintenance, staff and conservation, especially at a historic site. It should remain affordable, and students or local residents could receive discounts. Some public buildings should be free because they provide a community service. The decision depends on the site's costs and purpose, but visitors should be able to see clearly how the money supports the place.

A new building usually offers modern wiring, lifts and better insulation, while an older building may have a distinctive layout and a more established neighbourhood. The condition matters more than age: a well-maintained older home can be comfortable, and a poorly built new one can create problems. I would compare safety, transport, cost and natural light before deciding.

title: 朋友自学
prompt: Describe one of your friends who learned something without a teacher
cues: And explain whether it would be easier to learn from a teacher
questions: Is it necessary to keep learning after graduating from school?
Should teachers make learning in their classes fun?
Do you think there are too many subjects for students to learn?
Is it better to focus on a few subjects or to learn many subjects?
Do you think enterprises should provide training for their employees?
Do you think it is good for older adults to continue learning?

answers.part2: A friend from my university society taught himself basic video editing for a welcome project. Our group needed a short introduction for new students, but none of us had used the editing software before. He wanted the video to include captions and short clips from different activities, so he found free tutorials online and practised on a test file. When the first export was too large to upload, he checked the settings and changed the resolution without making the text difficult to read. He asked us to review the draft and used our comments to shorten two sections. I think the project would have been easier with a teacher at the beginning, because an instructor could explain the main tools in order and point out mistakes immediately. However, learning independently suited this small task: he could search for help only when he reached a particular problem and practise at his own pace. By the time we showed the video at orientation, he could make simple edits confidently. I admired his initiative, especially because he tested each technique instead of copying a tutorial without understanding it. For advanced editing, he would probably benefit from a course, but this project showed that a beginner can make useful progress alone.
part3: Yes, because work, technology and people's interests continue to change after formal education ends. Learning does not always mean taking another degree; it can be a short course, reading or asking an experienced colleague for guidance. I expect to keep developing data and communication skills after graduation. Ongoing learning helps people adapt, but it should remain manageable alongside work and family life.

Teachers should make lessons engaging, but fun should support learning rather than replace it. A short game or practical example can help students remember a difficult idea and take part more confidently. Some subjects still require careful practice, so not every class needs to feel like entertainment. A good teacher varies the approach and checks that students understand the material, not just that they enjoyed the activity.

Some students do feel overloaded when they have many subjects, frequent homework and little time to explore any topic deeply. A broad curriculum is useful because children may discover an interest they would not otherwise try. Schools need to balance that range with realistic workloads and time for practice. The problem is not simply the number of subjects, but how much work is expected in each one.

Students need a broad foundation first, because knowledge from different subjects helps them see connections and discover what interests them. As they get older, focusing on a smaller number can give them enough depth to develop useful skills. I would not make the choice too early; a balance between breadth and specialisation is more helpful than treating them as opposites.

Yes, employers should provide training when staff need new skills to do their jobs safely and effectively. It can improve performance and help a company adapt to new technology or regulations. Employees also benefit by gaining experience they can use later. Training works best when it is practical, relevant to the role and followed by a chance to apply what people learned.

Yes. Learning gives older adults a way to stay curious, meet people and keep using their skills. It could be a language class, a computer course or something enjoyable like local history. The purpose does not have to be getting a qualification or finding a job. Classes should be accessible and welcoming, so people can learn at a comfortable pace without feeling judged.

title: 机智解决问题的人
prompt: Describe a person who solved a problem in a smart way
cues: And explain why you think he/she did it in a smart way
questions: Do you think children are born smart or they learn to become smart?
How do children become smart at school?
Why are some people well-rounded and others only good at one thing?
Why does modern society need talents of all kinds?
Do you think smart children are happier than other children?
Is it important for schools to identify and develop each student’s talents?

answers.part2: A classmate solved a problem smartly during our statistics project. We were close to the deadline when we noticed that two group members had used different definitions for the same variable. He did not ask everyone to redo the analysis straight away. Instead, he opened the original instructions, traced where each definition came from and checked which one matched the question. Then he listed the charts affected by the difference, so we could correct those results and leave the rest of the work alone. He asked both members to show their sources before settling the definition. He recorded the agreed definition in our shared document so no one would use the old version again. We added a short note to the presentation explaining the change rather than hiding it. I thought this was a smart solution because he separated the source of the error from the work that was still valid. Under pressure, it would have been easy to rebuild everything or choose whichever result looked better. His checklist gave each person a clear task, and we finished on time with a more accurate explanation. I felt reassured by how calmly he handled the disagreement. Since then, when I find a mistake in my own work, I try to check the assumptions first instead of changing several steps at once.
part3: Children may start with different strengths, but experience, teaching and practice have a large effect on how those strengths develop. A child who asks questions and receives patient feedback can make progress in a subject that once seemed difficult. Calling someone naturally smart can overlook the effort behind their achievement. I think ability grows when children get support and opportunities to try.

Children develop their abilities when lessons match their level, teachers give useful feedback and they have room to ask questions. A student may understand a difficult idea after seeing it explained in a different way or applying it to a small project. Practice matters, but so does confidence to make mistakes. Schools should help each child find strengths rather than label some as naturally smart.

People become well-rounded when they have chances to try different subjects and activities, while others focus deeply on one area because it interests them or suits their goals. Family expectations, school opportunities and time all play a role. Neither path is automatically better. Broad experience can help people connect ideas, while specialisation builds expertise; many careers need a mix of both.

Modern society faces problems that cannot be solved by one kind of expertise. Engineers may design a system, but communities also need teachers to explain it, artists to communicate ideas and organisers to make it work. Different strengths help teams see risks that one specialist might miss. A society benefits when it values practical, creative and caring skills instead of treating only a few careers as important.

Not necessarily. A child who learns quickly may enjoy school, but they can also feel pressure to keep getting high marks or struggle to connect with classmates. Happiness depends on relationships, confidence and feeling safe, not only on academic ability. Schools should give bright children suitable challenges while helping them develop interests and friendships outside their strongest subject.

Yes, schools should help students notice what they are good at, whether that is science, sport, art or working with other people. A talent can grow when a teacher gives useful feedback and a chance to practise. Identification should not become a fixed label, because children may develop new interests later. The aim is to open opportunities, not rank students too early.

title: 爱护自然之人
prompt: Describe a person who likes to look after the natural world
cues: How he or she does it
How often he or she does it
And explain how you feel about this person
questions: Do you think parents should teach their children how to protect the environment?
What laws about the environment are effective in your country?
Which do you think people prefer, rewards or punishment, when it comes to government intervention in environmental protection?
Is it easy for children in cities to get close to the natural world?
What can people do to protect the natural world?
Is it important to teach students environmental protection at school?

answers.part2: A person I know who cares about the natural world is a friend who volunteers at a local park. She joined a monthly clean-up after noticing plastic cups and food wrappers along a path she uses for evening walks. During each visit, she collects litter, separates recyclable items and reports damaged bins to the park staff. She brings reusable gloves and bags for the group. She checks that the clean-up area is clear before the group leaves. She also grows native plants on her balcony and gives spare seedlings to neighbours. I joined one clean-up with her last month. We spent about an hour along the riverside path and filled two bags; afterwards, the group sorted the recyclable items for collection. She did not claim that one morning would solve pollution, but explained that a cleaner path is safer for wildlife and more pleasant for everyone who uses it. I like her practical attitude because she acts consistently without blaming individuals for larger environmental problems. Her example has made me more careful about leaving rubbish behind and more willing to take part in community activities. I admire that she makes looking after nature feel manageable: she gives a little time regularly and invites other people to help when they can.
part3: Yes, parents can make environmental care part of ordinary routines, such as sorting waste, saving water and respecting animals outdoors. Children are more likely to follow those habits if adults explain why they matter and do the same themselves. Parents should also show that responsibility is shared; families can make small choices, while companies and governments need to address larger sources of pollution.

The most effective environmental laws are clear, enforceable and aimed at major sources of damage. Limits on industrial emissions can make a measurable difference when factories are monitored and violations lead to meaningful penalties. Waste rules are useful too, but people need convenient collection systems. I would judge a law by whether air, water or recycling outcomes improve, rather than by how strict it sounds on paper.

I think a mix works better than either one alone. Rewards can encourage households or businesses to adopt greener habits, particularly when the change takes effort at first. Serious pollution still needs penalties because a company should not gain financially by ignoring the rules. The government should make the standards clear and apply them consistently. Incentives build cooperation; enforcement protects the public when voluntary action is not enough.

It depends on where they live. Children with a park, school garden or safe walking route nearby can see plants and insects regularly, but some dense neighbourhoods have little green space. Families may need to travel to a larger park at weekends. Schools can help by organising outdoor activities, although city planning also needs to make nature accessible in everyday life.

People can reduce waste, use public transport where possible and avoid disturbing wildlife, but individual action has limits. Local groups can organise clean-ups or report damage, while residents can support businesses that use fewer disposable materials. Governments and companies have greater influence over infrastructure and production, so responsibility should be shared. Small habits matter most when services make the sustainable choice practical and affordable.

Yes, school is a good place to explain how everyday choices connect with larger environmental problems. Students can learn why waste sorting matters, how ecosystems support people and what actions are actually effective. A clean-up or small garden project makes the subject concrete. Lessons should avoid suggesting individuals can solve everything alone; governments and businesses also have responsibility for pollution and resource use.

title: 禁用手机的场合
prompt: Describe an occasion when you were not allowed to use your mobile phone
cues: Why you were not allowed to use your mobile phone
And how you felt about it
questions: How do young and old people use mobile phones differently?
What positive and negative impact do mobile phones have on friendship?
Is it a waste of time to take pictures with mobile phones?
Do you think it is necessary to have laws on the use of mobile phones?
What are examples of good and poor phone manners?
How does the internet benefit people?

answers.part2: I was not allowed to use my phone during a final examination at university. Before the paper began, we had to switch our phones off and leave them in our bags at the front of the room. The invigilator explained the rule before handing out the exam papers and reminded us that even a phone on silent could cause a problem. We were allowed to use the calculator provided by the department, so nobody needed a phone for calculations. I placed my bag where I could see it and then stopped thinking about messages. The clear instructions helped me accept the restriction because everyone had to follow the same procedure. The rule was there to prevent cheating, including looking up information or using a calculator app. At first I felt slightly uneasy because I normally check the time on my phone, but there was a clock above the whiteboard. Once I started answering questions, I forgot about it and concentrated on the exam. The room was quiet, and not receiving notifications actually helped me focus. After the exam, everyone collected their belongings and checked messages in the corridor. I did not miss anything urgent, so the restriction felt reasonable. It reminded me that being without a phone is manageable when the reason is clear and the period is limited.
part3: Young people often use phones for messaging, video, games and social media throughout the day. Older adults may focus more on calls, family photos and practical services, although many are comfortable with apps too. The difference often comes from what someone has learned and needs, rather than age itself. Clear design and patient support make it easier for everyone to use a phone confidently.

Phones make it easy to share plans and check in, especially when friends are busy or live far apart. The downside is that quick messages can replace a proper conversation, and people may feel ignored when someone keeps looking at a screen. I use group chats for everyday updates, but for anything personal I prefer to talk directly.

Not necessarily. Phone photos are a quick way to remember a trip, a family occasion or useful information, and they are easy to share. It becomes a waste when someone spends the whole event framing pictures and barely experiences it. I usually take a few, then put my phone away and enjoy what is happening.

Some rules are necessary when phone use can put people at risk, especially while driving or crossing a busy road. Schools and workplaces may also limit phones during tasks that need concentration. A total ban in every setting would be excessive, because phones are useful for emergencies and learning. Rules should target the situation, explain the reason and allow sensible exceptions.

Good phone manners include keeping the volume low in shared spaces, putting a phone away during a conversation and asking before using speakerphone. Poor manners would be watching videos loudly on a bus or checking messages repeatedly while someone is speaking to you. Context matters: answering an urgent call is understandable, but people should briefly explain and return their attention afterward.

The internet gives people quick access to information, public services, learning materials and communication across long distances. Someone can attend an online class or arrange an appointment without travelling across town. It also helps small businesses reach customers. The benefit depends on access and the ability to judge information, because unreliable sources and scams can make the same convenience harmful.

title: 给别人建议
prompt: Describe a time when you gave advice to others
cues: When it was To whom you gave the advice
And explain why you gave the advice
questions: Should people prepare before giving advice?
Is it good to ask advice from strangers online?
What are the personalities of people whose job is to give advice to others?
What are the problems if you ask too many people for advice?
Why do some people think it is better to ask for advice from friends than from parents?
When would old people ask young people for advice?

answers.part2: I once gave advice to a friend who was unsure whether to enter a public-speaking competition. This happened earlier this year, after she had volunteered to introduce a guest speaker in one of our department events. She enjoyed preparing the introduction but worried that a larger audience would make her freeze. I asked what part made her most nervous before suggesting anything. Once she said it was forgetting her words, we discussed using brief cue cards instead of memorising a full speech. That made my suggestion specific to her concern rather than a general pep talk. She wanted to try, but worried that a mistake in front of an audience would make her look unprepared. I suggested choosing a topic she already knew well and treating the first round as practice rather than expecting to win. I also shared how nervous I had been before a class presentation, so she knew I was not dismissing her concern. She entered the competition and did not win, but afterwards she said she felt more comfortable speaking in front of people. I was glad she tried it, while recognising that it had to remain her decision. I gave the advice because I thought she would regret not trying more than making a small mistake. I learned to offer a manageable first step instead of telling someone what they must do.
part3: Yes, they should understand enough about the situation before offering an opinion. Advice based on one assumption can make a problem worse, even when the intention is kind. Asking a few questions first helps reveal what the person has already tried and what they actually need. It is also useful to make advice optional, because the person facing the decision has the most context.

It can be useful for hearing different experiences, especially when someone has a question they feel embarrassed to ask locally. However, strangers may not know the full situation, and some advice can be misleading or promotional. I would avoid sharing private details, check whether the person has relevant experience and compare reliable sources before acting. Online opinions can inform a choice, but should not make it for you.

People who give advice professionally need to listen carefully, ask clear questions and avoid judging someone too quickly. They should be calm and honest about what they know, while respecting privacy. A counsellor, for instance, cannot make a decision for a client but can help them see options. Empathy matters, but so does knowing when a problem needs a specialist or a different kind of support.

Asking many people can expose someone to useful perspectives, but it can also create confusion because each person has different values and experience. They may delay a decision while trying to satisfy everyone. It helps to choose two or three people who understand the issue, compare their reasons and then decide based on one's own priorities. Advice should inform a choice, not transfer responsibility for it.

Some people ask friends because they feel less pressure and expect them to understand their current life, especially with relationships or study. Parents may have more experience and know the person's history, but their advice can feel protective or old-fashioned. Neither source is always better. People should consider who understands the particular problem and be willing to hear a different point of view.

Older people may ask younger relatives for help with new apps, online services or current trends, because younger people often use those tools more regularly. They might also ask about education or job choices when a family member has recent experience. Advice can go both ways, though. Older adults usually have practical knowledge of their own, so the best conversation shares expertise rather than treating one generation as the teacher.

title: 自行车/摩托车/汽车旅行
prompt: Describe a bicycle/motorcycle/car trip you would like to go
cues: Who you would like to go with
Where you would like to go
When you would like to go
And explain why you would like to go by bicycle/motorcycle/car
questions: Which form of vehicle is more popular in your country, bikes, cars or motorcycles?
Do you think air pollution comes mostly from mobile vehicles?
Do you think people need to change the way of transportation drastically to protect the environment?
How are the transportation systems in urban areas and rural areas different?
Why do more people own and drive private vehicles now?
What do you think of the future of electric cars?

answers.part2: A trip I would like to take is a bicycle ride from my university to a lake on the edge of the city, probably after my final exams in early autumn. I would go with a classmate I often work with; we both spend a lot of time indoors, so a relaxed day outside would suit us. We would leave in the morning, follow a riverside cycle path and stop for lunch in a small town rather than ride at full speed. It should not be too difficult because most of the route is flat, although we would check the weather and avoid the main roads. If we wanted to stay longer, we could lock the bikes and walk around the lakeside before riding back. I like travelling by bicycle because I can notice small things along the way, such as people fishing or shops opening for the day, and I do not have to plan around parking. It would be a manageable challenge, not an extreme adventure, and a good way to celebrate finishing university work. At the lake, we could leave the bicycles at a marked rack, walk to a bird-watching area and find a small cafe for lunch before riding back. I like that cycling gives us a gradual change of scenery and lets us stop safely when something catches our eye. It would make the journey part of the day, not just transport to the destination.
part3: Motorcycles are probably the most common private vehicle in many Chinese cities because they are relatively affordable and easy to park, although electric bikes are especially widespread for short trips. Cars are more common among families who travel longer distances. The balance varies by region and income. Good public transport also affects what people choose, so popularity is not only about personal preference.

Vehicles are an important source of air pollution in busy cities, but they are not the only one. Power generation, factories, construction and heating can also produce emissions, depending on the region and season. Traffic is visible, so people may notice it first. Better public transport and cleaner vehicles help, but governments need to measure all major sources before deciding where policy will have the greatest effect.

People need to use cleaner transport more often, but change should be practical rather than abrupt. Reliable buses, safe cycle lanes and walkable neighbourhoods give people real alternatives to driving. Some rural residents have no convenient public transport, so private vehicles may remain necessary. Governments can encourage gradual changes while improving the infrastructure first; asking people to change without offering another option is unlikely to work.

Cities usually have more buses, metro lines and ride-hailing options because many people travel along the same routes. Rural areas may rely more on private cars or infrequent buses, since homes and services are farther apart. Urban transport can be crowded, while rural journeys may take longer. Investment should reflect local needs instead of copying one system everywhere.

Private vehicles are more common because rising incomes make them affordable to more families, and they offer flexibility when public transport is limited. A car is convenient for carrying children or shopping, while motorbikes suit short trips through crowded streets. The downside is congestion and pollution, especially when many people drive at the same time. Reliable public transport can reduce the need to own one.

Electric cars are likely to become more common as batteries improve and charging points spread. They can reduce exhaust pollution in cities, although their overall environmental impact also depends on how electricity and batteries are produced. For drivers, price, charging time and access to a home charger will matter as much as range. I expect gradual growth rather than every household switching immediately.

title: 花很久时间回复信息
prompt: Describe a time when you received a message or email and it took you a long time to reply
cues: Why you spent a lot of time replying
And explain how you felt about the experience
questions: When do people spend a long time responding to others’ messages?
In what situations do people not respond to messages right away?
What would you do if you haven’t received a reply after sending out a message?

answers.part2: An old school friend messaged me to ask if I could join a reunion dinner and help estimate how many classmates would attend. I saw it while revising for a difficult university exam; because the dinner fell on the same weekend, I needed to check the timetable before confirming. She had suggested two possible evenings, so I compared them with my revision plan and tried to decide whether I could attend without cancelling later. I had turned off notifications to concentrate and intended to reply after finishing a problem set, but the evening ran late and I forgot to reopen the chat. When I noticed it again two days later, I drafted a reply, then changed it because I wanted to explain my uncertainty politely rather than sound uninterested in seeing everyone. By then, the group had booked the table and the dinner had taken place. I apologised and explained what had happened; my friend was understanding, but I still felt embarrassed because silence could sound like a refusal. I was also disappointed to have missed the chance to catch up. Since then, I send a short acknowledgement if I need time to check my schedule, then confirm by a clear time.
part3: People take longer to reply when a message needs a thoughtful answer, such as discussing a disagreement, giving advice or confirming plans with several people. They may also be busy at work or want time to check details before responding. A delay does not always mean they are ignoring the sender. For an urgent issue, a short call is usually clearer than waiting for a detailed text.

People often delay replying when they are in class, working, driving or spending time with someone face to face. They may also want to check a detail before giving an answer. A late reply does not automatically mean they are upset or uninterested. If I need a quick decision, I say when I need it; for an ordinary message, I think it is fair to allow people time.

If a message needed an answer by a particular time, I would state that clearly in a follow-up and explain why it mattered. For something casual, I would leave it for a while rather than keep checking the chat. If the person still did not respond and the plan depended on them, I would make an alternative arrangement. Different people have different habits with their phones.

title: 花费超过预期的物品
prompt: Describe an item on which you spent more than expected
cues: How much you spent on it
And explain why you think you spent more than expected
questions: Do you often buy more than you expected?
What do you think young people spend most of their money on?
Do you think it is important to save money?
Why?
Do people buy things they don’t need?
Do you think it is the rich people’s responsibility to donate money to people in need?
What kind of things are people happy to pay a high price for?

answers.part2: I spent more than I planned on a laptop for my university coursework. I had set a budget for a basic model, but the cheapest options did not have enough memory for the data software I needed. I compared several machines, checked student discounts and chose one with a stronger battery and enough storage. The model cost about six thousand yuan, roughly twenty percent above my original budget. Most of the difference paid for memory and battery capacity, not a fashionable design. I waited a month for a student sale and checked the warranty before buying. I also needed a protective sleeve and an adapter, which made the final checkout higher than the price I had first seen. Those extras were useful, but they were not part of my original estimate. I bought it because I use a laptop every day for assignments and group work, and I wanted it to last through the rest of my degree. I was cautious about spending the extra money, but the decision made sense once I compared the specifications with my actual needs. I learned to consider long-term use as well as the price on the label, while still setting a limit before shopping.
part3: Occasionally, especially when I buy groceries while hungry or add small items to an online order. I try to set a budget and make a list before shopping, which helps me notice when something is an impulse purchase. It does not work every time, but waiting a day before buying a non-urgent item often shows whether I actually need it.

Young people often spend money on food, transport, clothes, devices and social activities. Those still living with family may save more, while students living independently face rent and daily costs. Spending also depends on income and priorities. I think many are willing to pay for experiences with friends, but a budget helps them avoid letting convenience purchases take money away from longer-term plans.

Yes, saving gives people a buffer for unexpected costs and more freedom to make future choices. A student might save for a laptop, while a family may need money for rent or medical bills. The amount depends on income, so advice should be realistic rather than make people feel guilty. Even a small regular contribution can be useful over time.

Savings give people some protection when an unexpected bill or change in income occurs. They can also help someone pay for a larger goal, such as further study or a home, without relying entirely on borrowing. The amount depends on income and responsibilities; even a small, regular amount can build a useful habit over time.

Yes, people sometimes buy things they do not need because of advertising, discounts or the excitement of something new. Online shopping makes it especially easy to add an item without thinking much about it. People may also buy for social reasons, such as keeping up with a trend. A budget and a short pause before checkout can help separate a real need from a passing want.

People with significant wealth have more ability to support others, so donating can make a real difference. I would not say charity is their only responsibility; paying taxes fairly and treating employees well also matter. Donations are most useful when they support effective services and respect the needs of recipients. Society should not rely only on individual generosity to address problems that need public solutions.

People are willing to pay more for things they trust or use every day, such as a reliable phone, comfortable shoes or a good meal on a special occasion. Some also pay for experiences that feel memorable. A high price is not automatically good value, though. Buyers usually compare quality, durability and how much they will use the item before deciding it is worth the cost.

title: 近期看过且享受的电影
prompt: Describe a movie you watched and enjoyed recently
cues: When and where you watched it
And explain why you watched this movie
questions: What kinds of movies do you think are successful in your country?
What are the factors that make a successful movie?
Do Chinese people prefer to watch domestic movies or foreign movies?
Do you think only well-known directors can create the best movies?
Do you think successful movies should have well-known actors or actresses in leading roles?
Why do people prefer to watch movies in the cinema?

answers.part2: I watched The Wandering Earth 2 with two classmates after we handed in a project. We chose an evening showing at a cinema near campus and bought tickets in advance because it was a popular release. The film was long, so we shared a snack and took a short break before discussing it on the way home. One classmate had read about the production, while the other mainly wanted to see the special effects. Hearing their different reactions made me notice details I might not have thought about on my own. We chose it because we all enjoy science fiction and wanted an evening away from coursework. The story follows people trying to protect Earth, but the characters also have to make difficult choices about family and responsibility. The space elevator scenes were impressive, though what stayed with me was a conversation where one character questioned whether a sacrifice was fair. My friend focused on the technology, while I kept thinking about the decision itself. What I liked most was that the film made us disagree about a character's choice without making one answer obvious. We kept discussing it as we walked back, and I left thinking about the story rather than only the effects. Since we had just finished a project, watching it together felt like a proper evening off.
part3: In China, films often do well when they combine an engaging story with themes audiences recognise, such as family, friendship or national history. Comedy and action are also popular because they offer a shared, entertaining experience. Marketing and release timing can help, but people still recommend a film when they enjoy it. Success can mean ticket sales, lasting discussion or both.

A successful movie needs a story that holds attention, convincing performances and pacing that suits its audience. Visual effects may attract people, but they cannot replace characters viewers care about. Distribution and promotion also matter because audiences need to hear about the film. A smaller film can succeed through strong word of mouth, while a large production may earn money without being remembered for long.

Chinese audiences watch both domestic and foreign films, and their preference depends on genre, story and what is available in cinemas. Domestic films may feel culturally familiar and reflect local experiences, while foreign films can offer different settings and styles. A strong film can succeed regardless of where it was made. Friends' recommendations and online discussion also influence what people choose to watch.

No. Established directors have experience, funding and a reputation that may help a film reach audiences, but a new director can still make an original and moving film. Strong writing, performances and editing matter more than fame alone. Some independent films succeed because they offer a fresh perspective. I would judge a movie by what it achieves, not just who directed it.

Well-known actors can attract an audience and help a film secure funding, but they do not guarantee a strong story or performance. New actors may fit a role better and bring a fresh energy. A successful film needs a combination of writing, direction and acting that works together. I am more likely to remember a convincing character than recognise every person in the cast.

People choose the cinema for its large screen, strong sound and the feeling of watching with an audience. It can make an action or science-fiction film more absorbing than a phone or laptop. Going out also turns the film into a social event. The disadvantages are ticket prices and fixed showtimes, so many people save cinema visits for films that feel worth seeing on a big screen.

title: 遇到困难终成功的人
prompt: Describe a person who met difficulties but succeeded
cues: And explain how you feel about him
questions: In your country, what industry is it easier to be successful in?

answers.part2: A friend from my mathematics department wanted to join a university research project, but his first application was unsuccessful. I knew he cared about the opportunity because he had spent several evenings preparing his proposal after classes. The rejection was disappointing, particularly because he had expected his mathematical results to speak for themselves. He later realised that the panel also needed to understand why the work mattered and how he would contribute to the team. I saw him practise explaining the project to classmates, which made his improvement clear before he applied again. He had strong ideas, yet his proposal did not explain them clearly to people outside his course. He asked a lecturer for feedback, revised the introduction and volunteered on a smaller project so he could learn how the team handled data. The following semester he applied again and was accepted. I admired that he treated the rejection as information about what to improve rather than proof that he was not capable. His progress took several months and involved unglamorous work, such as rewriting sections and checking references. I felt proud when he told me the result, because I had seen the effort behind it. His experience showed me that persistence is most useful when it includes a willingness to change one's approach.
part3: There is no single industry where success is easy, but technology, online retail, healthcare and education offer opportunities in China because demand is changing quickly. Each field also has strong competition and requires different skills. A person is more likely to do well when they understand a real need and keep learning, rather than choosing an industry only because it is currently popular.

title: 鼓励别人做不愿做的事
prompt: Describe a time when you encouraged someone to do something that he/she didn't want to do
cues: What you encouraged him/her to do
And explain why you encouraged him/her to do it
questions: How can leaders encourage their employees?
When should parents encourage their children?
What kind of encouragement should parents give?
Do you think some people are better than others at persuading?
Should children do everything their parents ask them to do?
How can employers encourage their staff?

answers.part2: I once encouraged a friend to try a beginner badminton session, even though she worried that she would be the least skilled person there. We were talking after class when she said she wanted to learn but worried that she would slow everyone down. I showed her the club's sign-up message, which welcomed beginners, and offered to go with her to one session. She hesitated, then agreed to try it for half an hour. Before we went in, I introduced her to the organiser, who showed her where to leave her bag and explained how the beginner session worked. At first she watched a few rallies and asked how to hold the racket; after we practised serving together, she started joining short games. Nobody minded when the shuttle went off course, and she stopped apologising whenever she missed a shot. By the end, she was smiling and asked whether the group would meet again the following week. I felt genuinely pleased because she had tried something that interested her, but I did not treat one session as a commitment. I encouraged her because I could make the first visit less intimidating while leaving the decision to continue in her hands.
part3: A leader can encourage employees by explaining why a task matters, recognising specific contributions and giving people some say in how they complete it. Regular feedback is more useful than praise only at the end of a project. Leaders should also notice whether someone needs clearer guidance or more responsibility. People are more motivated when expectations are fair and their work is taken seriously.

Parents should encourage children when they are trying something difficult, recovering from a setback or building a new habit. Specific encouragement, such as noticing that a child kept practising, is more useful than saying they are perfect. Children also need honest feedback, so praise should not hide a problem they can work on. Support helps most when it respects the child's effort and interests.

Parents should give encouragement that recognises effort, persistence and kindness rather than only high marks or winning. They can say what the child did well and suggest one next step, which makes praise feel believable. Constantly comparing a child with a sibling may create pressure. Encouragement should help children feel capable while making it clear that mistakes are a normal part of learning.

Yes. Persuasive people often explain an idea clearly, understand what their audience cares about and support claims with evidence. Confidence can help, but pressuring or misleading someone is not good persuasion. A skilled speaker should be willing to hear objections and change their view if the facts do not support the original argument. Good persuasion leaves room for the listener to decide.

No, not automatically. Parents need to set firm rules about safety and basic responsibilities, but children should be able to ask questions and express a different view on less serious choices. For example, a parent can require a child to wear a helmet while letting them choose which sport to try. That balance teaches respect as well as independent judgement.

Employers can support staff through fair pay, predictable schedules, training and a safe way to raise concerns. These are broader workplace conditions, not just a manager's day-to-day encouragement. Benefits should reflect what employees actually need; for some, flexible hours matter more than a one-off reward. When a company follows through on its promises, staff are more likely to trust its efforts to motivate them.

title: Dream and ambition
questions: What was your childhood dream?
Are you the kind of person who sticks to dreams?
What is your dream job?
Do you think you are an ambitious person?

part1: When I was young, I thought being a scientist would be exciting because I liked asking how things worked. I did not know what the job involved, but the idea of investigating a question appealed to me. My interests have become more specific as I have studied mathematics.

I try to stay committed, but I am willing to adjust the route when I learn more. I am exploring analytical careers while finishing my degree, and I see that as refining a goal rather than giving up on it.

I would like to work as a data analyst, using mathematics to answer practical questions. I would enjoy checking whether a pattern is reliable and explaining the result clearly to other people. The role would combine problem-solving with communication, which suits me.

I would say I am moderately ambitious. I want to use my mathematics degree in a role where I can keep learning and take on more responsibility over time. At the same time, I do not want work goals to take over my health or relationships.

title: Evening time

What do you hate doing in the evening?

part1: I prefer the evening because I can slow down after classes and decide how to spend my time. I try to finish demanding coursework earlier, though, since I become less focused if I work late at night.
I usually have dinner, finish any urgent coursework and then read or watch a short programme. Before bed, I pack what I need for the next day so I am not looking for notes in the morning.

When I was little, I often played badminton or hide-and-seek with children in our neighbourhood after dinner. We came home when it got dark or our parents called us. I remember those evenings as simple and carefree.

I liked playing outside because it gave me a chance to move around and make up games with other children. We could decide what to do ourselves, which made the evening feel relaxed after a day at school.

When I was younger, I usually played outside after dinner, but now I spend more evenings finishing coursework or catching up with friends. I have more freedom to choose what to do, although deadlines make weekdays less relaxed than they used to be.

No. On weekdays I usually finish coursework, have dinner and relax for a short time before bed. At weekends I have more freedom to meet friends, watch a film or stay up later, so the evening feels less structured.

I hate having to deal with a long list of small chores just as I am ready to relax. I prefer to finish laundry and prepare my bag earlier, so the evening does not disappear into tasks I could have done sooner.

title: Films/cinemas
