part1: I like character-driven mysteries because I enjoy following clues and working out what someone has overlooked. A believable plot matters more to me than impressive effects. I often keep thinking about a film if its ending changes how I understand an earlier scene.

Yes, I watched animated films with my family, usually at home on weekends. I did not understand every story when I was young, but I enjoyed the characters and music. A few of those films still remind me of relaxing evenings at home.
I watched films with my family as a child, usually at home rather than at a cinema. Going with friends is a good way to spend time together, since you can talk about the film afterwards.

Not very often, perhaps every couple of months. We usually choose a film that several of us want to see, then get something to eat and compare our favourite scenes afterwards. It is an easy way to spend an evening together.

Yes, if everyone wants to see the same film. It gives friends a shared activity, and they can talk about it afterwards over a meal. For a proper catch-up, though, a cafe is better because people can talk throughout.
I watch films at home most weeks, but I go to the cinema for a film I really want to see. Home is more convenient, but a cinema makes a new release feel like a shared event.

Usually at home, because it is more convenient and I can pause the film. I choose the cinema for a new release or something with strong visuals, where the large screen and sound make a noticeable difference.

title: History
questions: Have you ever been to historical museums?
Do you like history?
When was the last time you read about history?
Did you like history when you were young?

part1: Yes, I visited a local history museum on a school trip. It displayed old maps, household objects and photographs of streets I recognised. Seeing the objects helped me picture daily life in the past more easily than reading a list of dates.

Yes, when it is connected to real people and places I can still visit. Personal stories make the past easier to follow, and comparing an old street with a modern one helps me picture how daily life changed.

Last month I read an online article about how my city's railway station had changed over time. I was looking for information before meeting a friend nearby, and the old photographs made me curious about what the area used to look like.

A visit to an old street made a history lesson feel more real than a list of dates. Personal stories make the past easier to follow and remember. I remember it better when I can connect it with a real place.

title: Morning routines
questions: What do you do right after getting up in the morning?
Is breakfast important?
What is your morning routine?
Do you like to get up early in the morning?

part1: The first thing I do is open the curtains and wash my face. I usually make a cup of tea next, then check the time of my first class. I try not to start scrolling on my phone before I am properly awake.

Yes, it is important for me because I have morning lectures and find it harder to concentrate when I am hungry. I usually have something simple, such as fruit, eggs or bread, rather than a large meal.

On a class day I get up around seven, wash, eat something simple and pack my laptop and notes. I leave a little extra time for the bus, since arriving flustered makes it harder to focus in my first lecture.

I like early mornings when I have slept well because the streets and campus are quieter. I am not naturally an early riser, though, so on free days I let myself sleep longer instead of setting an unnecessary alarm.

title: Old buildings
questions: Have you ever seen old buildings in the city？?

part1: Yes, there are a few historic buildings near the centre, including an old gate and several traditional houses. I first noticed them during a school visit, when our teacher explained how the neighbourhood had developed around them.

Yes, when a building has historical or architectural value. It can show how a neighbourhood developed and give a city a recognisable character. Preservation should include repairs and a useful new purpose, rather than leaving the building empty until it deteriorates.

I would choose a modern apartment for everyday life because it is usually easier to maintain and has better heating and wiring. For a visit, though, I prefer an old building with original details. My choice depends on whether I am living there or exploring it.

I would like to visit a traditional courtyard house that is open to the public. I am interested in how the rooms are arranged around a shared space and how that design reflects family life in the past.

I would like to see a traditional courtyard house because its layout shows how families used to share space. It would be interesting to compare that design with the apartments people live in now. That contrast would make the visit memorable.

title: Sports programs

part1: I enjoy watching close games, especially when the players have to change tactics as the match develops. I prefer watching with a small group because it is more fun to react and discuss the game together.

Yes, if there is a match nearby and the tickets are affordable. The crowd makes the game feel more immediate than watching on television, and I can see how players communicate. I do not go often, but I enjoy the atmosphere.

I usually watch with friends or classmates who follow the same sport. We can talk about the players and react to the match, which makes a long game more engaging than watching by myself. It feels more social.

I will probably keep watching basketball and badminton, especially when a close match is available online. I would also like to see more university games in person after graduation if I have time. I enjoy the tactics as much as the final score.
I prefer watching with a small group of friends. We can react to the same moments and discuss the tactics, but a very large group can be distracting if I am trying to follow a close match.

Yes, I watched a university basketball match in a small stadium with classmates. It was much louder than watching on television, and being surrounded by other supporters made the close final minutes feel especially exciting.

title: 交通拥堵
prompt: Describe a time when you were stuck in a traffic jam for a very long time
cues: And explain how you felt in the traffic jam
questions: How can we solve the traffic jam problem?
Do you think developing public transport can solve traffic jam problems?
Do you think the high ways will help reduce traffic jams?
What are good ways to manage traffic?
Do you like to use public transport?
Would you rather be in a car or a bus in a traffic jam?

answers.part2: The longest traffic jam I remember was on the way to a family dinner across town on a rainy Friday evening. I was in the car with my parents, and several roads had slowed down after a collision near a junction. We checked a map app, tried a side road and then stopped again behind a line of buses. The journey normally took around forty minutes, but that evening it stretched close to two hours. My father kept the car moving slowly while my mother checked the road updates, and I sent the restaurant a message so they would not think we had forgotten the booking. I leaned back and listened to a radio programme while my parents followed the traffic updates. At first I was impatient because we had left early, but after a while I accepted there was nothing useful to do except wait. Sitting still for nearly two hours left me stiff and tired, even though listening to the programme helped pass the time. We eventually arrived about an hour late, and the restaurant had kept our table. I felt tired and frustrated, though the evening itself was still pleasant. Since then, I check traffic before leaving and allow more time for a cross-city trip at rush hour.
part3: Cities can reduce traffic jams by making buses and trains frequent, connecting them well and providing safe routes for walking and cycling. Staggered work hours can also spread the morning rush. Wider roads may help at one junction, but they can encourage more people to drive later. Good traffic management combines public transport, sensible parking rules and planning that puts daily services closer to where people live.

Better public transport can reduce traffic jams by giving commuters a reliable alternative to driving, especially during rush hour. It works best when buses and trains are frequent, affordable and connect easily with walking or cycling routes. It cannot solve every traffic problem because deliveries and some jobs require vehicles. Still, shifting everyday passenger trips away from private cars can make roads move more smoothly.

A new highway can reduce congestion on a particular route by giving drivers another way through, but it may also encourage more people to use cars over time. That can move the traffic problem elsewhere. Highways help most when they connect to a wider transport plan and avoid busy residential areas. Better public transport and sensible land use are usually needed as well.

Traffic can be managed more effectively with reliable public transport, clear junction design and information that helps drivers avoid delays. Cities can adjust signals at busy times, enforce parking rules and encourage employers to stagger work hours. These steps manage existing demand, while better buses and safe cycling routes give people alternatives. Adding road space alone may not help for long if more people then choose to drive.

Yes, I like public transport when it is frequent and easy to navigate. I can read or listen to something during the trip instead of watching traffic, and it is usually cheaper than driving. Crowded buses at rush hour can be uncomfortable, so service quality matters. For most city journeys, a reliable bus or metro is a practical choice for both passengers and the environment.

I would rather be on a bus if it had a dedicated lane, because I could read or rest instead of concentrating on the traffic. If the bus were stuck in the same queue, I would prefer a car for privacy and temperature control. The best option depends on the route and whether public transport can avoid the congestion.

title: 在成功公司工作的人
prompt: Describe a person who works in a successful company
cues: What he/she does in the company
And explain why you think it is a successful company
questions: Do you think governments should provide financial support to companies?
Do you think companies should donate money to help society?
Do you think customer satisfaction is important for a company?

answers.part2: My cousin works as a data analyst for an online retail company. The company sells household goods and clothing through its website, so it handles a large number of orders every day. My cousin checks which products are often returned and whether deliveries are arriving on time. She says the managers use that information to adjust stock and improve the site. I have seen her explain a chart to colleagues who do not work with data, which shows why communication matters as much as technical skill in her role. One report showed that a popular item was often returned after its packaging changed, so she presented the pattern to the product team. She checks messy records before drawing conclusions, because a neat chart can still tell the wrong story. She says the company grew by making ordering convenient, but reliable delivery and clear customer support are what keep people coming back. Success also depends on teams sharing information: stock managers, delivery staff and analysts all affect the customer's experience. I find her job interesting because it uses numerical skills to answer practical questions. I think the company is successful because it listens to customers and adjusts its service, rather than relying only on early growth. Her example has shown me that good analysis matters when someone acts on it.
part3: Governments can support companies when the help protects jobs, encourages useful research or helps an industry change to cleaner practices. The support should have clear conditions and a time limit, otherwise public money may simply protect an unsuccessful business. Small firms may need access to loans or training more than a direct grant. Any programme should publish who receives funding and what results it achieves.

Companies can support society by donating to local services, education or environmental projects, especially when the cause connects with the community they operate in. Donations should be transparent and not used to distract from poor working conditions or harmful products. A company also helps society by paying staff fairly and reducing waste. Financial support is valuable, but responsible daily behaviour matters just as much.

Yes. Satisfied customers are more likely to return and recommend a business, which is important for long-term success. A company can learn from complaints and improve a product before a small problem becomes widespread. However, pleasing every customer is impossible, so firms need to balance feedback with safety, costs and fair treatment of staff. Trust grows when a company responds honestly and fixes mistakes.

title: 想有空时去旅游的地方
prompt: Describe a place you would like to visit in your free time
cues: How long you will stay there
And explain why you would like to visit it
questions: Why do you think some people choose not to travel abroad?
Do you think a gap period in life is important?

answers.part2: I would like to spend a free weekend in Hangzhou, especially around West Lake, and would probably go in spring with a friend. I have visited once, but our schedule was tight and we moved quickly between the main sights. On the first day, I would walk beside the water, stop for tea and visit one of the older streets nearby. I would take a light jacket and comfortable shoes, since we would be outside for much of the day and could decide the route as we went. We could pause whenever the lakeside path became busy, then choose a quieter lane for dinner instead of rushing to another landmark. On the second day, I would take local transport to a quieter neighbourhood, have lunch at a small restaurant and leave time for an unplanned walk through a market or beside a canal. I would stay two nights, which would give us time to rest and explore without turning the trip into a checklist. I want to return because I enjoyed the lake but saw little of the city beyond its best-known attractions. A slower visit would let me notice how residents use the area in their ordinary routines, as well as enjoy the scenery.
part3: Some people avoid travelling abroad because it can be expensive, time-consuming or difficult to plan around work and family. Others may feel uncomfortable with language differences or prefer exploring their own country first. Not travelling does not necessarily mean they dislike other cultures; it may simply be a practical choice. International travel is enjoyable, but it is not essential for everyone.

A gap period can be valuable, but it is not essential for everyone. Time away from study or work may let someone rest, travel or gain experience before making a longer-term choice. On the other hand, it costs money and can be difficult to organise without a clear purpose. I think it works best when the person has a realistic plan and something they hope to learn from it.

title: 收到特殊蛋糕
prompt: Describe a special cake you received from others

questions: What are the differences between special food in China and other countries?
Is there any food in your country that is eaten at special times or on special occasions?
Why are some people willing to spend a lot of money on meals on special days?
Do you think it’s good to communicate when eating with your family?
In your country, do people nowadays cook at home as frequently as people did in the past?
What do you think of people using their mobile phones during a meal?

answers.part2: A special cake I received was a homemade chocolate cake from a friend after I finished a demanding semester. She brought it to our shared study room one afternoon while I was sorting revision notes. She had made it the night before and wrote a short message in icing, choosing chocolate because I had mentioned liking it earlier in the term. Two classmates joined us, so we cut it into small pieces and took a proper break from studying. My friend stayed for a while and asked how the exam preparation was going; we talked about plans for the holiday rather than reviewing notes. She had chosen a small cake because there were only a few of us in the room, and wrapped it carefully so it would survive the walk across campus. The cake was a little uneven, but that made it feel personal rather than shop-bought. I had been worried about an exam that week, and her visit changed the mood in the room. I felt noticed because she remembered a small detail and chose to celebrate the end of the semester with me. It was special for the thought behind it, not its size or decoration, and I still associate that flavour with finishing a difficult period.
part3: Special foods differ across countries because they reflect local ingredients, climate and history. In China, dumplings or mooncakes are linked with particular festivals, while other countries may serve roast dishes, pastries or seasonal sweets. The foods are not directly comparable, but they often have a similar role: families prepare or share them to mark an important occasion. I find the stories behind a dish as interesting as its taste.

Dumplings are often eaten during the Spring Festival in many parts of China, although customs vary between families and regions. Preparing them can be a shared activity, and the meal gives relatives time to catch up. Other celebrations have their own dishes, such as birthday noodles. The food matters partly because of its taste, but also because people associate it with a particular gathering.

People may spend more on a special meal because it marks a wedding, birthday or family reunion and gives everyone a chance to celebrate together. Choosing a good restaurant can make the occasion feel different from an ordinary day. Some also see an expensive meal as a way to show care, though that is not necessary. Shared time matters more than the price of the menu.

Yes, mealtimes can be an easy chance for family members to catch up without arranging a separate meeting. Even a short conversation about the day helps people stay connected. It should not become compulsory, though; someone may need quiet after work or study. I think putting phones aside for part of the meal can help, as long as the conversation remains relaxed.

People in China may cook at home less often than previous generations because many work long hours and can order food quickly. At the same time, some young adults are learning to cook for health or budget reasons, and families still prepare meals together on weekends. The pattern varies by age and city. Convenience has changed routines, but home cooking remains important for many households.

A quick check for an urgent message is understandable, but scrolling through a meal can make companions feel ignored. Meals are one of the few times families or friends can talk without a formal plan, so attention matters. I think people should agree on a simple expectation, such as putting phones away unless someone is waiting for important news. It is about courtesy, not banning devices completely.

title: 组织快乐活动
prompt: Describe a time when you organized a happy event successfully
cues: Who helped you to organize it
And explain why you think it was a successful event
questions: How can parents help children to be organized?
On what occasions do people need to be organized?
Does everything need to be well prepared?
Do people need others’ help when organizing things?
How would you feel when you were not well prepared for something?
Do you prefer to prepare and organize an activity or just take part in an activity?

answers.part2: I helped organise a welcome event for new students in my department at the start of a semester. A few classmates and I booked a classroom, prepared a short quiz and invited senior students to answer questions about courses and campus life. We started planning about two weeks beforehand and asked the department office which room would be available. We sent a reminder to the new students the day before. We put a simple sign by the entrance so visitors could find the room. One classmate designed the quiz, another contacted the senior students, and I checked the equipment and arranged refreshments. On the day, the projector failed briefly, but we had printed the questions and could continue while someone restarted it. The small backup plan kept the event moving and helped me see why checking practical details matters. We mixed students from different years into small teams so newcomers could ask questions while they completed the quiz. One senior stayed afterwards to talk about choosing electives, and several first-years exchanged contact details. The event worked because everyone had a clear role and our printed sheets kept the activity moving despite the projector problem. I felt pleased when the new students stayed to talk instead of leaving as soon as it ended.
part3: Parents can help by keeping a predictable routine and showing children how to prepare for the next day. A child could pack a school bag before bed and use a simple checklist for homework. Adults should give reminders at first, then let the child take more responsibility. The aim is to build a habit, not to control every detail of a child's schedule.

People need to be organised when several tasks depend on one another, such as preparing for an exam, travelling or running an event. A wedding or university presentation can involve deadlines, bookings and other people's schedules, so missing one detail affects everyone. Everyday routines need less planning. I would put more effort into preparation when mistakes would be costly or difficult to fix.

No. Important events, work deadlines and travel usually benefit from preparation, but a casual afternoon or conversation does not need a detailed plan. Overplanning can make people anxious and leave little room to respond to something unexpected. I try to prepare enough to avoid obvious problems, then leave some flexibility for ordinary situations that can unfold naturally.

It depends on the size and complexity of the task. One person can organise a weekly schedule alone, but a family event or group project needs input from the people involved. Sharing jobs prevents one person from carrying everything and helps catch details they may miss. The organiser still needs to coordinate decisions and make sure everyone knows what they agreed to do.

I would feel anxious at first, especially if other people were depending on me. I would try to work out what was essential and deal with that before worrying about the parts I could no longer change. Afterwards, I would note what I had overlooked. Being unprepared is uncomfortable, but reviewing it can help me plan more realistically next time.

I usually prefer helping to organise a small activity because I like making sure people know where to go and what to bring. For a larger event, I am happy just to take part because planning can become a lot of work. It depends on my time and interest. I enjoy organising most when tasks are shared and everyone can contribute.

title: 花费甚少的外出日
prompt: Describe a special day out that cost you little money/didn’t cost you much
cues: And explain how you feel about the day
questions: Do people like to spend their leisure time out in your country?
How do people spend their leisure time in your country?
How does technology affect the way people spend their leisure time?
Do you think only old people have time for leisure?
Why do people like to have days off?

answers.part2: A low-cost day out I remember was an afternoon walk through a public park with a university friend last October, just after our midterm exams. We spent less than thirty yuan between us, mainly on bus fare and a small snack; we had packed water and fruit at home. The park was close enough to reach by bus, so transport cost very little as well. We had not planned an activity beyond walking, which meant we could change direction when we saw a path beside the water. I liked that the day felt full without needing a ticket or a reservation. We spent part of the afternoon watching a group practise badminton, then rested on a bench and talked about how our exams had gone. Neither of us needed a paid activity to make the day feel different from a normal afternoon. Afterwards, we took the bus home and compared which path we would try next time. I went home feeling relaxed, even though we had not travelled far or done anything unusual. The day was special because we had time to catch up without checking the clock or deciding what to buy next. It reminded me that a change of scenery does not need to be expensive to feel worthwhile.
part3: Many people in China enjoy spending free time outside the home, especially by eating with friends, visiting a shopping centre or walking in a park. These activities are easy to arrange and suit different budgets. Still, some people prefer staying home after a demanding week. The choice depends on work hours, weather and whether someone wants company or quiet time.

People in China spend free time meeting friends, eating out, watching films, exercising, travelling nearby or relaxing with online entertainment. The choice depends on age, location and how much time someone has. Students may meet at a cafe after class, while families often choose a meal or a park at weekends. More people also use short periods of free time for hobbies at home.

Technology gives people more ways to relax, from streaming films and playing games to joining an online class. It can also make hobbies easier to share with friends. The downside is that passive scrolling can take up more time than intended and crowd out sleep or exercise. I think it works best when people choose an activity deliberately instead of opening an app whenever they have a free moment.

No. People of every age need leisure, but they may have different amounts of free time at different stages of life. Students and working adults often fit it around classes or jobs, while some retired people have more control over their schedule. Caring responsibilities and health matter too, so age alone does not determine who has time to relax.

Days off give people time to recover from work or study, spend time with family and do things that do not fit into a busy weekday. Rest can improve concentration when people return to their responsibilities. Some use a day off for travel or appointments, while others prefer staying home. A break is valuable even when it is ordinary, because people need time that is not controlled by deadlines.

title: 语言学习
prompt: Describe a thing you did to learn another language
cues: How it helped you learn the language
And how you felt about it
questions: What difficulties do people face when learning a language?
Do you think language learning is important?
Why?
Which is better, to study a language alone or to study it in a group?
What's the best way to learn a language?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of learning a language?
Some people think that technology has made it unnecessary to learn languages. What do you think?

answers.part2: One thing I did to improve my English was listen to a short podcast each morning and write down a few phrases I could reuse. I chose episodes that lasted about ten minutes and replayed one section if I missed how a phrase was pronounced. I kept the notes in a small file on my phone, with one example sentence beside each expression. After a few days, I tried using one phrase in a conversation rather than merely recognising it when I heard it. That helped me remember the wording and made the practice feel connected to speaking. I chose everyday topics, such as study and travel, so the language felt relevant to conversations I might have. At first I paused whenever I heard an unfamiliar word, but later I tried to follow the main idea and checked only the expressions that seemed useful. I repeated a few sentences aloud to notice the rhythm and reviewed my notes on the bus. The routine took around fifteen minutes, which made it possible to continue during a busy semester. After several weeks, I found it easier to respond in class without translating every sentence in my head. I liked seeing that small improvement. Listening regularly gave me more confidence than memorising a long vocabulary list in one sitting.
part3: Learners often find it difficult to remember vocabulary, understand unfamiliar grammar and speak quickly enough to join a conversation. Pronunciation can also feel uncomfortable, especially when they worry about making mistakes. Regular practice helps, but progress is gradual. A teacher or language partner can correct errors and give learners a reason to speak. Short daily practice is usually more manageable than trying to master everything in a few weeks.

Language learning is important because it lets people communicate more directly and understand another culture beyond translated words. It can help with work or travel, but it is also satisfying to read or watch something in its original language. Not everyone needs to become fluent in several languages. Even a basic level can make everyday interactions easier and show respect for the people someone meets.

It allows people to communicate more directly and understand ideas that may be lost in translation, including humour and cultural references. It can also make travel and work easier. Not everyone needs to become fluent in several languages, but learning even the basics can make daily interactions more respectful and help someone feel less dependent on translation tools.

Studying alone gives learners control over their pace and lets them repeat difficult material. A group provides conversation practice, feedback and encouragement, which are important for speaking. I would combine both: review vocabulary independently, then use it in a class or with a language partner. The best balance depends on the learner's goals and confidence.

The best approach combines regular exposure with active use. Learners can listen to short podcasts or videos, note useful phrases and then use them in conversation or writing. A class provides structure and feedback, while independent practice lets people focus on their own interests. It is better to practise a little most days than to memorise long lists once a week. The method should fit the learner's schedule and goals.

Learning another language can help people travel, study or work with less dependence on translation tools. It also gives them a closer understanding of humour and cultural references. The main drawbacks are the time and effort required, and learners may feel embarrassed when they cannot express a complex idea. Those difficulties become manageable with practice. Even basic ability can be useful, so fluency is not the only worthwhile outcome.

Translation tools are useful for signs, basic messages and unfamiliar words, but they cannot always capture tone, humour or cultural meaning. Learning a language also lets people build relationships without depending on a device. I would use technology to support practice, for example by listening to a podcast, but I do not think it makes language learning unnecessary. It changes how we learn, not why communication matters.

title: 重要河流/湖泊
prompt: Describe an important river/lake in your country
cues: And explain why it is important
questions: Are rivers and lakes important to a country?
What are the popular water sports in your country?
Are rivers and lakes good for transport?
Why?
How do rivers and lakes affect local tourism?
Do you think rivers and lakes attract tourists?
How can rivers and lakes benefit local people?

answers.part2: The Yangtze is one of the most important rivers in China. It is about 6,300 kilometres long, flowing from the Tibetan Plateau across central China before reaching the East China Sea. I saw it near Wuhan on a family trip when I was younger. There, it looked broad and busy, with cargo boats moving beside smaller vessels and low green banks visible in the distance. From the bridge, the opposite bank looked hazy, and the water seemed to stretch much farther than I could judge from the road. The steady movement of boats made it clear that the river is part of the city's working life, not just a landscape in the background. People were also walking along the riverfront, taking photographs and watching the vessels pass, so it served as a public space as well as a transport route. It also provides water for farming and communities along its route, while its influence appears in Chinese history and literature. At the same time, flooding and pollution can affect people who live nearby, so protecting the river matters for future generations. I would like to see another section one day, since the landscape around it must change considerably along its long course.
part3: Yes, they provide water, support farming and wildlife, and can be used for transport or recreation. Some rivers have also shaped settlement and trade over many generations. Their importance varies by region, but pollution or drought can affect a large number of people. Protecting water quality is therefore a practical concern for public health and the economy, as well as for nature.

Swimming is the most accessible water activity, while boating, kayaking and paddleboarding are popular in places with lakes or a safe coastline. Competitive sports such as rowing also have a following, especially at universities. Access depends on facilities and safety, so not every region offers the same choices. People are more likely to try a sport when lessons and equipment are affordable.

They can be useful when waterways connect towns or carry heavy goods, since boats can move large loads efficiently. However, rivers are not available everywhere, and journeys may be slower or affected by weather and water levels. Roads and railways are more flexible for many routes, so waterways work best as part of a wider transport network.

For example, the Yangtze has historically carried passengers and heavy goods between inland cities and coastal ports. Boats can move bulky loads without adding to road congestion, but that only works where there are maintained docks and reliable water levels. Smaller rivers may serve local routes, or become less useful during dry seasons. So their value depends on both geography and infrastructure.

Rivers and lakes attract visitors for walks, boat trips, fishing and views, so nearby cafes and guesthouses may benefit. A clean waterfront can also become a public space that residents use every day. However, heavy tourism can create litter, noise and pressure on wildlife. Local authorities need to manage access and waste carefully; otherwise the attraction may be damaged by the very visitors it brings.

Yes, clean rivers and lakes attract people who want to enjoy scenery, go boating or spend time outdoors. They can also support local restaurants and guesthouses. The attraction depends on access and water quality; polluted banks or overcrowded paths can put visitors off. Local authorities need to manage litter and protect habitats so tourism does not damage the natural feature people came to see.

Rivers and lakes provide water for households and farming, support wildlife and can give communities places to exercise or relax. Some are also important for transport, fishing or tourism, depending on the region. The benefits depend on water quality, so pollution can quickly affect people's health and local livelihoods. Protecting the river is practical as well as environmental; residents, businesses and authorities all need to keep waste out of it.
